title: Syllabus
section: Course Objectives
text:
Course Objectives
This course introduces the mathematical principles underlying diffusion-based generative models used in modern AI. Students will learn how noise is progressively added to data and how neural networks are trained to reverse this process to generate realistic samples. The course builds on probability, Gaussian distributions, and optimization to explain diffusion processes, denoising objectives, and sampling algorithms. Emphasis is placed on intuitive derivations, geometric interpretation of probability distributions, and connections to familiar machine learning concepts such as maximum likelihood and variational inference. By the end of the course, students will understand diffusion models both conceptually and mathematically.

title: Syllabus
section: Course Outcomes
text:
Course Outcomes
At the end of this course, students will be able to:

Explain the forward and reverse diffusion processes.
Derive the Gaussian noise perturbation model used in diffusion models.
Understand and interpret the denoising training objective.
Connect diffusion models with likelihood-based learning.
Implement and analyze simplified diffusion sampling algorithms.
Compare diffusion models with GANs and VAEs.
Read and interpret recent diffusion model research papers.

Reference: title, authors, and a link to the paper.
Core idea: the result or algorithm to understand and implement.

section: Interpreting a small-scale implementation
text:
Interpreting a small-scale implementation
The aim is to reproduce and examine a paper’s central mechanism at a tractable scale. A successful toy experiment does not reproduce the paper’s full benchmark results. Each project will distinguish the original method from the reduced experiment and state what can reasonably be concluded.
The Papers section in the navigation contains separate reading tutorials, such as Binomial Diffusion. Their presence does not by itself make a paper an implementation-project choice.

title: 00 · Introduction and Motivation
text:
What this course is about
The first note of the course. It says what the subject is, what the rest of the material is for, and then earns the claim that organises everything with the smallest possible example. Interactive version: Sampling as a Map.
A generative model is a thing that produces samples. Show it a pile of handwritten digits and it should produce new handwritten digits — not ones from the pile, and not noise, but plausible new members of the same population.
The difficulty is that nobody hands you the population. You get a finite pile of examples, and from that pile you must build something that can generate more. Put formally: given samples \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) drawn from an unknown \(p_{\text{data}}\), construct a procedure that draws fresh samples from something close to \(p_{\text{data}}\).
Two observations shape everything that follows.
Sampling is not the same as knowing the density. You do not need a formula for \(p_{\text{data}}(x)\) in order to draw from it, and — as the course will show — for images you could not write one down anyway. What you need is a procedure.
Every such procedure turns simple randomness into structured output. Somewhere in the machine there is a coin flip, a uniform draw, or a burst of Gaussian noise, and everything downstream of it is arithmetic. That is the picture this note builds, and the rest of the course is about how to learn the arithmetic when the target is complicated.

title: 00 · Introduction and Motivation
text:
The route, in one paragraph
We start with probability itself — random variables, joints, conditionals, Bayes — because generation runs forward from a latent cause to an observation while inference runs backward, and Bayes is the bridge. Then distributions and maximum likelihood in one dimension, where fitting has closed forms. Then the multivariate Gaussian, the one family closed under everything linear, which is why every tractable calculation in this subject goes through it. Then the wall: in high dimension, estimating a density directly stops working, even with structure. That failure is what forces the modern approach — stop describing distributions and start comparing them, which is why distances and divergences become central. Diffusion models are then one particular, very effective answer.


How the material is organised
Lecture Notes are the numbered spine, in reading order, and follow the lectures. Tutorials sit alongside and go deeper on one thing. The Curriculum page lists the sequence and maps it to weeks.


Where to start
Read this note, then 01 · The World’s Smallest Diffusion Model, which builds a complete working diffusion model on a dataset of two points, with every step in closed form. Nothing in it is approximated and nothing is learned — which makes it the clearest possible statement of what we are trying to do in high dimensions, and of exactly which step stops being computable once the data is images rather than two numbers.

title: 00 · Introduction and Motivation
section: The simplest generative model there is
text:
The simplest generative model there is
The rest of this note presents one tiny generator twice — first as a hierarchy you sample conditionally (a Bayesian model), then as a deterministic map applied to uniform randomness — and then makes the claim that carries the rest of the course: every modern generative sampler, diffusion included, is the second picture, once all of its random inputs are exposed, with a learned ingredient in place of the formula.

title: 00 · Introduction and Motivation
section: View 1: conditional generation (a hierarchical model)
text:
View 1: conditional generation (a hierarchical model)
The simplest latent-variable model:
\[
\mathbb{P}(z = 1) = \pi, \quad \mathbb{P}(z = 2) = 1 - \pi, \qquad
x \mid z \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(\mu_z,\, \sigma^2).
\]
Ancestral sampling generates by following the arrows: draw the latent coin \(z\), then draw \(x\) from the selected component. The observed marginal is obtained by summing out the latent:
\[
p(x) \;=\; \sum_{z} p(z)\, p(x \mid z)
\;=\; \pi\, \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_1, \sigma^2) + (1-\pi)\, \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_2, \sigma^2)
\]
— exactly the two-component mixture from the playground. A mixture is not just a formula; it is a generative story: population \(\to\) subpopulation \(\to\) individual.
Inference is the same hierarchy, run backwards. Given an observed \(x\), Bayes’ rule gives the posterior over the hidden coin:
\[
\mathbb{P}(z = 1 \mid x)
= \frac{\pi\, \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_1, \sigma^2)}
       {\pi\, \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_1, \sigma^2) + (1-\pi)\, \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_2, \sigma^2)} .
\]
For \(\mu_{1,2} = \mp 1\) and \(\pi = \tfrac12\) this equals \(\operatorname{sigmoid}(-2x/\sigma^2)\); its companion \(\mathbb{P}(z = 2 \mid x) = \operatorname{sigmoid}(2x/\sigma^2)\) is exactly the posterior W01 computed for the \(+1\) component, and the posterior mean of \(\mu_z\) is the tanh denoiser: W01’s denoising step was latent-variable inference all along. Generation and inference are the two directions of one arrow.

title: 00 · Introduction and Motivation
section: View 2: the coin disappears into a map
text:
View 2: the coin disappears into a map
Theorem (inverse-CDF / probability integral transform). Let \(F\) be a CDF with generalized inverse \(F^{-1}(u) = \inf\{x : F(x) \ge u\}\), and let \(U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\). Then \(X = F^{-1}(U)\) has CDF \(F\).
Proof. \(\mathbb{P}(F^{-1}(U) \le x) = \mathbb{P}(U \le F(x)) = F(x)\), since \(F^{-1}(u) \le x \iff u \le F(x)\) by monotonicity. \(\square\)
For our mixture, \(F(x) = \pi\,\Phi\!\big(\tfrac{x-\mu_1}{\sigma}\big) +
(1-\pi)\,\Phi\!\big(\tfrac{x-\mu_2}{\sigma}\big)\) is continuous and strictly increasing, so \(F^{-1}\) is an honest function, and
\[
u \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1), \qquad x = F^{-1}(u)
\]
generates the mixture with no coin anywhere — the explicit coin has been marginalized out. One caution about where it went: under this map, the event \(u < \pi\) selects the lowest \(\pi\)-fraction of the mixture distribution, which is not the same as the ancestral label \(z = 1\) when the components overlap — both Gaussians have full support, so each contributes on both sides of any quantile. (In the well-separated limit \(\sigma \to 0\) the two events do coincide, and the packed map below is the construction in which \(u < \pi\) genuinely encodes the coin.) Randomness in, structure out, everything in between deterministic.

title: 00 · Introduction and Motivation
section: The two-point limit
text:
The two-point limit
Send \(\sigma \to 0\) with \(\mu_{1,2} = \mp 1\). The CDF collapses to a staircase: a jump of height \(\pi\) at \(-1\), a flat plateau at height \(\pi\) across the empty middle, a jump to \(1\) at \(+1\). The map becomes
\[
x = \begin{cases} -1, & u < \pi \\ +1, & u > \pi \end{cases}
\qquad\text{i.e.}\quad x = \operatorname{sign}(u - \pi),
\]
W01’s dataset, generated by thresholding a uniform (almost surely: the single point \(u = \pi\) has probability zero). The plateau is the geometric image of the empty region: no value of \(u\) lands there. The map is the inverse CDF for this discrete distribution. (In the demo, slide \(\sigma\) down and watch the staircase form.)

title: 00 · Introduction and Motivation
section: Maps are not unique
text:
Maps are not unique
\(F^{-1}\) is the monotone map pushing \(\text{Uniform}(0,1)\) to \(p\), but not the only map. The “packed” two-stage construction
\[
x = \begin{cases}
\mu_1 + \sigma\, \Phi^{-1}\!\big(u/\pi\big), & u < \pi,\\[2pt]
\mu_2 + \sigma\, \Phi^{-1}\!\big(\tfrac{u-\pi}{1-\pi}\big), & u \ge \pi,
\end{cases}
\]
also pushes uniform to the mixture (each branch rescales its segment of \([0,1]\) back to a full uniform — Exercise 3), and it is literally ancestral sampling written as one formula. Different map, same distribution: what is canonical is the distribution, not the transport. (In higher dimensions, choosing among the many maps is its own subject — optimal transport — which we will brush against later.)

title: 00 · Introduction and Motivation
section: The claim that organizes everything
text:
The claim that organizes everything

Once all of its random draws are exposed, a generative sampler is a deterministic map from base randomness to a sample.










Model
Random input(s)
Sampling mechanism
Typical fitting




This note

quantile \(F^{-1}(u)\) (numerical in the demo)
the CDF is known


GAN
\(z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\)

adversarial objective

\(z\), plus decoder noise \(\varepsilon\)

The outer skeleton is shared — simple randomness, a sampling mechanism, data — while the learned object, the structural constraints, and the sampler differ. For diffusion in particular, determinism is a sampler choice: the probability-flow ODE is a deterministic map from \(x_1\); the reverse SDE consumes fresh noise at every step and is a deterministic function only of \((x_1, \text{all step noises})\).
In one dimension with a known CDF, the map is a formula. For images, the population law is unknown and no tractable multivariate inverse-CDF construction exists — so deep generative models learn a transport, density, score, or other ingredient of a sampler rather than writing the map down. And you have already run one: W01’s probability-flow ODE numerically transported a moment-matched Gaussian to within \(\approx \sigma_{\min}\) of the two-point data (W01 lists the approximations involved); with the exact terminal law, score, and integration, it is an exact deterministic transport — an inverse-CDF-like map built not from the CDF but from the score, which is exactly the object a neural network can learn in high dimension. That construction, done properly, is Modules 4–6.

title: 00 · Introduction and Motivation
section: Exercises
text:
Exercises

Complete the inverse-CDF proof for a general (possibly non-strictly-increasing) \(F\) using the generalized inverse.
Derive \(\mathbb{P}(z = 1 \mid x)\) above, and show that for \(\mu_{1,2} = \mp 1\), \(\sigma = 1\), \(\pi = \tfrac12\) its companion \(\mathbb{P}(z = 2 \mid x)\) equals W01’s \(\operatorname{sigmoid}(2x)\) posterior (mind which component carries the \(+\) sign); compute the posterior mean of \(\mu_z\).
Verify the packed map: show that conditional on \(u < \pi\), the rescaled variable \(u/\pi\) is \(\text{Uniform}(0,1)\), and conclude that the branch produces \(\mathcal{N}(\mu_1, \sigma^2)\) with the correct probability.
Construct the inverse-CDF map for a three-component mixture and describe its staircase limit as \(\sigma \to 0\). How many plateaus, at what heights?
The map \(x = F^{-1}(u)\) is monotone increasing. Exhibit a decreasing map with the same pushforward, and a map that is neither monotone nor continuous. (Hint: \(1 - u\) is also uniform.)

title: 01 · The World’s Smallest Diffusion Model
text:
The dataset
The second note of the introduction, and the reason the course exists. It builds a complete diffusion model on a dataset of two points: forward noising, the optimal denoiser, the score, and reverse-time generation — every step exact, in closed form, with nothing learned and nothing approximated.
Read it as a statement of the goal. This is what we want to understand in high dimensions. Everything the course does later is an attempt to recover these same five objects when the data is images instead of two numbers, and the closed forms are gone. The final section names precisely which step breaks first.
Our data distribution puts equal mass on two points:
\[
p_{\text{data}}(x_0) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\,\delta(x_0 + 1) \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\,\delta(x_0 - 1),
\qquad x_0 \in \{-1, +1\}.
\]
Generative modeling asks: given samples from \(p_{\text{data}}\), produce more samples. For this dataset the answer is a coin flip — which is exactly why it is the right dataset: the machinery becomes transparent.

title: 01 · The World’s Smallest Diffusion Model
section: Forward process: noise melts the data
text:
Forward process: noise melts the data
Corrupt a clean sample with Gaussian noise of size \(\sigma\):
\[
x_\sigma \;=\; x_0 + \sigma z, \qquad z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1) \text{ independent of } x_0.
\]
Since \(x_0 = \pm 1\) with probability \(\tfrac12\) each, the density of the corrupted sample is a two-component Gaussian mixture:
\[
p_\sigma(x) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{N}(x;\, -1,\, \sigma^2)
\;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{N}(x;\, +1,\, \sigma^2).
\]
Two facts, both visible in the demo:

Small \(\sigma\): two sharp bumps at \(\pm 1\) — the data is intact.
Large \(\sigma\): the bumps merge. Indeed \(\mathbb{E}[x_\sigma] = 0\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(x_\sigma) = \mathbb{E}[x_0^2] + \sigma^2 = 1 + \sigma^2\), and for \(\sigma \gtrsim 3\) the mixture is indistinguishable in practice from \(\mathcal{N}(0,\, 1 + \sigma^2)\) — at \(\sigma = 3\) its excess kurtosis is only \(-0.02\). (It is never exactly Gaussian at finite \(\sigma\); the precise statement is \(x_\sigma / \sqrt{1+\sigma^2} \Rightarrow \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) as \(\sigma \to \infty\).)

This is the first design principle of diffusion models: destroying structure is easy, fully understood, and ends somewhere known (a Gaussian), no matter what the data was.

title: 01 · The World’s Smallest Diffusion Model
section: Denoising: Bayes’ rule gives the optimal denoiser in closed form
text:
Denoising: Bayes’ rule gives the optimal denoiser in closed form
Now invert: we observe a noisy \(x_\sigma = x\) and want the clean \(x_0\). The best guess under squared error is the posterior mean \(\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_\sigma = x]\) (we will prove this optimality claim in Module 1; for now, take it).
The posterior over the two candidates follows from Bayes’ rule:
\[
\mathbb{P}(x_0 = +1 \mid x)
= \frac{\tfrac12\,\mathcal{N}(x; +1, \sigma^2)}
       {\tfrac12\,\mathcal{N}(x; +1, \sigma^2) + \tfrac12\,\mathcal{N}(x; -1, \sigma^2)}
= \frac{1}{1 + \exp\!\big(-\tfrac{2x}{\sigma^2}\big)}
= \operatorname{sigmoid}\!\Big(\frac{2x}{\sigma^2}\Big),
\]
where the middle step divides through by \(\mathcal{N}(x; +1, \sigma^2)\) and uses \(\exp\!\big(-\tfrac{(x+1)^2}{2\sigma^2}\big) \big/ \exp\!\big(-\tfrac{(x-1)^2}{2\sigma^2}\big)
= \exp\!\big(-\tfrac{2x}{\sigma^2}\big)\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{\;\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_\sigma = x]
= (+1)\,\mathbb{P}(+1 \mid x) + (-1)\,\mathbb{P}(-1 \mid x)
= \tanh\!\Big(\frac{x}{\sigma^2}\Big).\;}
\]
The optimal denoiser is a tanh — an activation function you already know, produced by nothing but probability. Sanity-check its two regimes:

\(\sigma \to 0\): \(\tanh(x/\sigma^2)\) becomes a hard step — snap to the nearer data point.
\(\sigma \to \infty\): \(\tanh(x/\sigma^2) \approx x/\sigma^2 \to 0\) — the observation is all noise, so the best guess is the prior mean \(0\).

title: 01 · The World’s Smallest Diffusion Model
section: The score function (a preview of Module 4)
text:
The score function (a preview of Module 4)
Differentiate \(\log p_\sigma\) directly. With \(\varphi_\pm(x) = \mathcal{N}(x; \pm 1, \sigma^2)\) and \(\varphi_\pm'(x) = -\tfrac{x \mp 1}{\sigma^2}\varphi_\pm(x)\),
\[
\nabla_x \log p_\sigma(x)
= \frac{\tfrac12\varphi_-'(x) + \tfrac12\varphi_+'(x)}{p_\sigma(x)}
= -\frac{x - \mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x]}{\sigma^2}
= \frac{\tanh\!\big(\tfrac{x}{\sigma^2}\big) - x}{\sigma^2}.
\]
Rearranged, this is Tweedie’s formula, one of the two or three most important identities of the course:
\[
\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_\sigma = x] \;=\; x + \sigma^2\, \nabla_x \log p_\sigma(x).
\]
Denoising and knowing the score are the same thing — for additive Gaussian noise of known size \(\sigma\), which is exactly the diffusion setting. The score \(\nabla_x \log p_\sigma\) points from \(x\) toward where the (noised) data is denser; the denoiser just moves by \(\sigma^2\) times the score. One caveat: the score is a local quantity — at \(x = 0\) it vanishes by symmetry even though, in the two-bump regime, \(x = 0\) is a density minimum. It is an unstable equilibrium: the reverse dynamics leave a particle sitting exactly there alone, and push a particle on either side away toward the nearer mode.

title: 01 · The World’s Smallest Diffusion Model
section: Reverse process: run the diffusion backwards
text:
Reverse process: run the diffusion backwards
Generation now works by annealing: start from pure noise at a large \(\sigma_{\max}\), and lower \(\sigma\) along a grid \(\sigma_{\max} = \sigma_0 > \sigma_1 > \cdots > \sigma_K \approx 0\), nudging the sample along the score at every step. (We write \(y_k\) for the reverse iterate at noise level \(\sigma_k\), keeping \(x_0\) reserved for the clean data point; \(y_0\) is pure noise and \(y_K\) is the generated sample.)
\[
y_{k+1} \;=\; y_k \;+\; \frac{\sigma_k^2 - \sigma_{k+1}^2}{2}\,
\nabla_y \log p_{\sigma_k}(y_k)
\;=\; y_k + \frac{\sigma_k^2 - \sigma_{k+1}^2}{2}\cdot
\frac{\tanh\!\big(y_k/\sigma_k^2\big) - y_k}{\sigma_k^2}.
\]
This deterministic rule is the explicit Euler discretization of the probability-flow ODE in the variance clock \(\tau = \sigma^2\). (Strictly, to speak of dynamics across noise levels we couple them: \(x_\tau = x_0 + w_\tau\) with \(w\) a Brownian motion — Module 5 makes this precise; nothing below needs it yet.) The stochastic variant both doubles the score drift and injects fresh independent noise at each step,
\[
y_{k+1} = y_k + \big(\sigma_k^2 - \sigma_{k+1}^2\big)\,\nabla_y \log p_{\sigma_k}(y_k)
+ \sqrt{\sigma_k^2 - \sigma_{k+1}^2}\; z_k, \qquad z_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)
\text{ i.i.d.},
\]
giving the Euler–Maruyama discretization of the reverse-time SDE. Where these updates come from is the business of Modules 5–6 (Fokker–Planck, reverse-time dynamics); today we only need to watch them work: a cloud of particles started from \(\mathcal{N}(0,\, 1+\sigma_{\max}^2)\) splits, condenses, and lands within \(\approx \sigma_{\min}\) of \(\{-1, +1\}\), in equal proportions up to sampling error.
To be honest about the word “exact”: the formulas are exact, but the sampler carries four small approximations — we initialize from the moment-matched Gaussian rather than the true mixture \(p_{\sigma_{\max}}\) (indistinguishable at \(\sigma_{\max} = 3\), but not equal); we stop at \(\sigma_{\min} = 10^{-2} > 0\), so samples end a hair’s width from the atoms; the Euler steps discretize the flow; and any finite run has sampling noise. Each vanishes in the appropriate limit — and every one of them has a counterpart in real diffusion models.
The full sampler, with no neural network anywhere:
import numpy as np

def score(y, s2):                 # ∇ log p_σ(y), exact for the two-point data
    return (np.tanh(y / s2) - y) / s2

smax, smin, K, N = 3.0, 1e-2, 500, 100_000
sig = smax * (smin / smax) ** (np.arange(K + 1) / K)    # geometric σ grid
y = np.sqrt(1 + smax**2) * np.random.randn(N)           # start from pure noise

for k in range(K):                                       # probability-flow ODE
    d = sig[k]**2 - sig[k + 1]**2
    y += 0.5 * d * score(y, sig[k]**2)

err = np.abs(np.abs(y) - 1).max()      # worst distance to the nearest data point
print(err, (y > 0).mean())   # ≈ 0 and ≈ 0.5, up to σ_min + discretization + sampling

title: 01 · The World’s Smallest Diffusion Model
section: Why the course exists: what breaks for images
text:
Why the course exists: what breaks for images
Everything above was exact because the posterior mean had a formula. For images there is no usable one. (Exercise 4 gives a closed form for any finite training set — but a sampler built on it can only ever reproduce the training points; what we actually want is the posterior mean under the unknown population distribution.) Nor can it be tabulated: a \(64 \times 64\) RGB image lives in a space of \(256^{12288}\) configurations, and the data occupies a vanishingly thin filament of it (Module 1: the curse of dimensionality). The entire role of the neural network in a diffusion model is to approximate the map \((x, \sigma) \mapsto \mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x]\) — to be the tanh we can no longer derive. Every other ingredient of this note survives unchanged, and each becomes a module of the course:







In this note
In the course




The “produce more samples” problem; why direct density estimation fails
M1 — Foundations of generative modeling


Gaussian mixture, conditioning, \(\operatorname{Var} = 1+\sigma^2\)
M2 — Gaussians and noise accumulation


The discrete \(\sigma\) grid; denoising as the training target
M3 — DDPM framework


\(\nabla_x \log p_\sigma\), Tweedie’s formula
M4 — Score matching and denoising


The \(\sigma\)-continuum, densities evolving with \(\sigma\)
M5 — SDEs and Fokker–Planck


The reverse update and the probability-flow ODE
M6 — Reverse-time dynamics

title: 01 · The World’s Smallest Diffusion Model
section: Exercises
text:
Exercises

Fill in the algebra for \(\mathbb{P}(x_0 = +1 \mid x) = \operatorname{sigmoid}(2x/\sigma^2)\) and \(\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x] = \tanh(x/\sigma^2)\).
Show \(\operatorname{Var}(x_\sigma) = 1 + \sigma^2\), and more generally \(\operatorname{Var}(x_\sigma) = \operatorname{Var}(x_0) + \sigma^2\) for any data distribution with finite variance (independence of \(z\) and \(x_0\) is all you need — zero mean is not required).
Unequal weights. Let \(\mathbb{P}(x_0 = +1) = \pi\) with \(0 < \pi < 1\). Show \(\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x] = \tanh\!\big(\tfrac{x}{\sigma^2} + \tfrac12 \log\tfrac{\pi}{1-\pi}\big)\) — the denoiser acquires a bias. Check that as \(\sigma \to \infty\) this tends to \(2\pi - 1\), the prior mean, and work out what happens in the degenerate cases \(\pi \in \{0, 1\}\) by taking limits.
More points. For data uniform on \(\{a_1, \dots, a_m\}\), show \(\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x] = \sum_i a_i\, w_i(x)\) with \(w_i(x) \propto \exp\!\big(\tfrac{a_i x}{\sigma^2} - \tfrac{a_i^2}{2\sigma^2}\big)
\propto \exp\!\big(-\tfrac{(x - a_i)^2}{2\sigma^2}\big)\) — a softmax with Gaussian-kernel weights. (So the optimal denoiser for a finite dataset under Gaussian corruption is attention-like: an RBF-weighted average of the training points. For non-uniform weights \(\pi_i\), each logit gains \(\log \pi_i\).)
Run the sampler above with the SDE update instead of the ODE. Compare the RMS distance of the final samples to the nearest data point for both, as a function of \(K\) and of \(\sigma_{\min}\). (You should find that increasing \(K\) removes discretization error but both samplers retain a terminal width \(\approx \sigma_{\min}\) — lowering \(\sigma_{\min}\), not raising \(K\), is what sharpens the atoms.)

title: 02 · Probability & Random Variables
text:
The sample space, events, and the probability measure
A standalone tutorial (used in W02): the probability the course actually uses, built from the ground up — sample spaces, events, random variables, and expectation. Joints, conditionals and Bayes’ rule follow in the next concept. Readers already comfortable with these notions may proceed directly to Distributions and Maximum Likelihood.
Probability theory is built on two distinct maps: the probability measure, which assigns numbers to events, and the random variable, which assigns numbers to outcomes. Distinguishing the two carefully at the outset prevents most of the common confusions, and this tutorial is organized accordingly.
A random experiment is modeled by three objects.
All further rules are consequences of the axioms; two used constantly are \(P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)\) and \(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\).
A remark on the continuous case. For \(\Omega = [0,1]\) with the uniform measure, every singleton event \(\{\omega\}\) has probability zero, although some outcome certainly occurs. Probability zero therefore does not mean impossibility; it means a vanishing fraction of the possibilities. This is also the reason \(P\) is defined on events rather than on individual outcomes: in the continuous case, individual outcomes are too small to carry probability.

title: 02 · Probability & Random Variables
text:
The sample space \(\Omega\) is the set of all possible outcomes of the experiment, with one element \(\omega \in \Omega\) per complete outcome. For a single die, \(\Omega = \{1, \dots, 6\}\). For two coin tosses, \(\Omega = \{HH, HT, TH, TT\}\); note that an outcome specifies the result of the entire experiment, i.e. both tosses. For a point drawn from the interval \([0,1]\), \(\Omega = [0,1]\), an uncountable set.
An event is a subset \(A \subseteq \Omega\); events are the objects to which probabilities are assigned. “The die shows an even number” is the event \(\{2, 4, 6\}\); “at least one head” is the event \(\{HH, HT, TH\}\). An event is a collection of outcomes, not an outcome.
Worth pausing on the asymmetry here, because it is the source of a lot of early confusion. Exactly one outcome occurs, but many events occur at once. Roll a \(4\) and the single outcome is \(\omega = 4\) — yet “even”, “at most \(5\)”, “not a \(6\)” and \(\Omega\) itself have all occurred simultaneously, because \(4\) belongs to all of them. Outcomes are exclusive; events are not.
The probability measure is the first of the two maps:
\[
P : \text{events} \longrightarrow [0, 1],
\]
required to satisfy Kolmogorov’s axioms: (i) \(P(A) \ge 0\) for every event \(A\);

\(P(\Omega) = 1\); (iii) for mutually exclusive events \(A_1, A_2, \dots\), \(P\big(\bigcup_i A_i\big) = \sum_i P(A_i)\) (countable additivity).

title: 02 · Probability & Random Variables
section: Random variables
text:
Random variables
The second map is the random variable. A random variable is a function
\[
X : \Omega \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}
\]
that assigns a numerical value to each outcome. For the two-coin experiment with \(X\) the number of heads: \(X(HH) = 2\), \(X(HT) = X(TH) = 1\), \(X(TT) = 0\). Despite the name, \(X\) is a fixed, deterministic function; the randomness resides entirely in which outcome \(\omega\) the experiment produces.






WarningA random variable is not a function of events



The single most common misreading is that a random variable takes events to numbers. It does not. Its input is a single outcome \(\omega\), never a set.
Take a die and the indicator of oddness,
\[
Y(\omega) = \begin{cases} 1 & \omega \in \{1,3,5\},\\ 0 & \omega \in \{2,4,6\}. \end{cases}
\]
It is tempting to read this as “\(Y\) sends the event even to \(0\).” It does not. \(Y\) sends the outcome \(2\) to \(0\), and the outcome \(4\) to \(0\), and the outcome \(6\) to \(0\) — three separate outcomes that happen to receive the same number. Nothing is ever evaluated at the set \(\{2,4,6\}\).
The direction that is available runs the other way: a random variable manufactures events by taking preimages. From \(Y\) we recover
\[
\{\omega : Y(\omega) = 0\} = \{2,4,6\}, \qquad
\{\omega : Y(\omega) = 1\} = \{1,3,5\},
\]
so the chain is random variable \(\to\) numerical condition \(\to\) event \(\to\) probability. Getting this arrow the right way round is most of what the two-map picture buys you.


The two maps combine as follows. A statement such as \(\mathbb{P}(X = 1)\) is evaluated by first identifying the event determined by the condition and then applying \(P\) to it:
\[
\mathbb{P}(X = 1)
\;=\; P\big(\{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) = 1\}\big)
\;=\; P(\{HT, TH\}) = \tfrac{2}{4}.
\]
Carrying this out for every value (or set of values) of \(X\) yields the distribution of \(X\), a probability assignment on the real line. Once the distribution is available, the underlying sample space is usually suppressed and one works with the distribution directly; this is standard practice, and the remainder of the course follows it. The present section records what that convention leaves implicit.
A discrete random variable is described by its probability mass function (pmf) \(p(x) = \mathbb{P}(X = x)\), with \(\sum_x p(x) = 1\). A continuous random variable is described by its probability density function (pdf) \(f(x) \ge 0\), with \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\, dx = 1\); probabilities are obtained as areas under the density,
\[
\mathbb{P}(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\, dx .
\]
Three properties of densities deserve emphasis.

A density value is not a probability and may exceed 1; the Uniform distribution on \([0, \tfrac12]\) has \(f \equiv 2\). Only areas under the density are probabilities.
\(\mathbb{P}(X = x) = 0\) for every individual \(x\), by the singleton remark above. The informal reading of a density is \(f(x)\,dx \approx\) the probability of an outcome within \(dx\) of \(x\); densities compare the relative plausibility of neighborhoods.
The cumulative distribution function (CDF) \(F(x) = \mathbb{P}(X \le x)\) applies to discrete and continuous variables alike, and its derivative, where it exists, is the pdf. The CDF appears in Generative AI, in Its Simplest Form as the sampling map \(F^{-1}\).

title: 02 · Probability & Random Variables
section: What \(\Omega\) actually is when the variable is continuous
text:
What \(\Omega\) actually is when the variable is continuous
Write \(T \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) for tomorrow’s temperature and it is natural to assume the sample space is \(\mathbb{R}\). It is not — or at least, it need not be, and thinking it must be obscures what the notation says.
The experiment is tomorrow. Its outcomes are the ways tomorrow could turn out: every physically possible state of the world, an enormous set with no numbers in it anywhere. Call it \(\Omega\). The temperature is a reading taken from such a state,
\[
T : \Omega \longrightarrow \mathbb{R},
\]
which extracts one number from each possible world and discards everything else about it — the wind, the cloud cover, who won the match. Humidity would be a second reading \(H : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) of the very same worlds, which is precisely why \(T\) and \(H\) can be correlated: they are two numbers pulled from one outcome.
So \(T \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) is not a claim about \(\Omega\) at all. It is a claim about the distribution induced by \(T\) on the real line: the probability that lands on each region of \(\mathbb{R}\) once \(P\) is pushed through \(T\). The underlying \(\Omega\) stays exactly where it was, unmentioned.

The canonical shortcut
Nobody ever constructs the set of possible worlds. What statistics does instead is take the induced distribution and make it the model:
\[
\Omega = \mathbb{R}, \qquad
P = \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2), \qquad
X(\omega) = \omega .
\]
Sample space the real line, probability the Gaussian itself, random variable the identity function — the outcome is the number. This is the canonical probability space, and it is what is silently in play whenever a textbook says “let \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\)” and never mentions an experiment.
The shortcut is legitimate because every probability statement about the value of \(T\) depends only on the induced distribution, and the canonical space reproduces that distribution exactly. It costs you nothing as long as you want statements about one variable’s value. It costs you something the moment you want two variables to live on the same outcome — then you need a sample space rich enough to carry both, which is the subject of the next section.

title: 02 · Probability & Random Variables
section: Expectation
text:
Expectation
The expectation of a random variable is the probability-weighted average of its values,
\[
\mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_x x\, p(x)
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\mathbb{E}[X] = \int x\, f(x)\, dx ,
\]
the center of mass of the distribution. The expectation need not be an attainable value; a fair die has \(\mathbb{E}[X] = 3.5\). More generally, for a function \(g\),
\[
\mathbb{E}[g(X)] = \sum_x g(x)\, p(x)
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\int g(x)\, f(x)\, dx ,
\]
so that the distribution of \(g(X)\) itself need never be computed (a fact sometimes called the law of the unconscious statistician).
Two properties carry most of the weight in this course.

Linearity. \(\mathbb{E}[aX + bY] = a\,\mathbb{E}[X] + b\,\mathbb{E}[Y]\) holds for all random variables on a common sample space, with no independence assumption. (Independence is required for the separate statement \(\mathbb{E}[XY] = \mathbb{E}[X]\,\mathbb{E}[Y]\).)
Variance. \(\operatorname{Var}(X) =
\mathbb{E}\big[(X - \mathbb{E}X)^2\big] =
\mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}X)^2\) measures spread about the mean, and for independent random variables variances add. The identity \(\operatorname{Var}(x_0 + \sigma z) = 1 + \sigma^2\) of W01 is an instance.

Finally, the conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = y]\) is the mean of the conditional distribution of \(X\) given \(Y = y\), regarded as a function of \(y\). It is the minimum-mean-squared-error prediction of \(X\) from the observation \(Y = y\) (proved in Distributions and Maximum Likelihood), and the denoiser \(\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_\sigma]\) of W01 is precisely a conditional expectation.

title: 02 · Probability & Random Variables
section: The four objects, in one table
text:
The four objects, in one table









Object
Form
What it does
Common misreading




Sample space \(\Omega\)
a set
lists every way the experiment could turn out
that it must be numbers


Event \(A\)
\(A \subseteq \Omega\)
a yes/no question about the outcome
that only one can occur


Probability \(P\)
\(P(A) \in [0,1]\)
assigns probability to events
that it applies to outcomes


Random variable \(X\)
\(X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\)
assigns a number to outcomes
that it applies to events



The two maps point at different arguments, and that is the whole distinction: probabilities attach to events, numbers attach to outcomes. A distribution is what you get by combining them — push \(P\) through \(X\) and read off the result on the real line.

section: Correspondence with this course
text:

Object

title: 02 · Probability & Random Variables
section: Exercises
text:
Exercises

For two fair coin tosses with \(X\) the number of heads: write out \(\Omega\), the values \(X(\omega)\) for all four outcomes, and the pmf of \(X\); verify that the pmf sums to 1 using the additivity axiom.
Exhibit (a) a pdf exceeding 3 at some point; (b) a random variable whose expectation is not an attainable value; (c) two dependent random variables for which \(\mathbb{E}[X + Y] = \mathbb{E}[X] + \mathbb{E}[Y]\) nevertheless holds, illustrating that linearity requires no independence.
Let \(U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\) and \(X = U^2\). Compute \(\mathbb{E}[X]\) twice: directly via \(\mathbb{E}[g(U)]\), and by first deriving the CDF and pdf of \(X\). Compare the effort required.

title: 03 · Joint, Conditional, Marginal — and Bayes
text:
Two numbers on one outcome
The second concept in the spine, and the point at which probability starts being useful. One new move — put two numbers on the same outcome instead of one — produces the whole multivariate vocabulary: joints, marginals, conditionals, and Bayes’ rule. Everything here is elementary and uses the standard discrete and continuous probability tools from the preceding note.
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be two random variables defined on the same sample space — two numerical features read off the same outcome \(\omega\). Height and weight of one person; today’s price and tomorrow’s price of one stock; the clean image and its noisy version from one generation run.
That sharing is the whole idea. “\(X\) and \(Y\) are jointly distributed” is not an extra assumption bolted on; it is the statement that a single \(\omega\) determines both numbers at once, which is exactly why they can be correlated.

title: 03 · Joint, Conditional, Marginal — and Bayes
section: Joint distributions
text:
Joint distributions
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be two random variables defined on the same sample space — two numerical features of the same outcome. Their joint distribution specifies \(p(x, y) = \mathbb{P}(X = x \text{ and } Y = y)\) in the discrete case, or a joint density \(f(x, y)\) whose volumes are probabilities in the continuous case. The joint distribution is a complete description of the pair: every probabilistic statement about \((X, Y)\) can be computed from it.
The following discrete joint distribution serves as the running example (the state of a morning sky and the occurrence of rain):

title: 03 · Joint, Conditional, Marginal — and Bayes
section: Marginal distributions
text:
Marginal distributions
The marginal distribution of \(X\) describes \(X\) alone, with \(Y\) disregarded. It is obtained by summing (or, for densities, integrating) the joint distribution over the other variable:
\[
p(x) = \sum_y p(x, y),
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
f(x) = \int f(x, y)\, dy .
\]
In the table these are the row and column sums — the margins of the table, which is the origin of the term: \(\mathbb{P}(\text{cloudy}) = 0.45\) and \(\mathbb{P}(\text{rain}) = 0.25\). The operation is justified directly by the additivity axiom: the event “cloudy” is the disjoint union of “cloudy and rain” and “cloudy and no rain”. Marginalization recurs throughout the course; in the mixture model of Generative AI, in Its Simplest Form, the observed density \(p(x) = \sum_z p(z)\, p(x \mid z)\) is precisely the joint distribution of \((x, z)\) with the latent variable summed out.

title: 03 · Joint, Conditional, Marginal — and Bayes
section: Conditional distributions and Bayes’ rule
text:
Conditional distributions and Bayes’ rule
The conditional distribution of \(Y\) given \(X = x\) is defined, whenever \(p(x) > 0\), by
\[
p(y \mid x) = \frac{p(x, y)}{p(x)} .
\]
The definition restricts attention to the outcomes consistent with \(X = x\) and renormalizes their probabilities to total 1. In the running example, \(\mathbb{P}(\text{rain} \mid \text{cloudy}) = 0.20 / 0.45 \approx 0.44\), compared with the unconditional \(\mathbb{P}(\text{rain}) = 0.25\).
Applying the definition in both directions and eliminating the joint yields Bayes’ rule,
\[
\boxed{\;p(x \mid y) = \frac{p(y \mid x)\, p(x)}{p(y)}\;}
\]
which converts a conditional in one direction into the conditional in the other. The tanh denoiser of W01 is an application of this identity, with \(x\) the clean data point and \(y\) the noisy observation; it is derived in full in The World’s Smallest Diffusion Model.
\(X\) and \(Y\) are independent if \(p(x, y) = p(x)\, p(y)\) for all \(x, y\) — equivalently, if \(p(y \mid x) = p(y)\), so that conditioning on \(X\) conveys no information about \(Y\). In the table, \(0.20 \ne 0.45 \times 0.25\), so the two variables are dependent. The i.i.d. assumption underlying the likelihoods of Distributions and Maximum Likelihood are an independence statement applied to repeated observations.

title: 03 · Joint, Conditional, Marginal — and Bayes
section: Bayes’ rule, and why inference is the inverse problem
text:
Bayes’ rule, and why inference is the inverse problem

Generation runs forward; inference runs backward
Almost every model in this course is written in the forward direction. You posit some unobserved state, and you write down a mechanism that turns it into data:
\[
\underbrace{z}_{\text{latent, what we care about}}
\;\longrightarrow\;
\underbrace{x}_{\text{observed, what we get}} ,
\qquad \text{specified by } p(x \mid z).
\]
Writing \(p(x \mid z)\) is usually the easy half. It is a mechanism — a simulator, a physical story, a noise model — and you can often just state it.
But that is rarely what you want. You do not observe \(z\); you observe \(x\), and you want to reason back to the cause. That is the inverse problem:
\[
\underbrace{x}_{\text{observed}} \;\longrightarrow\; \underbrace{z}_{\text{inferred}},
\qquad \text{wanted: } p(z \mid x).
\]









Forward
Inverse




Direction
cause \(\to\) effect
effect \(\to\) cause


Object
\(p(x \mid z)\)
\(p(z \mid x)\)


Typical status
given, by modelling
wanted, must be computed


Names
generative model, sampling distribution, simulator
inference, inversion, the posterior



You cannot simply invert the arrow, because the forward map is generally many-to-one: different latent states can produce the very same observation. Knowing \(x\) therefore does not determine \(z\) — it only makes some values of \(z\) more plausible than others. Something extra is needed to break the tie, and that something is what you believed about \(z\) before looking. Bayes’ rule is exactly the bookkeeping that combines the two:
\[
\underbrace{p(z \mid x)}_{\text{posterior}}
\;=\;
\frac{\overbrace{p(x \mid z)}^{\text{likelihood}}\;\overbrace{p(z)}^{\text{prior}}}
     {\underbrace{p(x)}_{\text{evidence}}},
\qquad
p(x) = \sum_z p(x \mid z)\,p(z).
\]
This is the single most useful thing in the course’s toolkit: it is the bridge from the direction you can write down to the direction you want.


A toy example: did the student understand “or”?
A student is set ten short questions on the logical connective or. We would like to know whether they have actually grasped it — but “understanding” is not something we can measure. We can only mark the answers.

Latent \(z \in \{0, 1\}\): the student understands the concept, or does not. This is the inferential goal.
Observable \(x \in \{0, 1, \dots, 10\}\): the number of questions correct. This is all we ever see.

Now the forward model — the sampling distribution that says how marks are produced given the latent state. A student who understands still slips occasionally; one who does not can still get items right by guessing or by luck in which items came up. Take each item as independent with
\[
x \mid z = 1 \;\sim\; \text{Binomial}(10,\ 0.9),
\qquad
x \mid z = 0 \;\sim\; \text{Binomial}(10,\ 0.4).
\]






NoteThe marks scale does not matter



Nothing above depends on marks running \(0\) to \(10\). The same structure works for a single right/wrong item (\(x \in \{0,1\}\), a Bernoulli), or a percentage score \(0\)–\(100\), or a graded rubric. All that changes is the count distribution you put on the observable. What stays fixed is the shape of the problem: a latent you want, an observable you get, and a sampling distribution connecting them.


Suppose the student scores \(x = 7\). Take a neutral prior \(p(z=1) = 0.5\). Then
\[
\frac{p(z=1 \mid x=7)}{p(z=0 \mid x=7)}
= \underbrace{\frac{\binom{10}{7} 0.9^{7} 0.1^{3}}{\binom{10}{7} 0.4^{7} 0.6^{3}}}_{\text{likelihood ratio}}
\times \underbrace{\frac{0.5}{0.5}}_{\text{prior odds}}
= \Big(\tfrac{0.9}{0.4}\Big)^{7}\Big(\tfrac{0.1}{0.6}\Big)^{3}
= 1.352 ,
\]
so \(p(z = 1 \mid x = 7) = 1.352 / 2.352 = \mathbf{0.575}\).
Two things are worth noticing. The binomial coefficient \(\binom{10}{7}\) appears in both the numerator and the denominator and cancels — it describes how many ways the marks could have been arranged, which is the same under either hypothesis, so it carries no evidence. And \(7/10\), which sounds like a decent score, is barely informative here: it moves us from \(50\%\) to \(58\%\).
Across the range of possible scores:



Score \(x\)

The posterior is not a smooth reflection of the mark — it is nearly flat at the extremes and swings sharply in the middle, where the two hypotheses actually disagree.
And the prior genuinely matters. At the same score \(x = 7\):



Prior \(p(z=1)\)
0.2

Posterior \(p(z=1 \mid x=7)\)

Same evidence, three different conclusions. This is not a defect. It is the honest statement that seven out of ten is weak evidence, and weak evidence does not overturn what you already knew.


The sampling distribution is the likelihood
The expression \(p(x \mid z)\) has been doing two jobs above, and it is worth separating them, because this is the distinction Distributions and Maximum Likelihood makes in the parametric setting.









Hold fixed
Vary
You get

the sampling distribution — how marks come out

the likelihood — how well each \(z\) explains what we saw

It is one formula read in two directions. Forward, it generates. Backward, it scores. Bayes’ rule is what converts the backward reading into an actual probability distribution over \(z\), by weighting with the prior and renormalising.


Bayesian Knowledge Tracing
The toy example freezes the student in time. Real learners learn, so the latent state changes as they work — and the natural extension is exactly the model used in intelligent tutoring systems: Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (Corbett and Anderson, 1995, User Modeling and User-Adapted Interaction).
BKT keeps the same two-layer structure and lets the latent evolve:

a hidden binary skill state \(z_t \in \{\text{not known}, \text{known}\}\);
an observed response \(x_t \in \{\text{incorrect}, \text{correct}\}\) at each opportunity \(t\).

Four parameters specify it, and each is a conditional probability:







Parameter
Meaning




\(P(L_0)\)
probability the skill is known before any practice — the prior


\(P(T)\)
probability of learning it at an opportunity, if not yet known — the transition


\(P(G)\)
probability of answering correctly without knowing it — the guess


\(P(S)\)
probability of answering incorrectly while knowing it — the slip



So the emission model is \(P(\text{correct} \mid \text{known}) = 1 - P(S)\) and \(P(\text{correct} \mid \text{not known}) = P(G)\). Standard BKT assumes no forgetting.
Tracing a student is then a two-step recursion, repeated per question — and the first step is precisely Bayes’ rule:

Update on the evidence. With \(L\) the current probability the skill is known, a correct answer gives \[
L^{+} \;=\; \frac{L\,(1 - P(S))}{L\,(1 - P(S)) + (1-L)\,P(G)} ,
\] and an incorrect answer gives \(L^{-} = L\,P(S) \,/\, [\,L\,P(S) + (1-L)(1 - P(G))\,]\).
Predict forward through learning. \(L \leftarrow L^{\pm} + (1 - L^{\pm})\,P(T)\).

For instance with \(L = 0.4\), \(P(S) = 0.10\), \(P(G) = 0.25\), \(P(T) = 0.20\), a correct answer raises the belief to \(0.36 / 0.51 = 0.706\), and the learning step then carries it to \(0.706 + 0.294 \times 0.20 = 0.765\) before the next question. An incorrect answer instead drops it to \(0.04/0.49 = 0.082\).






TipThe shape to remember



A latent state you care about, an observable you actually get, a forward model connecting them, and Bayes running the inference backwards — repeated over a sequence. That is BKT, and it is also a hidden Markov model, a Kalman filter, and, as the next few weeks will show, a diffusion model.




Why this is the shape of the whole course
Diffusion models are an inverse problem, and it is worth being blunt about the terminology, because it inverts what you might expect.

The forward process of a diffusion model is the corruption: \(x_0 \to x_\sigma = x_0 + \sigma z\). We write it down ourselves, in closed form, and it is trivial to sample. This is the easy direction.
Generating an image means going the other way — recovering a plausible clean \(x_0\) from a noisy \(x_\sigma\). The clean signal is the latent; the noisy observation is the data.

So in a diffusion model, generation is the inference problem. That is why the central object of the course is a posterior, and why the optimal denoiser is a posterior mean:
\[
\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_\sigma]
= \tanh\!\Big(\frac{x_\sigma}{\sigma^2}\Big)
\quad\text{for the two-point dataset of }
\] W01 — which is Bayes’ rule applied to two Gaussian components and then averaged. Swap “understands the concept” for “was a \(+1\)”, and “ten marks” for “one noisy measurement”, and it is the same calculation you did above.

title: 03 · Joint, Conditional, Marginal — and Bayes
section: Exercises
text:
Exercises

Two fair coin tosses. Let \(X\) be the result of the first toss and \(Y\) the total number of heads. Write the joint as a table, compute both marginals, and compute both families of conditionals. Verify Bayes’ rule on \(\mathbb{P}(X = H \mid Y = 1)\).
For the sky-and-rain table above, compute \(\mathbb{P}(\text{cloudy} \mid \text{rain})\) by Bayes’ rule from \(\mathbb{P}(\text{rain} \mid \text{cloudy})\) and the marginals, then confirm it by reading the table directly.
Construct two different joint distributions on \(\{0,1\}^2\) that have the same pair of marginals. What does this show about whether marginals determine a joint?
Show that if \(p(x,y) = p(x)p(y)\) then every conditional \(p(y \mid x)\) equals \(p(y)\) — independence means the conditional does not move as you change what you condition on.
In the mixture model \(z \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi)\), \(x \mid z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_z, \sigma^2)\): identify the joint \(p(x,z)\), both marginals, and both conditionals. State which of these the W01 denoiser computes, and which the ancestral sampler of Generative AI, in Its Simplest Form uses.
A generative model produces a noisy observation \(x_t\) from a clean signal \(x_0\). Which direction is easy to write down, \(p(x_t \mid x_0)\) or \(p(x_0 \mid x_t)\)? Which one does generation require? Name the rule that converts one into the other.

title: 04 · Distributions and Maximum Likelihood
text:
The cast of distributions
Standalone tutorial accompanying W02. Interactive versions: the Distribution Playground and the Likelihood Lens.
This note walks one loop twice: distribution → samples → fitted distribution → new samples. First visually (the playground), then analytically (maximum likelihood for the Gaussian, derived in full). It doubles as a compact reference for the distribution families used throughout the course.
A sentence of habitat for each: the Uniform encodes total ignorance on an interval; the Normal is what sums of many small independent effects look like (W01’s warm-up demo is this statement); the Gamma models positive, right-skewed quantities such as waiting times; the Beta lives on \((0,1)\) and models proportions and probabilities; a mixture models data with subpopulations — clusters — and is the recurring character of this course.

title: 04 · Distributions and Maximum Likelihood
section: How sampling actually works
text:
How sampling actually works
Every sampler in the playground reduces to uniform random numbers:

Inverse CDF. If \(F\) is a CDF and \(U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\), then \(X = F^{-1}(U)\) has CDF \(F\) (proved in the companion note Generative AI, in Its Simplest Form). This handles Uniform (\(x = a + (b-a)u\)) and anything with a computable \(F^{-1}\).
Box–Muller for the Normal: with \(U_1, U_2\) independent uniforms, \(\sqrt{-2\log U_1}\,\cos(2\pi U_2)\) is exactly \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\). This is the sampler inside every demo of this course.
Pick-then-sample for mixtures: draw the component index with probabilities \(\pi_i\), then sample that component — ancestral sampling, the subject of the companion note.
Gamma and Beta use clever rejection samplers (the playground uses Marsaglia–Tsang); we treat them as black boxes.

title: 04 · Distributions and Maximum Likelihood
section: Likelihood
text:
Likelihood
Fix a family \(f(x;\theta)\) and observe an i.i.d. dataset \(x_1, \dots, x_n\). The likelihood and log-likelihood are
\[
L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i; \theta),
\qquad
\ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \log f(x_i; \theta),
\]
and the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) is \(\hat\theta = \arg\max_\theta \ell(\theta)\). The log changes nothing about the argmax (monotonicity) and everything about the algebra and the numerics: a product of 3000 numbers of size \(10^{-2}\) underflows; a sum of their logs is a perfectly pleasant \(\approx -13{,}800\).

title: 04 · Distributions and Maximum Likelihood
section: PDF vs likelihood: the same function, two readings
text:
PDF vs likelihood: the same function, two readings
The chronic confusion, settled: \(f(x;\theta)\) is one formula with two arguments.









Fix
Vary
You get
Area under the curve

\(= 1\), always

parameters \(\theta\)

The Likelihood Lens shows both as slices of the same surface \(f(x;\mu) = \mathcal{N}(x; \mu, \sigma^2)\): the horizontal slice (fix \(\mu\)) is a density in \(x\); the vertical slice (fix \(x\)) is a likelihood in \(\mu\). For the Gaussian the two slices happen to have the same bell shape, because \(f(x;\mu) = f(\mu;x)\) — a symmetry of this family, not a general fact (repeat the exercise mentally with a Gamma in \(\theta\)). What is general: the likelihood is not a probability distribution over \(\theta\) — it need not integrate to 1, and only its argmax and local shape carry meaning.

title: 04 · Distributions and Maximum Likelihood
section: The Gaussian MLE, in full
text:
The Gaussian MLE, in full
\[
\ell(\mu, \sigma^2)
= -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu)^2 .
\]
Maximize over \(\mu\). Only the second term involves \(\mu\):
\[
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \mu}
= \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu)
= \frac{n}{\sigma^2}(\bar{x} - \mu)
\;\stackrel{!}{=}\; 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{\ \hat\mu = \bar{x}\ }
\]
for every \(\sigma\) — which is why, in the Lens, changing \(\sigma\) sharpens the log-likelihood parabola but never moves its peak.
Maximize over \(\sigma^2\) (treat \(v = \sigma^2\) as the variable):
\[
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial v}
= -\frac{n}{2v} + \frac{1}{2v^2}\sum_i (x_i - \hat\mu)^2
\;\stackrel{!}{=}\; 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{\ \hat\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2\ }
\]
(One should check this is a maximum, not merely critical: \(\ell \to -\infty\) as \(v \to 0^+\) and as \(v \to \infty\), and this is the only critical point.) Note the divisor \(n\): the MLE of the variance is biased — \(\mathbb{E}[\hat\sigma^2] =
\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2\) — which is where the familiar \(n-1\) estimator comes from. For this course the distinction is a footnote; the MLE is what the theory produces.

title: 04 · Distributions and Maximum Likelihood
section: Aside: binary cross-entropy is a likelihood
text:
Aside: binary cross-entropy is a likelihood
The most familiar loss in machine learning is a maximum-likelihood problem in disguise, and the disguise falls away the moment classification is read as a (conditional) generative model.
The model. For the \(i\)-th sample with features \(x_i\), model the binary label as a Bernoulli trial,
\[
y_i \mid x_i \;\sim\; \text{Bernoulli}(\pi_i), \qquad y_i \in \{0, 1\},
\]
and let a neural network supply the logit — the log-odds, not the log-probability:
\[
s_i = f_\theta(x_i) = \log \frac{\pi_i}{1 - \pi_i}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\pi_i = \operatorname{sigmoid}(s_i).
\]
The likelihood. The Bernoulli pmf can be written in one line as \(p(y \mid \pi) = \pi^{y} (1-\pi)^{1-y}\), so for independent samples
\[
L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n \pi_i^{\,y_i} (1 - \pi_i)^{1 - y_i},
\qquad
-\ell(\theta) = -\sum_{i=1}^n \Big[ y_i \log \pi_i + (1 - y_i)\log(1 - \pi_i) \Big].
\]
The right-hand side is exactly binary cross-entropy. Training a classifier with BCE is maximum likelihood for a conditional Bernoulli model whose log-odds are the network output — nothing more. (The name is also earned: \(-\ell/n\) is the cross-entropy between the empirical distribution of each label and the model’s Bernoulli.)
The \(\pm 1\) convention. With labels \(y_i \in \{-1, +1\}\), the identity \(\operatorname{sigmoid}(-s) = 1 - \operatorname{sigmoid}(s)\) collapses both cases into \(p(y_i \mid s_i) = \operatorname{sigmoid}(y_i s_i)\), and the negative log-likelihood becomes the logistic loss,
\[
-\ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \log\!\big(1 + e^{-y_i s_i}\big)
\]
— the same objective, rewritten.
The connection to this course. The latent posterior of W01 \(\mathbb{P}(z = 2 \mid x) = \operatorname{sigmoid}(2x/\sigma^2)\) is precisely this model with logit \(s(x) = 2x/\sigma^2\): the optimal classifier of the hidden component is a Bernoulli model whose log-odds are linear in the observation. Classification, denoising, and latent inference are all the same likelihood computation wearing different clothes.

title: 04 · Distributions and Maximum Likelihood
section: Fitting the other families — honestly
text:
Fitting the other families — honestly

Uniform. The likelihood is \((b-a)^{-n}\) if all points lie in \([a,b]\) and \(0\) otherwise: to maximize, squeeze the interval as tight as the data allows — \(\hat a = \min_i x_i\), \(\hat b = \max_i x_i\). (No calculus; the maximum is on the boundary of the constraint. That is Exercise 2.)
Gamma and Beta have no closed-form MLE. Setting the derivatives to zero produces equations involving the digamma function, solvable only numerically. The playground therefore uses the method of moments (MoM): equate the family’s mean and variance to the sample’s \(\bar x\) and \(s^2\) and solve —
\[
\text{Gamma: } \hat k = \frac{\bar{x}^2}{s^2},\ \ \hat\theta = \frac{s^2}{\bar{x}};
\qquad
\text{Beta: } c = \frac{\bar{x}(1-\bar{x})}{s^2} - 1,\ \
\hat\alpha = \bar{x}\,c,\ \ \hat\beta = (1-\bar{x})\,c .
\]
MoM is a respectable estimator in its own right (consistent, and a standard warm start for numerical MLE); the honest label matters because “just maximize the likelihood” quietly assumes machinery we haven’t built.
Mixtures. Even MoM gets awkward; the right tool is expectation–maximization (EM), which belongs to a later conversation. Today the mixture plays a different role — see below.

title: 04 · Distributions and Maximum Likelihood
section: The trap: right method, wrong family
text:
The trap: right method, wrong family
In the playground: generate 3000 samples from the two-bump mixture, then fit a single Normal by maximum likelihood. The fit is optimal within its family — and its peak sits exactly in the empty valley between the clusters, because the best single Gaussian matches the overall mean and variance, not the shape.
Two lessons. First, MLE optimizes within the family you chose; the choice of family is a modeling decision the likelihood cannot rescue. Second, we currently have no number that says how wrong this fit is. Constructing that number — the KL divergence, and its identity with maximum likelihood — is the next lecture.

title: 04 · Distributions and Maximum Likelihood
section: Exercises
text:
Exercises

Re-derive \(\hat\sigma^2\) for the Gaussian, including the argument that the critical point is a maximum.
Show that the Uniform MLE is \((\hat a, \hat b) = (\min_i x_i, \max_i x_i)\), and explain why calculus alone would miss it.
Derive the Gamma method-of-moments estimators from \(\mathbb{E}X = k\theta\) and \(\operatorname{Var} X = k\theta^2\).
For a single observation \(x\) from \(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma\) known, sketch the likelihood in \(\mu\). Now hold \(\mu\) known and sketch the likelihood in \(\sigma\) — is it bell-shaped? Symmetric? (This kills the “likelihood looks like a pdf” illusion outside the Gaussian-mean case.)
BCE gradient. For the Bernoulli model of the aside with a linear logit \(s_i = \theta^\top x_i\), show that \(\nabla_\theta(-\ell) = \sum_i (\pi_i - y_i)\, x_i\) — prediction error times input, the cleanest gradient in machine learning. Verify that the \(\pm 1\) logistic form gives the same gradient.
For a mixture \(\sum_i \pi_i f_i\) with component means \(\mu_i\) and variances \(\sigma_i^2\), show \(\operatorname{Var}(X) = \sum_i \pi_i \sigma_i^2 + \sum_i \pi_i (\mu_i - \bar\mu)^2\) with \(\bar\mu = \sum_i \pi_i \mu_i\) — within-component plus between-component spread. Use it to predict what \(\hat\sigma\) the single-Gaussian fit in the trap will report.

title: 05 · The Multivariate Gaussian — A Working Reference
text:
1. The definition, and the one-line reason for its shape
A standalone tutorial accompanying W03, and deliberately built as a reference rather than a narrative: the results you will keep needing, each with enough derivation to see why it is true. The organising fact is that the multivariate normal is closed under everything linear, which is why it is the only distribution this course ever propagates through a computation.
A random vector \(X \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is multivariate normal, written \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma)\), when it has density
\[
p(x) \;=\; \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2}\,(\det\Sigma)^{1/2}}
\exp\!\Big(\!-\tfrac12 (x-\mu)^{\!\top}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\Big),
\]
with \(\mu \in \mathbb{R}^d\) the mean vector and \(\Sigma\) a symmetric positive definite \(d \times d\) covariance matrix, \(\Sigma_{ij} = \operatorname{Cov}(X_i, X_j)\).
Everything in the exponent is the scalar
\[
\Delta^2(x) \;=\; (x-\mu)^{\!\top}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu),
\]
the squared Mahalanobis distance — distance from the mean, measured in units of the spread in each direction. So the density depends on \(x\) only through \(\Delta^2\), and its level sets \(\{\Delta^2 = c\}\) are ellipsoids centred at \(\mu\), with axes along the eigenvectors of \(\Sigma\) and semi-axis lengths proportional to \(\sqrt{\lambda_i}\).

title: 05 · The Multivariate Gaussian — A Working Reference
text:
NoteWhy the constant out front is what it is



\((\det\Sigma)^{1/2}\) is the volume factor of the linear map that turns a round unit ball into that ellipsoid — see §4. The \((2\pi)^{d/2}\) is \(d\) copies of the univariate \(\sqrt{2\pi}\). Neither is arbitrary; both are forced by requiring \(\int p = 1\).



What it costs to go multivariate
A single Gaussian is \(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\): two numbers. The \(d\)-dimensional version needs a mean vector and a covariance matrix, so the parameter count jumps from \(2\) to
\[
d + \binom{d+1}{2} \;=\; \frac{d(d+3)}{2},
\]
which for a \(784\)-pixel image is \(308{,}504\). Worth seeing where that growth comes from: not from the means, which contribute only \(d\), but from the covariance, which has to record how every coordinate co-varies with every other. This is the whole of the “high-dimensional density estimation is hard” problem in one line, and it is what motivates the structured and low-rank alternatives.

title: 05 · The Multivariate Gaussian — A Working Reference
section: 2. Identity covariance: the joint is a product
text:
2. Identity covariance: the joint is a product
This is the fact worth internalising first. Take \(\mu = 0\) and \(\Sigma = I\). Then \(\det I = 1\), \(I^{-1} = I\), and \(x^\top x = \sum_i x_i^2\), so
\[
p(x) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2}} e^{-\frac12 \sum_i x_i^2}
     = \prod_{i=1}^{d} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-x_i^2/2}
     = \prod_{i=1}^{d} p(x_i).
\]
The exponential turns a sum in the exponent into a product of factors, and each factor is a standard univariate normal. So \(\mathcal{N}(0, I)\) in \(d\) dimensions is nothing more than \(d\) independent standard normals stacked into a vector — there is no extra content in the multivariate object at all.
More generally, whenever \(\Sigma\) is diagonal, \(\Sigma = \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1^2,\dots,\sigma_d^2)\), the same factorisation gives \(p(x) = \prod_i \mathcal{N}(x_i; \mu_i, \sigma_i^2)\): diagonal covariance means independent coordinates.






WarningDiagonal \(\Sigma\) means independent — but only because it is Gaussian



For a general joint distribution, zero correlation does not imply independence. What makes the implication valid here is joint normality. Gaussian marginals are not enough; the pair must be jointly Gaussian.


This is also why diffusion models add \(\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I)\) noise and never worry about the dimension: isotropic Gaussian noise is per-pixel independent noise, and the \(784\)-dimensional statement is \(784\) one-dimensional statements.

title: 05 · The Multivariate Gaussian — A Working Reference
section: 4. Linear transformations, which is the whole engine
text:
4. Linear transformations, which is the whole engine
The result. If \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)\) and \(Y = AX + b\), then
\[
\boxed{\;Y \sim \mathcal{N}\big(A\mu + b,\; A\Sigma A^{\!\top}\big).\;}
\]
Why the mean and covariance are those. No normality needed for this part — it is just linearity of expectation and the definition of covariance:
\[
\mathbb{E}[Y] = A\,\mathbb{E}[X] + b = A\mu + b,
\] \[
\operatorname{Cov}(Y) = \mathbb{E}\big[(Y - A\mu - b)(\cdot)^{\!\top}\big]
= \mathbb{E}\big[A(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^{\!\top}A^{\!\top}\big] = A\Sigma A^{\!\top}.
\]
Why the result is still Gaussian. That is the content, and it deserves more than one line. The argument runs through the moment generating function, so we build that first.

The moment generating function
For a random vector \(X\) in \(\mathbb{R}^d\), define
\[
M_X(t) \;=\; \mathbb{E}\big[e^{t^{\!\top}X}\big], \qquad t \in \mathbb{R}^d .
\]
It is called moment generating because differentiating at the origin returns the moments. In one dimension, expanding \(e^{tX} = \sum_k t^k X^k / k!\) and differentiating term by term gives \(M^{(k)}(0) = \mathbb{E}[X^k]\). In \(d\) dimensions the same expansion gives
\[
\nabla M_X(0) = \mathbb{E}[X] = \mu, \qquad
\nabla^2 M_X(0) = \mathbb{E}\big[XX^{\!\top}\big] = \Sigma + \mu\mu^{\!\top} .
\]
So the MGF packages every moment into a single function of \(t\).
The property we actually need is stronger than that. It is the uniqueness theorem: if \(M_X(t) = M_Y(t)\) for all \(t\) in some open neighbourhood of the origin, then \(X\) and \(Y\) have the same distribution. The MGF does not merely summarise a law — it determines it. That is what licenses an argument of the form “compute an MGF, recognise it, conclude”.






WarningOne caveat, stated honestly



The MGF characterises a distribution when it exists in a neighbourhood of \(0\), and not every distribution has one — \(\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]\) is infinite for all \(t \ne 0\) for a Cauchy, and for all \(t > 0\) for a lognormal. The fix is the characteristic function \(\varphi_X(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{i t^{\!\top}X}]\), which exists for every distribution because \(|e^{i\theta}| = 1\), and which satisfies the same uniqueness theorem. Every argument below goes through verbatim with \(\varphi\) in place of \(M\) and \(it\) in place of \(t\). For the Gaussian the MGF exists for all \(t \in \mathbb{R}^d\), so we may use the simpler object.




The MGF of a Gaussian
Take the scalar case first, \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\):
\[
M_X(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{tx}\,
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\, e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2\sigma^2}\, dx .
\]
Everything is in the exponent, so complete the square there. Writing the two terms over a common denominator and grouping,
\[
tx - \frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}
\;=\;
\underbrace{\mu t + \tfrac12 \sigma^2 t^2}_{\text{free of } x}
\;-\; \frac{\big(x - \mu - \sigma^2 t\big)^2}{2\sigma^2} .
\]
(Multiply out both sides to check it; the cross terms are what force the \(\tfrac12\sigma^2t^2\).) The first part comes outside the integral, and what is left is a Gaussian density with mean \(\mu + \sigma^2 t\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), which integrates to \(1\). Hence
\[
\boxed{\;M_X(t) = \exp\!\Big(\mu t + \tfrac12 \sigma^2 t^2\Big).\;}
\]
Note the shape: the exponent is a quadratic in \(t\). Everything that follows is a consequence of that one fact.
Now \(d\) dimensions. For \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_d)\) the coordinates are independent standard normals, so the expectation factorises:
\[
M_{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}(t) = \mathbb{E}\Big[\textstyle\prod_i e^{t_i \varepsilon_i}\Big]
= \prod_i \mathbb{E}\big[e^{t_i \varepsilon_i}\big]
= \prod_i e^{t_i^2/2}
= e^{\frac12 t^{\!\top}t} .
\]
For general \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)\), factor \(\Sigma = LL^{\!\top}\) and substitute \(x = \mu + Lu\) in the defining integral. The Jacobian is the constant \(\det L\), which cancels against the \((\det\Sigma)^{1/2} = |\det L|\) in the normalising constant, and the quadratic form becomes \(u^{\!\top}u\). What remains is the standard-normal integral evaluated at \(L^{\!\top}t\):
\[
M_X(t) = e^{t^{\!\top}\mu}\, M_{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}\big(L^{\!\top}t\big)
= e^{t^{\!\top}\mu}\, e^{\frac12 (L^{\!\top}t)^{\!\top}(L^{\!\top}t)}
= \exp\!\Big(t^{\!\top}\mu + \tfrac12 t^{\!\top}LL^{\!\top}t\Big),
\]
so
\[
\boxed{\;M_X(t) = \exp\!\Big(t^{\!\top}\mu + \tfrac12\, t^{\!\top}\Sigma\, t\Big).\;}
\]
This is a change of variables inside an integral, not an appeal to the affine theorem — so there is no circularity in using it to prove that theorem next.


The affine theorem, one step at a time
Compute the MGF of \(Y = AX + b\) and see what it turns out to be.
\[
M_Y(t) \;=\; \mathbb{E}\big[e^{t^{\!\top}Y}\big]
\;=\; \mathbb{E}\big[e^{t^{\!\top}(AX+b)}\big]
\qquad\text{(definition, then substitute } Y)
\]
\[
=\; e^{t^{\!\top}b}\; \mathbb{E}\big[e^{t^{\!\top}AX}\big]
\qquad\text{($b$ is constant, so } e^{t^{\!\top}b} \text{ leaves the expectation)}
\]
\[
=\; e^{t^{\!\top}b}\; \mathbb{E}\big[e^{(A^{\!\top}t)^{\!\top}X}\big]
\qquad\text{(since } t^{\!\top}A = (A^{\!\top}t)^{\!\top})
\]
That third line is the move that makes the whole thing work: the matrix has been pushed off the random vector and onto the argument of the MGF. The expectation is now \(M_X\) evaluated at the point \(A^{\!\top}t\), and we know \(M_X\):
\[
=\; e^{t^{\!\top}b}\, \exp\!\Big((A^{\!\top}t)^{\!\top}\mu
+ \tfrac12 (A^{\!\top}t)^{\!\top}\Sigma\,(A^{\!\top}t)\Big)
\qquad\text{(apply the Gaussian MGF)}
\]
\[
=\; \exp\!\Big(t^{\!\top}b + t^{\!\top}\!A\mu
+ \tfrac12\, t^{\!\top}\!A\Sigma A^{\!\top} t\Big)
\qquad\text{(transpose each piece)}
\]
\[
=\; \exp\!\Big(t^{\!\top}\big(A\mu + b\big)
+ \tfrac12\, t^{\!\top}\big(A\Sigma A^{\!\top}\big) t\Big)
\qquad\text{(collect the linear terms)}
\]
Now read the answer. It has the form \(\exp\big(t^{\!\top}m + \tfrac12
t^{\!\top}S\,t\big)\) — a linear term plus a quadratic term, which is precisely the shape of a Gaussian MGF, with \(m = A\mu+b\) and \(S = A\Sigma A^{\!\top}\). By the uniqueness theorem, a distribution with that MGF is \(\mathcal{N}(A\mu+b,
A\Sigma A^{\!\top})\). \(\square\)
What made it work. A Gaussian MGF is the exponential of a quadratic in \(t\). Substituting \(A^{\!\top}t\) into a quadratic yields another quadratic — that is the entire mechanism, and it is why the family is closed. Push a distribution whose MGF is not the exponential of a quadratic through the same steps and you land on a function of a different shape, which is a different family. Closure under linear maps is not a lucky property of the Gaussian; it is a restatement of the fact that its log-MGF is quadratic.
Sampling and whitening are this result, read in the two directions. Factor \(\Sigma = LL^{\!\top}\) (Cholesky, or \(\Sigma^{1/2}\) from the eigendecomposition). Then

forward, \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I) \Rightarrow \mu + L\boldsymbol\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, LL^{\!\top}) = \mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)\) — this is how you sample any Gaussian from standard noise;
backward, \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma) \Rightarrow L^{-1}(X-\mu) \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)\) — this is whitening, and it is why one can always assume \(\mathcal{N}(0,I)\) without loss of generality.







TipThe reason this family and no other



Almost every operation in this course is linear: adding noise, taking a weighted average of a signal and noise, projecting, marginalising. The Gaussian family is closed under all of them, with the parameters transforming by a rule you can compute in closed form. Push almost any other family through a linear map and you leave the family and lose the closed form. That closure is the entire reason diffusion models are analytically tractable.


Degenerate case. If \(A\) has rank \(< d\) then \(A\Sigma A^{\!\top}\) is singular, \(\det = 0\), and the density formula of §1 breaks down — the law is still Gaussian, but it is concentrated on a lower-dimensional subspace and has no density with respect to Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb{R}^m\). The demo’s singular preset shows the cloud collapsing to a line.

title: 05 · The Multivariate Gaussian — A Working Reference
section: 5. Marginals and conditionals
text:
5. Marginals and conditionals
Split \(X\) into blocks, and \(\mu, \Sigma\) to match:
\[
X = \begin{pmatrix} X_1 \\ X_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\mu = \begin{pmatrix} \mu_1 \\ \mu_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} \Sigma_{11} & \Sigma_{12} \\ \Sigma_{21} & \Sigma_{22}\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Marginal. \(X_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_1, \Sigma_{11})\). Note how easy this is: you delete the blocks belonging to \(X_2\). No integration is needed, because marginalising is the linear map \(X \mapsto \begin{pmatrix} I & 0\end{pmatrix}X\), and §4 already tells you the answer.
Conditional.
\[
X_1 \mid X_2 = x_2 \;\sim\;
\mathcal{N}\Big(\underbrace{\mu_1 + \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}(x_2 - \mu_2)}_{\text{mean moves linearly in } x_2},\;
\underbrace{\Sigma_{11} - \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}\Sigma_{21}}_{\text{variance does not depend on } x_2}\Big).
\]
Two features are worth pausing on, because they are unusual and the course leans on both. The conditional mean is a linear function of what you observed — so the best predictor of \(X_1\) from \(X_2\) is linear, which is why linear regression is exactly right under joint normality and only an approximation otherwise. And the conditional variance does not depend on the observed value at all: you learn the same amount whatever \(x_2\) turns out to be.
In two dimensions with correlation \(\rho\) this reduces to: \(Y \mid X = x \sim \mathcal{N}(\rho x,\, 1-\rho^2)\) for standard marginals.

title: 05 · The Multivariate Gaussian — A Working Reference
section: 6. Sums, and why noise accumulates the way it does
text:
6. Sums, and why noise accumulates the way it does
If \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)\) and \(Y \sim \mathcal{N}(\nu,T)\) are independent, then \(X + Y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu+\nu,\ \Sigma+T)\): means add, covariances add. (Independence is essential — without it the covariance of the sum picks up cross terms, \(\Sigma + T + \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y) + \operatorname{Cov}(Y,X)\).)
This is the whole of the course’s forward process. With \(x_0\) fixed and \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)\),
\[
x_\sigma = x_0 + \sigma \boldsymbol\varepsilon \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(x_0,\ \sigma^2 I),
\]
and composing two such steps gives \(\mathcal{N}(x_0, (\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2)I)\): variances add, standard deviations do not. Noise accumulates like \(\sqrt{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2}\), which is the \(\sqrt{t}\) envelope of W01.

section: Exercises

Exercises

Verify directly from the density that \(\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I_d)\) factorises into \(d\) independent \(\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)\) coordinates. Where exactly does the argument use that \(\Sigma\) is diagonal?
Let \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_2)\) and \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\). Compute the law of \(AX\). Sketch its one-\(\sigma\) ellipse and check it against Act II of the demo.
Show that if \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)\) then \(a^{\!\top}X\) is univariate normal for every fixed \(a\), using §4 with \(A = a^{\!\top}\). Then explain why the converse (used as a definition of multivariate normality) is a strictly stronger statement than “every coordinate is normal”.
For the bivariate case with \(\mu = 0\), \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = 1\) and correlation \(\rho\), derive the conditional \(Y \mid X = x\) from the block formula of §5 and confirm you get \(\mathcal{N}(\rho x, 1-\rho^2)\).
Two independent noising steps of size \(\sigma_1\) then \(\sigma_2\) are applied to a fixed \(x_0\). Show the result is the same in law as one step of size \(\sqrt{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2}\). Why does this fail if the two noises are correlated?
(Degeneracy.) Take \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I_2)\). Compute \(A\Sigma A^{\!\top}\), show it is singular, and describe where the resulting law actually lives. Why does the density formula of §1 not apply?
(Entropy.) Using \(h(X) = \tfrac12\log((2\pi e)^d \det\Sigma)\), show that an affine map \(X \mapsto AX + b\) with \(A\) square and invertible changes the entropy by exactly \(\log|\det A|\) — and explain why \(b\) does not appear.

title: 06 · Estimating a Density in Many Dimensions
text:
1. The estimator, and its three-line derivation
We know what a multivariate Gaussian is. Now fit one. The maximum likelihood estimator is the sample covariance and the derivation is three lines — and then it collapses, because in almost every application that matters there are fewer samples than variables. This note is about what you do next: impose structure, estimate the inverse rather than the thing itself, and watch every classical method run into the same wall. It ends with the honest verdict on why an entire decade of statistics could not solve this and deep learning did.
Let \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) be i.i.d. draws from \(\mathcal{N}_p(\mu,\Sigma)\). The log-likelihood is
\[
\ell(\mu,\Sigma) = -\frac{n}{2}\log\det\Sigma
- \frac12 \sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\mu)^{\!\top}\Sigma^{-1}(x_i-\mu) + \text{const}.
\]
Differentiating in \(\mu\) gives \(\hat\mu = \bar x\), exactly as in one dimension. For \(\Sigma\) the clean route is to reparametrise by the precision matrix \(\Theta = \Sigma^{-1}\) and use the trace trick — a scalar equals its own trace, and the trace is cyclic:
\[
\sum_i (x_i-\bar x)^{\!\top}\Theta(x_i-\bar x)
= \sum_i \operatorname{tr}\!\big(\Theta (x_i-\bar x)(x_i-\bar x)^{\!\top}\big)
= n\operatorname{tr}(\Theta S),
\]
where
\[
S = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar x)(x_i - \bar x)^{\!\top}
\]
is the sample covariance. The log-likelihood becomes, up to constants,
\[
\boxed{\;\ell(\Theta) = \frac{n}{2}\Big(\log\det\Theta - \operatorname{tr}(S\Theta)\Big).\;}
\]
This is concave in \(\Theta\) (\(\log\det\) is concave on positive definite matrices, the trace term is linear), so setting the gradient to zero is enough. Using \(\partial \log\det\Theta/\partial\Theta = \Theta^{-1}\) and \(\partial \operatorname{tr}(S\Theta)/\partial\Theta = S\):
\[
\Theta^{-1} - S = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \hat\Sigma = S .
\]
The MLE of the covariance is the sample covariance, with divisor \(n\) rather than \(n-1\) — biased, exactly as in the univariate case. And since maximum likelihood is invariant under reparametrisation, the MLE of the correlation matrix is the sample correlation matrix: standardise \(S\) by its own diagonal.
Two things to notice, because both matter in a moment. The likelihood depends on the data only through \(\bar x\) and \(S\) — they are sufficient. And written in \(\Theta\), the problem is a concave maximisation, which is what will later let us bolt a penalty onto it and still have something solvable.
