Marginal score \(\partial_x\log p_t(x)\)
Converted from the noise predictor



Using \(b_n\) for a variance and \(\beta(t)\) for a rate avoids treating them as interchangeable. We retain \(\alpha_t\) for an amplitude throughout; it is not Ho’s one-step retention \(1-\beta_n\).


Where is the score in this forward process?
The forward corruption does not need the score. Its contraction and noise are prescribed. Their purpose is to supply a tractable density path and supervised training pairs.
The score becomes necessary when we want to generate data by reversing the progression of densities. It describes how the current noisy distribution depends on position. At a late time the distribution is simple; nearer the data it becomes increasingly structured. A time-conditioned network will estimate all these scores.

title: 15 · From Score to Sampling
section: 4. Small forward steps give the VP SDE
text:
4. Small forward steps give the VP SDE
Let \(h_n=t_n-t_{n-1}\) and take \(b_n=\beta(t_{n-1})h_n+O(h_n^2)\) for a smooth nonnegative rate. Expanding \(\sqrt{1-b_n}\) gives
\[X_{t_n}-X_{t_{n-1}}
\approx-\frac{\beta(t_{n-1})}{2}X_{t_{n-1}}h_n
+\sqrt{\beta(t_{n-1})h_n}\,Z_n.\]
The first term is proportional to elapsed time; the random term is proportional to its square root. These are the drift and Brownian increment of
\[\boxed{dX_t=-\frac{\beta(t)}2X_t\,dt+\sqrt{\beta(t)}\,dW_t.}\]
This is the variance-preserving SDE. Its conditional distribution remains Gaussian:
\[\alpha_t=\exp\left(-\frac12\int_0^t\beta(u)\,du\right),
\qquad \sigma_t^2=1-\alpha_t^2,
\qquad X_t=\alpha_tX_0+\sigma_t\varepsilon.\]
Equivalently, \(\beta(t)=-2\,d\log\alpha_t/dt\). Thus the rate in the SDE and the amplitudes in the training examples describe the same schedule. Appendix B derives the relation from the discrete chain. On a grid, choosing
\[b_n=1-\exp\left(-\int_{t_{n-1}}^{t_n}\beta(u)\,du\right)\]
makes the discrete conditional transition agree exactly with this linear SDE’s forward transition.






NoteWhat “variance preserving” and the terminal Gaussian mean



If \(X_0\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\), the forward VP process preserves that law. For arbitrary data, its variance need not remain constant. In fact,
\[\operatorname{Var}(X_t)=\alpha_t^2\operatorname{Var}(X_0)+1-\alpha_t^2.\]
With a finite integrated rate, \(\alpha_1>0\), so the terminal law generally retains a small data contribution. Starting generation from \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) is then an approximation to \(p_1\). Exact Gaussian termination for arbitrary data requires a limiting construction; we do not assume it for a finite schedule.



An SDE drift is not the whole transport velocity
The forward SDE has drift \(f(x,t)=-\beta(t)x/2\). But that drift alone does not describe its density evolution: the random increments also spread probability. To construct a deterministic ODE with the same density path, we must account for both effects. This is where the score enters the probability-flow velocity.

title: 15 · From Score to Sampling
section: 5. The same density path gives two reverse sampling dynamics
text:
5. The same density path gives two reverse sampling dynamics
For a general scalar forward SDE
\[dX_t=f(X_t,t)\,dt+g(t)\,dW_t,\]
the density evolves according to the Fokker–Planck equation:
\[\partial_t p_t=-\partial_x(f p_t)+\frac12g(t)^2\partial_x^2p_t.\]
The first term describes drift transport. The second describes random spreading. A deterministic ODE \(\dot x=v(x,t)\) instead has the continuity equation
\[\partial_t p_t=-\partial_x(p_tv).\]
Since \(\partial_xp_t=p_ts_t\), rewrite Fokker–Planck as
\[\partial_t p_t=-\partial_x\left[p_t\left(f-\frac12g^2s_t\right)\right].\]
We have identified the deterministic probability-flow velocity:
\[\boxed{v(x,t)=f(x,t)-\frac12g(t)^2s_t(x).}\]
For VP, this is \(v(x,t)=-\beta(t)[x+s_t(x)]/2\). It moves the density forward when integrated from zero to one. Integrating the same ODE toward decreasing \(t\) gives generation.

Put both reverse samplers on an increasing clock
To keep signs unambiguous, define the sampling clock \(\tau=1-t\) and write \(Y_\tau\) for the current generated particle. As \(\tau\) increases, the corruption time \(t\) decreases.







Dynamics
Equation in the increasing sampling clock, with \(t=1-\tau\)




Reverse SDE
\(dY_\tau=[-f(Y_\tau,t)+g(t)^2s_t(Y_\tau)]\,d\tau+g(t)\,d\overline W_\tau\)


Probability-flow ODE
\(dY_\tau/d\tau=-f(Y_\tau,t)+\tfrac12g(t)^2s_t(Y_\tau)\)



The reverse-SDE equation is a time-reversal result, stated here under the usual smoothness and density assumptions. It is not obtained by just negating the forward drift. Appendix C verifies that its density evolves along the same reversed path.
For the VP construction the two equations become
\[\boxed{dY_\tau=\beta(t)\left[\frac{Y_\tau}{2}+s_t(Y_\tau)\right]d\tau
+\sqrt{\beta(t)}\,d\overline W_\tau,}\]
\[\boxed{\frac{dY_\tau}{d\tau}=\frac{\beta(t)}2\left[Y_\tau+s_t(Y_\tau)\right].}\]
With the exact score and correct initial law \(Y_0\sim p_1\), their one-time densities agree: \(Y_\tau\sim p_{1-\tau}\). Their trajectories and joint distributions across times differ. Learned scores, finite numerical steps, and an approximate terminal prior can all cause discrepancies in practice.


Why merely removing the noise is wrong
Removing the Brownian increment from the reverse SDE leaves drift \(\beta(t)[x/2+s_t(x)]\). The probability-flow drift is \(\beta(t)[x+s_t(x)]/2\). The score coefficient must also change.
A standard Gaussian checks this immediately. Its score is \(-x\) at every time under VP. The probability-flow velocity is zero, so Gaussian particles stay where they are. The reverse SDE is an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process with drift \(-\beta x/2\) and noise amplitude \(\sqrt\beta\); the Gaussian is stationary. Removing its noise alone would instead contract the particles to zero.

title: 15 · From Score to Sampling
section: 6. Turn the dynamics into algorithms
text:
6. Turn the dynamics into algorithms
At the current corruption time \(t=t_n\), choose a positive backward step \(h_n=t_n-t_{n-1}\). Suppose we can evaluate \(s_\theta(x,t)\).

Deterministic sampler: Euler for the probability-flow ODE
Euler evaluates the velocity at the current particle and takes a short step:
\[\boxed{x_{t_{n-1}}=x_{t_n}+\frac{h_n\beta(t_n)}2
\left[x_{t_n}+s_\theta(x_{t_n},t_n)\right].}\]
The initial draw is random, but no new noise is added during this recursion. This is explicit Euler integrated backward in corruption time, not the implicit numerical method called backward Euler.


Stochastic sampler: Euler–Maruyama for the reverse SDE
The reverse SDE gives
\[\boxed{x_{t_{n-1}}=x_{t_n}+h_n\beta(t_n)
\left[\frac{x_{t_n}}2+s_\theta(x_{t_n},t_n)\right]
+\sqrt{h_n\beta(t_n)}\,z_n,}\]
where each \(z_n\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) is independent. Both this update and the ODE update use the score at the current time and position. They differ in the score coefficient and the presence of new Gaussian noise.


DDPM ancestral sampling is another discretization of the stochastic route
The one-step forward observation is \(X_{t_n}=\sqrt{1-b_n}X_{t_{n-1}}+\sqrt{b_n}Z_n\). Gaussian denoising gives \(\sqrt{1-b_n}\,\mathbb E[X_{t_{n-1}}\mid X_{t_n}=x]=x+b_ns_t(x)\), the single-step form of the identity derived in Section 7. Thus the score determines the reverse conditional mean. Ho’s parameterization replaces it by the learned score:
\[\mu_\theta(x,t_n)=\frac1{\sqrt{1-b_n}}
\left[x-\frac{b_n}{\sigma_{t_n}}\varepsilon_\theta(x,t_n)\right]
=\frac{x+b_ns_\theta(x,t_n)}{\sqrt{1-b_n}}.\]
The ancestral update samples from a modeled Gaussian reverse transition:
\[\boxed{x_{t_{n-1}}=\mu_\theta(x_{t_n},t_n)+\sqrt{\nu_n}\,z_n.}\]
Two fixed reverse-variance choices are \(\nu_n=b_n\) and \(\nu_n=\widetilde b_n=b_n\sigma_{t_{n-1}}^2/\sigma_{t_n}^2\). Ho’s sampling algorithm sets \(z_1=0\) at the final data step. This endpoint convention is separate from the interior reverse transitions.
For an interior step with standard Gaussian marginals, the exact score is \(-x\), so this mean becomes \(\sqrt{1-b_n}x\). Recurring with only that mean reduces variance from 1 to \(1-b_n\). Adding independent noise with variance \(b_n\) restores variance 1. The noise accounts for reverse conditional uncertainty; it is not an arbitrary perturbation added after denoising.
To see the SDE connection, first use \(\nu_n=b_n\) and expand the mean:
\[\frac{x+b_ns_\theta}{\sqrt{1-b_n}}
=x+b_n\left(\frac x2+s_\theta\right)+O(b_n^2).\]
With \(b_n=\beta(t_n)h_n+O(h_n^2)\), this has the leading drift of reverse-SDE Euler–Maruyama. Its noise variance also has the required leading term \(\beta(t_n)h_n\). The posterior-variance choice has the same limit on intervals bounded away from zero noise. Endpoint behavior needs separate care.
Thus DDPM and reverse-SDE Euler–Maruyama share a continuous limit; their finite updates need not be identical. The \(O(h_n^2)\) comparison concerns conditional means and variances, not a claim of second-order stochastic trajectory accuracy. Song et al.’s Appendix E develops this correspondence. The Gaussian reverse kernel is a modeling/small-step approximation for general data, even when its conditional mean is exact.


What happens to the DDIM noise term?
Deterministic DDIM is another discretization of the probability-flow route, using transformed coordinates rather than the direct Euler step above. The DDIM paper first gives a generalized update with fresh Gaussian noise, then sets its step-noise coefficient to zero in Section 4.1 after Eq. (12); Eq. (16) denotes this choice by \(\eta=0\). It is not obtained by deleting the noise from Ho’s ancestral update while keeping Ho’s mean. We keep DDIM’s derivation outside the main recipe here so that the two primary routes remain distinguishable.

title: 15 · From Score to Sampling
section: 7. Train the score using the same denoising regression as DDPM
text:
7. Train the score using the same denoising regression as DDPM
We have constructed the samplers assuming a score. Now we supply the missing function. At a selected time, form
\[X_t=\alpha_tX_0+\sigma_t\varepsilon,
\qquad X_0\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\quad\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,1).\]
The conditional score of this Gaussian observation is known:
\[U_t=\partial_x\log p_t(x\mid X_0)\big|_{x=X_t}
=-\frac{X_t-\alpha_tX_0}{\sigma_t^2}
=-\frac{\varepsilon}{\sigma_t}.\]
The training target \(U_t\) depends on the sampled clean/noisy pair. The network receives only \((X_t,t)\), so it cannot generally recover the particular \(X_0\) or \(\varepsilon\) used for every pair. Squared-error regression averages the possible labels conditional on those inputs.

Why conditional-score labels learn the marginal score
At a fixed positive time, differentiate the noisy marginal density:
\[\begin{aligned}
p_t(x)&=\int p_t(x\mid x_0)p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_0)\,dx_0,\\
\partial_x\log p_t(x)
&=\int \partial_x\log p_t(x\mid x_0)
\frac{p_t(x\mid x_0)p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_0)}{p_t(x)}\,dx_0\\
&=\int \partial_x\log p_t(x\mid x_0)p(x_0\mid X_t=x)\,dx_0\\
&=\mathbb E[U_t\mid X_t=x].
\end{aligned}\]
The posterior appears in this proof, but we never have to evaluate it during training. Drawing clean observations and independent noise supplies samples from their joint law. The regression identity
\[\mathbb E[(s_\theta(X_t,t)-U_t)^2\mid X_t,t]
=(s_\theta(X_t,t)-s_t(X_t))^2+\operatorname{Var}(U_t\mid X_t,t)\]
shows that the unknown conditional-variance term cannot affect the optimal predictor. This is why a known conditional score is a valid target for learning the unknown marginal score.


Noise prediction is a scaled version of this regression
Set \(s_\theta(x,t)=-\varepsilon_\theta(x,t)/\sigma_t\). Then, for each training time,
\[\boxed{(\varepsilon_\theta(X_t,t)-\varepsilon)^2
=\sigma_t^2\left(s_\theta(X_t,t)+\frac{\varepsilon}{\sigma_t}\right)^2.}\]
Unweighted noise prediction is score regression weighted by \(\sigma_t^2\). It avoids training directly against targets whose scale grows as \(1/\sigma_t\) near the clean endpoint. It does not mean the network knows the noise realization; its unrestricted optimum is the posterior mean
\[\varepsilon_*(x,t)=\mathbb E[\varepsilon\mid X_t=x],\qquad
s_t(x)=-\frac{\varepsilon_*(x,t)}{\sigma_t}.\]
Ho’s simplified DDPM loss uses a uniformly sampled discrete index:
\[\mathcal L_{\mathrm{DDPM}}=
\mathbb E_{\substack{n\sim\mathrm{Unif}\{1,\ldots,N\}\\X_0\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\ \varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,1)}}
\left[(\varepsilon_\theta(\alpha_{t_n}X_0+\sigma_{t_n}\varepsilon,t_n)-\varepsilon)^2\right].\]
The analogous continuous-time noise loss replaces \(n\) by an independently drawn \(t\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)\) and uses the continuous schedule. Song’s general score objective additionally permits a positive time weight \(\lambda(t)\). Choosing \(\lambda(t)=\sigma_t^2\) recovers the noise-prediction weighting above.
That is the precise meaning of almost the same training: the corruption and regression target can coincide, while the time distribution and loss weighting may differ. Positive time-only weights preserve the unrestricted pointwise optimum, but affect how a finite network allocates its capacity. A network trained only at integer steps also needs an explicit continuous time-conditioning or interpolation rule before off-grid ODE evaluations are justified. The original weighted ELBO loss is not numerically identical to Ho’s simplified noise loss.


The denoising interpretation through Tweedie’s formula
Since \(\varepsilon=(X_t-\alpha_tX_0)/\sigma_t\), conditional averaging gives
\[\boxed{D_*(x,t):=\mathbb E[X_0\mid X_t=x]
=\frac{x+\sigma_t^2s_t(x)}{\alpha_t}.}\]
For \(\alpha_t>0\) and \(\sigma_t>0\), the posterior-mean denoiser, noise predictor, and score are interchangeable descriptions of the same conditional information. The score itself is the scaled displacement \((\alpha_tD_*(x,t)-x)/\sigma_t^2\), not the posterior mean alone. The sampler uses this information locally over many times; a single denoising mean is not generally a sample from the clean distribution.

title: 15 · From Score to Sampling
section: 8. Solve one complete example before training a network
text:
8. Solve one complete example before training a network
Take
\[X_0\sim\mathcal N(2,0.25),\qquad\beta(t)=8.\]
The cumulative amplitudes are \(\alpha_t=e^{-4t}\) and \(\sigma_t^2=1-e^{-8t}\). Gaussian addition gives
\[p_t=\mathcal N(m_t,V_t),\qquad
m_t=2\alpha_t,\qquad V_t=0.25\alpha_t^2+\sigma_t^2.\]
Here \(V_t\) is the marginal variance, whereas \(\sigma_t^2\) is the conditional corruption variance. They are not the same. The exact marginal score and optimal noise predictor are
\[s_t(x)=-\frac{x-m_t}{V_t},\qquad
\varepsilon_*(x,t)=\frac{\sigma_t(x-m_t)}{V_t}.\]
Insert this score into either update in Section 6. No training is needed for this check. At time one,
\[p_1\approx\mathcal N(0.0366,0.99975),\]
which is close to, but not exactly, the standard Gaussian.

An exact ODE solution is available for verification
For a constant standardized label \(z\), the trajectory
\[x_t=m_t+\sqrt{V_t}\,z\]
satisfies the probability-flow ODE. Thus integrating from time one to zero gives the exact transport
\[\boxed{x_0=2+\sqrt{\frac{0.25}{V_1}}(x_1-m_1).}\]
If \(x_1\sim p_1\), the result has exactly the required data law. Starting instead from \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) gives a slightly different law even with an exact integrator. This separates terminal-prior error from numerical error.






Figure 2: Top: the known forward density path. Bottom: DDPM ancestral sampling, reverse-SDE Euler–Maruyama, and probability-flow Euler use the same analytic score. All are initialized from the exact terminal law for this diagnostic, isolating numerical error. There are 12,000 particles and 2,000 steps per sampler.



The reproducible simulation script contains all three samplers and generates both figures. It checks sampled moments against the exact finite-grid recurrences, verifies improvement under grid refinement, and compares ODE trajectories with the closed-form transport. Saved numerical checks record the results. This experiment verifies the equations and solvers; it is not a trained-model performance claim.

title: 15 · From Score to Sampling
section: 9. Assemble training and inference into one implementation
text:
9. Assemble training and inference into one implementation
The analytic example supplies an exact noise predictor. For unknown data, replace it with a neural network and train it using the regression in Section 7. Every other component remains prescribed.

Training algorithm
Inputs: clean observations, one consistent schedule \((\alpha_t,\sigma_t,\beta(t))\), and a time-conditioned noise predictor \(\varepsilon_\theta\).
Repeat for each training minibatch:
    Select clean observations x0 from the training set.
    Select times t independently (grid indices for DDPM, continuous times for an ODE model).
    Draw independent standard Gaussian noise epsilon.
    Form xt = alpha(t) * x0 + sigma(t) * epsilon.
    Predict epsilon_hat = network(xt, t).
    Compute mean squared error between epsilon_hat and epsilon.
    Update the network parameters using the gradient of this loss.
The network must receive time because the same observation value has different scores at different noise levels. Training needs neither reverse trajectories nor an ODE solve. A minibatch element supplies one independently selected time, not an entire forward trajectory.
For example, the continuous-time loss for a batch in PyTorch is:
# x0: a batch of scalar observations; noise_net(xt, t) returns the same shape.
# beta(t)=8, matching the example and the inference schedule below.
t = torch.rand_like(x0).clamp(min=1e-5, max=1 - 1e-5)
epsilon = torch.randn_like(x0)
alpha = torch.exp(-4 * t)
sigma = torch.sqrt(-torch.expm1(-8 * t))
xt = alpha * x0 + sigma * epsilon
loss = ((noise_net(xt, t) - epsilon) ** 2).mean()
optimizer.zero_grad()
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()
The small clipping interval is a numerical implementation choice that excludes the zero-noise endpoint. It slightly changes the time distribution. For images, draw one time per image and broadcast its amplitudes over pixels; replace scalar squared error by a sum or mean over coordinates.


Inference algorithm: choose the update after training
Draw x from a standard Gaussian reference.
For grid times t descending from 1 toward 0:
    Evaluate epsilon_hat = network(x, t).
    Convert to s = -epsilon_hat / sigma(t).

    Probability-flow ODE:
        x = x + h * beta(t) / 2 * (x + s).

    OR reverse-SDE Euler–Maruyama:
        draw a new standard Gaussian z;
        x = x + h * beta(t) * (x / 2 + s) + sqrt(h * beta(t)) * z.

    OR DDPM ancestral:
        use the matching discrete variance b;
        draw z, except use z=0 at the final step;
        x = (x + b * s) / sqrt(1-b) + sqrt(reverse_variance) * z.
Return the resulting approximate data sample.
Use one chosen update throughout a run. The standard Gaussian initialization approximates \(p_1\) for the finite VP schedule. In the analytic verification, replace it by a draw from the known exact \(p_1\).
All score evaluations occur at positive current times; there is no division by \(\sigma_0=0\). For data with a singular clean law or an unreliable learned endpoint, stop at a small positive time. A final posterior-mean denoising step is an optional additional approximation and changes the output distribution; it is not an exact replacement for the remaining transport.
For a complete learned example beyond the analytic check, the existing mixture training notebook implements training and inference with a small network. The recipe above is the same separation of tasks.

title: 15 · From Score to Sampling
section: 10. Reassemble the argument
text:
10. Reassemble the argument







Question
Answer supplied by this tutorial




What do we want?
New samples from a data distribution.


What distributional information will we learn?
The marginal score at each noise level.


Where do noisy distributions come from?
A prescribed contraction-plus-Gaussian-noise construction.


What is its continuous limit?
The forward VP SDE.


What labels can we compute?
The injected noise, equivalently the conditional Gaussian score.


Why do these labels recover the needed score?
Regression takes the conditional expectation of the target given the noisy input.


What changes between DDPM and probability flow?
The reverse dynamics and numerical sampling rule.


What is shared?
The forward density path, schedule, and compatible denoising predictor.


Where can approximation enter?
The learned predictor, terminal prior, reverse-kernel model, and finite integration steps.



A final check is to explain the standard Gaussian case without looking at the equations. Its score is \(-x\). Langevin needs noise to maintain its spread. The forward VP process preserves it. The reverse VP SDE also preserves it. Its probability-flow ODE has zero velocity. These facts would be inconsistent if we treated every appearance of the score as the same sampling rule.

Questions to answer before implementing a new sampler

Does time zero denote data or noise in this implementation?
Is the schedule parameter a one-step variance, a continuous rate, or a cumulative amplitude?
Is the network predicting noise, a clean posterior mean, or the score? What conversion is required?
Does the chosen update use the reverse-SDE score coefficient or the probability-flow coefficient?
Are the terminal law and score known exactly, or are we testing approximations to them?

title: 15 · From Score to Sampling
section: Appendix A. Langevin stationarity and its finite-step Gaussian bias
text:
Appendix A. Langevin stationarity and its finite-step Gaussian bias
For Langevin, the Fokker–Planck equation is
\[\partial_\tau q_\tau=-\partial_x(q_\tau s)+\partial_x^2q_\tau.\]
At the proposed stationary density \(q_\tau=p\), substituting \(s=p'/p\) gives
\[-\partial_x(p s)+\partial_x^2p=-p''+p''=0.\]
With suitable boundary behavior this establishes invariance. It does not by itself establish convergence from every starting distribution. For the standard Gaussian, the SDE is \(dX_\tau=-X_\tau d\tau+\sqrt2dW_\tau\). Its mean and variance obey
\[m'=-m,\qquad V'=-2V+2,\]
so \(m(\tau)=e^{-\tau}m(0)\) and \(V(\tau)=1+e^{-2\tau}(V(0)-1)\). This explicitly shows convergence of Gaussian initial laws.
The Euler–Maruyama chain is instead \(x_{k+1}=(1-\eta)x_k+\sqrt{2\eta}z_k\). For \(0<\eta<2\), its stationary variance solves
\[V=(1-\eta)^2V+2\eta
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad V=\frac1{1-\eta/2}.\]
At the figure’s step \(\eta=0.02\), this is about \(1.0101\). That discrepancy is a solver effect even with a perfect score.

title: 15 · From Score to Sampling
section: Appendix B. From discrete contraction to the cumulative schedule
text:
Appendix B. From discrete contraction to the cumulative schedule
For one step, expand the coefficient:
\[\sqrt{1-b_n}=1-\frac12b_n+O(b_n^2).\]
With \(b_n=\beta(t_{n-1})h_n+O(h_n^2)\), the conditional increment has mean \(-\beta(t_{n-1})x h_n/2+O(h_n^2)\) and variance \(\beta(t_{n-1})h_n+O(h_n^2)\). These identify the VP SDE’s drift and diffusion variance.
Across steps, the clean-data coefficient is \(\prod_j\sqrt{1-b_j}\). Therefore
\[\log\alpha_{t_n}=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^n\log(1-b_j)
\longrightarrow-\frac12\int_0^{t_n}\beta(u)\,du.\]
The conditional noise variance follows a recursion. If it is \(S_{n-1}\) before the next step, then
\[S_n=(1-b_n)S_{n-1}+b_n,\qquad S_0=0.\]
Consequently \(1-S_n=(1-b_n)(1-S_{n-1})=\prod_{j=1}^n(1-b_j)\), giving \(S_n=1-\alpha_{t_n}^2\). The limiting Gaussian conditional law has variance \(1-\alpha_t^2\). This derivation also explains why independently choosing incompatible formulas for \(\alpha_t\) and \(\beta(t)\) would train and sample different paths.

title: 15 · From Score to Sampling
section: Appendix C. Check the reverse density evolution and the factor of two
text:
Appendix C. Check the reverse density evolution and the factor of two
For the forward SDE, write
\[\partial_t p_t=-\partial_x(fp_t)+\frac12g^2\partial_x^2p_t.\]
The desired reverse-clock density is \(r_\tau(x)=p_{1-\tau}(x)\). It must satisfy
\[\partial_\tau r_\tau=\partial_x(fr_\tau)-\frac12g^2\partial_x^2r_\tau,\]
with coefficients evaluated at \(t=1-\tau\).
For the proposed reverse SDE with drift \(-f+g^2s_t\) and noise amplitude \(g\), its Fokker–Planck right-hand side is
\[\begin{aligned}
-\partial_x[(-f+g^2s_t)r_\tau]+\frac12g^2\partial_x^2r_\tau
&=\partial_x(fr_\tau)-g^2\partial_x(r_\tau s_t)+\frac12g^2\partial_x^2r_\tau\\
&=\partial_x(fr_\tau)-\frac12g^2\partial_x^2r_\tau,
\end{aligned}\]
because \(r_\tau s_t=\partial_xr_\tau\). The stochastic spreading cancels half of the score-induced contribution.
For the reverse probability-flow ODE with velocity \(-f+g^2s_t/2\), the continuity equation gives the same result directly:
\[-\partial_x[(-f+\tfrac12g^2s_t)r_\tau]
=\partial_x(fr_\tau)-\frac12g^2\partial_x^2r_\tau.\]
This verifies the matching density path and explains the coefficient difference. Density agreement alone does not prove that their trajectory couplings are the same; they are not. The identification of the stochastic process as the actual time reversal uses the reverse-time SDE theorem.

title: 15 · From Score to Sampling
section: Further reading within the course
text:
Further reading within the course

Denoising score matching and Langevin sampling: fixed-noise training and equilibrium sampling.
DDPM in Ho’s notation: training from the ELBO and the original sampling algorithm.
Probability-flow transport in one dimension: trajectories, densities, and construction of velocity fields.
Learning the score and Tweedie’s formula: denoising regression and posterior averaging in detail.
DDPM through the reverse VP SDE: finite-update comparisons and Song’s reverse-diffusion rule.
DDIM and the probability-flow ODE: deterministic and stochastic DDIM, with the transformed-coordinate Euler interpretation.

title: 11 · Langevin Diffusion
text:
This topic develops sampling through a stochastic dynamical system. Begin with a Gaussian target whose score is known, then extend the construction to estimated scores and more general target densities.

Gaussian Langevin Sampling derives a non-standard Gaussian score, substitutes it into Euler–Maruyama, and compares trajectories and densities with and without noise. It separates stationarity, convergence, and numerical error.
Denoising Score Matching and Langevin Sampling develops score estimation, sampling a fixed density, and annealing across noise levels. Its appendix explains the stationary-density argument.

The subsequent DDPM lecture introduces a reverse generative chain. Lecture 15: From Score to Sampling brings score training, DDPM, and probability-flow sampling together in one place.

title: 01 · Gaussian Langevin Sampling
text:
What this tutorial establishes
We want to generate observations from a specified probability density. One way is to initialize a collection of particles and repeatedly apply an update rule. The rule changes the distribution of the particles. To obtain the desired samples, we must choose dynamics whose distribution approaches the target, or whose finite-time transport reaches it.
This tutorial develops the first construction, Langevin sampling, entirely in one dimension. We use a non-standard Gaussian so that every part can be checked analytically:
\[\boxed{p(x)=\mathcal N(x;\mu,a^2),\qquad \mu=2,\quad a^2=4.}\]
Here \(a\) is the target standard deviation. It is not the coefficient of Brownian noise in the SDE. We derive the score, substitute it into a supplied numerical solver, and compare dynamics with and without noise. We then verify stationarity and examine the generated density.
The sampling recipe is:
This describes the iterative samplers studied here; it is not a claim that every sampling method requires an ODE or SDE. A Gaussian can be sampled directly, which gives us a useful reference for checking the dynamical sampler.

title: 01 · Gaussian Langevin Sampling
text:
Choose an initial law and draw independent starting particles.
Evaluate the score at their current positions.
Apply a numerical update, with fresh noise when the dynamics is stochastic.
Repeat and compare the final particle distribution with the target.

title: 01 · Gaussian Langevin Sampling
section: 1. Separate the target, the initial law, and the evolving density
text:
1. Separate the target, the initial law, and the evolving density
Write \(p(x)\) for the fixed target density. We initialize
\[X_0\sim P_{\mathrm{init}}=\mathcal N(-3,1).\]
Let \(q_\tau(x)\) denote the density of the particles after sampling time \(\tau\). Initially \(q_0=\mathcal N(-3,1)\); the aim is that \(q_\tau\) approaches \(p=\mathcal N(2,4)\).
The initial random draw and the Gaussian increments added later are different sources of randomness. We draw \(X_0\) independently of the driving Brownian motion. Each particle has its own initial draw and independent subsequent increments.
For this Gaussian target, the score is defined everywhere and the Langevin dynamics is well-defined from every finite starting position. Initial and target supports need not coincide: a fixed starting position is also valid. Targets that vanish on regions or have restricted support require additional care concerning the domain of the score, boundaries, and accessibility.

title: 01 · Gaussian Langevin Sampling
section: 2. Derive the score of the target
text:
2. Derive the score of the target
The density is
\[p(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi a^2}}\exp\left[-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2a^2}\right].\]
Take its logarithm and differentiate with respect to position:
\[\log p(x)=-\frac12\log(2\pi a^2)-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2a^2},\]
\[\boxed{s(x)=\frac{d}{dx}\log p(x)=-\frac{x-\mu}{a^2}.}\]
For our target,
\[\boxed{s(x)=-\frac{x-2}{4}.}\]
The score is positive to the left of 2, negative to its right, and zero at 2. It points toward the center. The scale \(a^2\) determines how strongly it acts at a given displacement.






NoteThe score does not change with sampling time



The target is fixed, so the score is \(s(x)\), not \(s_\tau(x)\). At successive steps, we evaluate the same function at different positions. The sampling density \(q_\tau\) changes, but the sampler uses the score of the target \(p\), not the score of its current particle density \(q_\tau\).

title: 01 · Gaussian Langevin Sampling
section: 3. First try: use the score as a deterministic velocity
text:
3. First try: use the score as a deterministic velocity
Suppose particles follow the ODE
\[\frac{dx}{d\tau}=s(x)=-\frac{x-\mu}{a^2}.\]
Set \(y=x-\mu\). Then \(\dot y=-y/a^2\), so
\[\boxed{x(\tau)=\mu+(x_0-\mu)e^{-\tau/a^2}.}\]
This solution defines a flow: each initial position is mapped to a later position. Every trajectory approaches \(\mu\). It does not retain the spread of the target Gaussian.
For an initial Gaussian \(X_0\sim\mathcal N(m_0,V_0)\), an affine transformation preserves Gaussianity. Consequently,
\[q_\tau^{\mathrm{ODE}}=
\mathcal N\left(\mu+(m_0-\mu)e^{-\tau/a^2},\ V_0e^{-2\tau/a^2}\right).\]
The mean approaches the correct value, but the variance approaches zero. Thus matching the mean is insufficient to establish successful sampling.

The supplied Euler update without diffusion
For step size \(\eta>0\), explicit Euler gives
\[\boxed{x_{k+1}=x_k-\frac{\eta}{a^2}(x_k-\mu).}\]
For \(0<\eta<a^2\), each update moves a fraction \(\eta/a^2\) of the distance toward the center without overshooting. More generally, convergence of this numerical recursion requires \(0<\eta<2a^2\). The continuous ODE has no numerical step-size restriction; this restriction belongs to its Euler approximation.

title: 01 · Gaussian Langevin Sampling
section: 4. Add Brownian diffusion: the Langevin SDE
text:
4. Add Brownian diffusion: the Langevin SDE
The Langevin dynamics for a fixed target is
\[\boxed{dX_\tau=s(X_\tau)\,d\tau+\sqrt2\,dW_\tau.}\]
A Brownian increment over an interval of length \(\eta\) has distribution \(\mathcal N(0,\eta)\) and is independent of the earlier increments. The score supplies the drift; the Brownian term supplies diffusion. Brownian noise is not another drift term.
Substitute the Gaussian score:
\[\boxed{dX_\tau=-\frac{X_\tau-\mu}{a^2}\,d\tau+\sqrt2\,dW_\tau.}\]
This is an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process. Its drift pulls particles toward \(\mu\), while its random increments spread them. The coefficient \(\sqrt2\) is paired with the unit coefficient multiplying the score. Changing one without adjusting the other generally changes the stationary density.

The supplied Euler–Maruyama update
We use the SDE counterpart of explicit Euler:
\[\boxed{x_{k+1}=x_k+\eta s(x_k)+\sqrt{2\eta}\,z_k,
\qquad z_k\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal N(0,1).}\]
There is no need to derive stochastic calculus to implement this rule. The noise variance is \(2\eta\) because the Brownian increment has variance \(\eta\) and the SDE multiplies it by \(\sqrt2\).
For the worked example,
\[\boxed{x_{k+1}=x_k-\frac{\eta}{4}(x_k-2)+\sqrt{2\eta}\,z_k.}\]
Removing the last term recovers the deterministic Euler update from Section 3. Starting all particles at 2 would leave them there without noise; with noise, their first positions would spread according to \(\mathcal N(2,2\eta)\).



The same initial positions under the deterministic and stochastic updates. The dashed line marks the target mean. Only eight particle trajectories are shown; the simulation uses 20,000 particles and step size 0.1.

title: 01 · Gaussian Langevin Sampling
section: 5. Why is the target stationary?
text:
5. Why is the target stationary?
The density \(q_\tau\) of the Langevin particles satisfies the supplied Fokker–Planck equation
\[\partial_\tau q_\tau=-\partial_x(sq_\tau)+\partial_x^2q_\tau.\]
The first term describes deterministic drift; the second describes Brownian spreading. Write this as a conservation equation:
\[\partial_\tau q_\tau=-\partial_x J_\tau,
\qquad J_\tau=sq_\tau-\partial_xq_\tau.\]
At the target density, the definition of the score gives
\[s(x)p(x)=\frac{p'(x)}{p(x)}p(x)=p'(x).\]
Therefore
\[J=sp-p'=0,\qquad \partial_\tau p=0.\]
So the target density is stationary: if \(X_0\) already follows \(p\), every later \(X_\tau\) also follows \(p\). For the Gaussian, we can check explicitly that
\[p'(x)=-\frac{x-\mu}{a^2}p(x),\]
which exactly cancels the score-driven flux. Individual particles still move at stationarity; it is their distribution that remains unchanged.






CautionStationarity is not a convergence proof



Showing that the target is preserved when already reached does not show that every initial distribution approaches it. Convergence is a separate question. For this Gaussian example, we can verify it directly from the known solution, without a general ergodicity proof. Finite running time and numerical discretization introduce further approximation errors.

title: 01 · Gaussian Langevin Sampling
section: 6. The Gaussian solution shows the evolving density
text:
6. The Gaussian solution shows the evolving density
For this SDE, the solution at any fixed time has the distributional representation
\[\boxed{X_\tau\overset{d}=\mu+e^{-\tau/a^2}(X_0-\mu)
+a\sqrt{1-e^{-2\tau/a^2}}\,Z,\qquad Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1),}\]
with \(Z\) independent of \(X_0\). The equality describes the law at a fixed time. Reusing one \(Z\) at all times would not reproduce a Brownian trajectory. Appendix A derives the formula.
For \(X_0\sim\mathcal N(m_0,V_0)\),
\[m_\tau=\mu+(m_0-\mu)e^{-\tau/a^2},\]
\[V_\tau=V_0e^{-2\tau/a^2}+a^2(1-e^{-2\tau/a^2}).\]
Hence \(m_\tau\to\mu\) and \(V_\tau\to a^2\). Because the distributions are Gaussian, this establishes convergence to the Gaussian target. More generally, the initial random term vanishes in probability for any initial probability law on \(\mathbb R\), independently of the Brownian motion, giving weak convergence in this example.
With our numerical choices,
\[\boxed{q_\tau=\mathcal N\left(2-5e^{-\tau/4},\ 4-3e^{-\tau/2}\right).}\]



Particle density evolution from the initial Gaussian toward the target. Histograms use Euler–Maruyama with step size 0.1. The dashed curves are the exact continuous-time SDE densities, which need not coincide exactly with the numerical histograms.





The mean approaches 2 in both dynamics. Brownian noise prevents the variance from collapsing: the SDE variance approaches 4, while the deterministic score ODE variance approaches zero.

title: 01 · Gaussian Langevin Sampling
section: 7. Implement sampling as a repeated update
text:
7. Implement sampling as a repeated update
The sampler carries a state, evaluates the same score function, and updates that state. The function below simulates independent particles in parallel. It does not call a Gaussian target sampler inside its update.
import numpy as np

mu, a2 = 2.0, 4.0

def score(x):
    return -(x - mu) / a2

def sample_langevin(n=20_000, eta=0.1, final_time=40.0, seed=7):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    x = rng.normal(loc=-3.0, scale=1.0, size=n)  # initial law
    steps = round(final_time / eta)
    if not np.isclose(steps * eta, final_time):
        raise ValueError("Choose final_time divisible by eta")
    for _ in range(steps):
        z = rng.standard_normal(n)             # fresh independent noise
        x = x + eta * score(x) + np.sqrt(2 * eta) * z
    return x
One terminal position per independently simulated particle supplies the final sample. Repeated positions along one trajectory are correlated and should not be treated as independent observations.

A finite-step sampler is not the exact SDE
Center the numerical recursion at \(\mu\) and define \(A=1-\eta/a^2\):
\[x_{k+1}-\mu=A(x_k-\mu)+\sqrt{2\eta}\,z_k.\]
Its mean and variance obey
\[m_{k+1}-\mu=A(m_k-\mu),\qquad V_{k+1}=A^2V_k+2\eta.\]
For \(|A|<1\), the stationary variance solves
\[V_\eta=A^2V_\eta+2\eta
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{V_\eta=\frac{a^2}{1-\eta/(2a^2)}.}\]
It exceeds \(a^2\) at every fixed positive step size in the stable range. Thus an arbitrarily long numerical run does not remove discretization bias. For our target variance 4, step sizes \(1,0.5,0.1\) give stationary variances approximately \(4.5714,4.2667,4.0506\).

title: 01 · Gaussian Langevin Sampling
section: 8. Compare the generated samples with the target
text:
8. Compare the generated samples with the target
We simulate 20,000 independent particles to \(\tau=40\) at each step size. The initial law is always \(\mathcal N(-3,1)\). The simulations are reproducible using the Python script; it produces the figures and numerical results.



Density comparisons at a common final time and with common histogram bins. The dashed red curve is the numerical chain’s stationary density; the black curve is the intended target. Larger stable steps produce visibly excessive spread.


A density plot is a qualitative diagnostic. To quantify the discrepancy without choosing bins, compare the empirical CDF \(\widehat F_M\) with the target CDF
\[F(x)=\Phi\left(\frac{x-\mu}{a}\right),\qquad
D_M=\sup_x|\widehat F_M(x)-F(x)|.\]
For sorted samples, compute
\[D_M=\max_i\left\{\frac{i}{M}-F(x_{(i)}),\ F(x_{(i)})-\frac{i-1}{M}\right\}.\]
Even exact samples have nonzero \(D_M\). We therefore generate 20 independent reference batches of 20,000 exact target samples and compare their discrepancies with those of the numerical sampler.

These are finite-sample diagnostics, not proofs of equality. Agreement of the mean can hide variance error. A numerical discrepancy within the exact-sample reference range does not establish zero discretization bias. Conversely, the analytic variance formula identifies that bias even when a particular empirical comparison is inconclusive. The reference range is descriptive, not a formal acceptance threshold.

title: 01 · Gaussian Langevin Sampling
section: 9. How this connects to ODE and reverse-SDE generation
text:
9. How this connects to ODE and reverse-SDE generation
The common computational structure is an initial draw followed by repeated state updates. The governing equation determines which update is appropriate and what distribution the dynamics produces.









Construction
Governing equation
Numerical update
Distributional objective




Deterministic transport
\(\dot x=v(x,t)\)
Euler
Reach a prescribed endpoint distribution through a designed flow


Fixed-target Langevin
\(dX=s(X)d\tau+\sqrt2dW\)
Euler–Maruyama
Approach a fixed target as sampling time increases


Reverse diffusion
Time-dependent reverse SDE
Euler–Maruyama or another stochastic solver
Follow a prescribed family of noisy densities back toward data



An ODE sampler obtains its randomness from the initial law. An SDE sampler also receives fresh random increments. In either case, repeatedly applying an arbitrary rule is not enough: the rule must have the required transport or equilibrium property. Our score ODE is an explicit example of a perfectly well-defined dynamical system that fails to sample the desired target.
For comparison with the later course notes, let a forward diffusion be
\[dX_t=f(X_t,t)dt+g(t)dW_t,\qquad s_t(x)=\partial_x\log p_t(x).\]
Data time is \(t=0\) and terminal noise time is \(t=1\). Write \(\tau=1-t\) and \(Y_\tau=X_{1-\tau}\) for an increasing reverse clock. Under the standard regularity assumptions, its reverse dynamics is
\[dY_\tau=\left[-f(Y_\tau,1-\tau)+g(1-\tau)^2s_{1-\tau}(Y_\tau)\right]d\tau
+g(1-\tau)d\overline W_\tau.\]
Unlike fixed-target Langevin, this score changes with diffusion time. The reversed forward drift also appears. The corresponding probability-flow ODE has velocity
\[\frac{dy}{d\tau}=-f(y,1-\tau)+\frac12g(1-\tau)^2s_{1-\tau}(y).\]
Simply deleting Brownian noise from the reverse SDE would leave the wrong score coefficient. With the exact score and correct initial terminal law, the reverse SDE and probability-flow ODE share marginal densities, not individual trajectories. These relations are developed in Song’s SDE discussion, the reverse-SDE notes, and the probability-flow series.
The worked Gaussian example separates three questions students can now ask of a sampler: which law initializes the state, which equation governs its updates, and why those dynamics produce the intended distribution. When the score is unknown, denoising score matching supplies a way to estimate it. The numerical sampling procedure remains a separate part of the model.

title: 01 · Gaussian Langevin Sampling
section: Appendix A. Deriving the Gaussian Langevin solution
text:
Appendix A. Deriving the Gaussian Langevin solution
This derivation is optional. Let \(U_\tau=X_\tau-\mu\). Multiplying
\[dU_\tau=-\frac{U_\tau}{a^2}d\tau+\sqrt2dW_\tau\]
by the deterministic integrating factor \(e^{\tau/a^2}\) cancels the drift:
\[d\left(e^{\tau/a^2}U_\tau\right)=\sqrt2e^{\tau/a^2}dW_\tau.\]
Integrating gives
\[X_\tau=\mu+e^{-\tau/a^2}(X_0-\mu)
+\sqrt2\int_0^\tau e^{-(\tau-u)/a^2}\,dW_u.\]
An Itô integral with a deterministic square-integrable integrand is a centered Gaussian. Its variance here is
\[2\int_0^\tau e^{-2(\tau-u)/a^2}du
=a^2\left(1-e^{-2\tau/a^2}\right).\]
Independence of the initial draw and Brownian motion makes the integral independent of \(X_0\). This yields the fixed-time representation used in Section 6. The deterministic integrand is why no additional random coefficient calculation is needed here.
For this special Gaussian problem, the exact transition over an interval of length \(\eta\) is also available:
\[X_{\tau+\eta}=\mu+e^{-\eta/a^2}(X_\tau-\mu)
+a\sqrt{1-e^{-2\eta/a^2}}\,Z,\]
where \(Z\) is a fresh independent standard Gaussian. It preserves the target exactly at finite step sizes, unlike Euler–Maruyama. General targets usually do not provide such an exact transition, which is why learning to use and assess numerical updates is useful.

title: 02 · Denoising Score Matching and Langevin Sampling
text:
1. Learn from clean/noisy pairs
For a smooth positive density \(p\), its scalar score is \(s(x)=\partial_x\log p(x)\). It measures the local rate of change of log density. We first learn this quantity for a Gaussian-smoothed data distribution, then use it as the drift in a sampling procedure. No probability-flow ODE is needed here.
Draw \(X_0\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}\) and independent \(\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\). At a fixed noise scale \(\sigma>0\), form
\[Y=X_0+\sigma\varepsilon,\qquad
p_\sigma(y)=\int\mathcal N(y;x_0,\sigma^2)p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_0)\,dx_0.\]
A denoiser trained with squared error estimates \(D_*(y,\sigma)=\mathbb E[X_0\mid Y=y]\). Tweedie’s formula connects it to the noisy marginal score:
\[s_\sigma(y)=\partial_y\log p_\sigma(y)
=\frac{D_*(y,\sigma)-y}{\sigma^2}.\]
The regression averages possible clean origins conditional on the noisy input. It does not recover the particular noise realization of every pair. The score is a property of the smoothed density \(p_\sigma\), not exactly the original clean density at finite \(\sigma\).

title: 02 · Denoising Score Matching and Langevin Sampling
section: 2. Denoising score matching
text:
2. Denoising score matching
The conditional Gaussian score is available for every constructed pair:
\[U=\partial_y\log p(Y\mid X_0)
=-\frac{Y-X_0}{\sigma^2}=-\frac{\varepsilon}{\sigma}.\]
Minimize
\[\mathcal L_{\mathrm{DSM}}(\theta;\sigma)
=\mathbb E_{X_0\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\,\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,1)}
[(s_\theta(X_0+\sigma\varepsilon,\sigma)+\varepsilon/\sigma)^2].\]
At the unrestricted optimum, \(s_*(y,\sigma)=\mathbb E[U\mid Y=y]=s_\sigma(y)\). The conditional target is known even though the marginal score is not. The loss differs from marginal-score regression by a conditional-variance term independent of the predictor. This is the denoising/score-matching connection developed by Vincent (2011).
To verify the identity, differentiate the marginal density:
\[\begin{aligned}
\partial_y p_\sigma(y)
&=\int \frac{x_0-y}{\sigma^2}p(y\mid x_0)p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_0)\,dx_0,\\
\partial_y\log p_\sigma(y)
&=\int \frac{x_0-y}{\sigma^2}
\frac{p(y\mid x_0)p_{\mathrm{data}}(x_0)}{p_\sigma(y)}\,dx_0\\
&=\int \frac{x_0-y}{\sigma^2}p(x_0\mid y)\,dx_0
=\mathbb E[U\mid Y=y].
\end{aligned}\]
Although the posterior is not explicitly available during training, sampling clean/noisy pairs supplies draws from their joint law. Squared-error regression performs the conditional averaging:
\[\mathbb E[(s_\theta(Y,\sigma)-U)^2\mid Y]
=(s_\theta(Y,\sigma)-\mathbb E[U\mid Y])^2
+\operatorname{Var}(U\mid Y).\]
The second term is independent of the predictor. For an empirical training distribution, the unrestricted population objective over corrupted training pairs targets its smoothed empirical score.
Equivalently, train a noise predictor with squared error and set \(s_\theta=-\varepsilon_\theta/\sigma\). Then
\[\mathbb E[(\varepsilon-\varepsilon_\theta)^2]=\sigma^2\mathcal L_{\mathrm{DSM}}.\]
This exact reparameterization will reappear in DDPM, with a different cumulative noise scale at every discrete step.

title: 02 · Denoising Score Matching and Langevin Sampling
section: 3. Once a fixed score is known: Langevin sampling
text:
3. Once a fixed score is known: Langevin sampling
For a fully worked example with trajectories, density plots, code, and numerical error checks, see Langevin Diffusion: Sampling a Gaussian Through Dynamics.
Let \(p\) be a smooth positive target density and \(s=\partial_x\log p\). Use sampling time \(\tau\), with \(p\) held fixed:
\[dX_\tau=s(X_\tau)\,d\tau+\sqrt2\,dW_\tau.\]
Brownian increments over an interval of length \(\eta\) are independent Gaussians with variance \(\eta\). Euler–Maruyama therefore gives
\[\boxed{x_{k+1}=x_k+\eta s(x_k)+\sqrt{2\eta}\,z_k,
\qquad z_k\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal N(0,1).}\]






NoteA fixed score, a chosen initial law, and fresh noise



The score \(s(x)=\partial_x\log p(x)\) has no explicit dependence on sampling time \(\tau\) or step index \(k\). Every Euler–Maruyama step evaluates the same function at the current position \(x_k\). Its value can change because the particle moves; the target density and its score field remain fixed. Changing the numerical step size does not change the target score.
Choose an initial law \(P_{\mathrm{init}}\) and draw \(X_0\sim P_{\mathrm{init}}\) independently of the driving Brownian motion. The initial law need not be Gaussian or equal to the target: it may, for example, be uniform, Gaussian, or a point mass at a chosen position. This initialization is separate from the fresh \(z_k\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) used at every step. Each \(z_k\) is independent of \(X_0\) and all earlier increments, and therefore of the current state \(x_k\). The initial law may itself be Gaussian, but its draw and the subsequent Gaussian increments have different roles. Initial and target supports need not coincide, but the dynamics must be defined at the starting positions. Restricted-support targets may require boundary conditions; zeros of the target density can make its score undefined. Convergence requires a separate argument, not merely a choice of initial law.
The score term is the drift; the Brownian term is the diffusion or noise term, not a Brownian drift. For a well-defined, ergodic Langevin process, suitable initializations approach the target as sampling time grows. Initialization affects how long this takes; neither an arbitrary finite running time nor a finite Euler step guarantees exact target samples. For example, the standard logistic target admits fixed starting points such as zero or six.


Score-directed drift and random spreading balance at the target distribution. For the continuous SDE, \(p\) is invariant under suitable conditions; convergence from a starting law requires additional ergodicity conditions. A finite unadjusted Euler step generally has bias, and a learned score adds approximation error. Appendix A derives the stationary density and illustrates convergence with a Gaussian target.
If the learned score is \(s_\sigma\), the intended stationary target is \(p_\sigma\). Langevin does not remove the smoothing merely by running longer. Its sampling clock is not a schedule that automatically reduces \(\sigma\).

title: 02 · Denoising Score Matching and Langevin Sampling
section: 4. First solved check: a standard Gaussian
text:
4. First solved check: a standard Gaussian
For \(p=\mathcal N(0,1)\), \(s(x)=-x\). Deterministic score ascent \(\dot x=-x\) collapses toward zero. Langevin instead gives
\[x_{k+1}=(1-\eta)x_k+\sqrt{2\eta}\,z_k.\]
For \(0<\eta<2\), the discrete chain’s stationary variance solves
\[V=(1-\eta)^2V+2\eta,
\qquad V=\frac1{1-\eta/2}.\]
It approaches the target variance 1 as \(\eta\to0\), but is not exactly 1 at a finite step. This separates finite-step sampling bias from score-estimation error.
crumbs: 02 · Denoising Score Matching and Langevin Sampling

title: 02 · Denoising Score Matching and Langevin Sampling
section: 5. Several noise levels and annealed Langevin dynamics
text:
5. Several noise levels and annealed Langevin dynamics
Train \(s_\theta(x,\sigma)\) at a decreasing sequence \(\sigma_1>\cdots>\sigma_L>0\), averaging the DSM loss over a stated distribution of noise levels with positive weights. At each level, perform several Langevin steps targeting \(p_{\sigma_i}\), then lower the noise scale. Large smoothing can make movement between modes easier; short runs at each level do not guarantee equilibrium.
This is the approach of Song and Ermon (2019). It differs from a reverse diffusion SDE designed to follow prescribed changing marginals without equilibrating at every level. The final positive noise level retains smoothing error.

title: 02 · Denoising Score Matching and Langevin Sampling
section: 6. Next: a learned reverse Markov chain
text:
6. Next: a learned reverse Markov chain
The training problem is now familiar: use known conditional Gaussian targets to estimate an unknown marginal score. Langevin supplies one sampling method, with a fixed target at each noise level. DDPM next builds a reverse Markov chain and motivates its training through the ELBO. Its simplified noise-prediction loss is another weighted denoising score objective, but its ancestral sampler follows different dynamics. After DDPM, Probability-Flow ODE develops deterministic transport and later reinterprets DDPM through a reverse SDE.

title: 02 · Denoising Score Matching and Langevin Sampling
section: Appendix A: why score-driven Langevin dynamics preserves the target density
text:
Appendix A: why score-driven Langevin dynamics preserves the target density

A.1. Target density and current particle density
Fix a smooth, strictly positive, normalized density \(p(x)\) on \(\mathbb R\). Its score is
\[s(x)=\partial_x\log p(x)=\frac{p'(x)}{p(x)}.\]
Consider the continuous-time Langevin SDE
\[\boxed{dX_\tau=s(X_\tau)\,d\tau+\sqrt2\,dW_\tau.}\]
Here \(\tau\) is sampling time. The target \(p\) remains fixed, while the density \(r_\tau\) of the moving particles can change. We assume the SDE is well posed and nonexplosive, and that the densities and boundary behavior justify the derivatives and probability balances below. On the real line, use vanishing probability flux at infinity; on a bounded interval, reflecting boundaries impose zero flux.
The question is: why should the equilibrium particle density be \(p\) when the drift is its score?


A.2. Probability flux and the Fokker–Planck equation
For a one-dimensional SDE \(dX_\tau=b(X_\tau)\,d\tau+g\,dW_\tau\) with constant \(g\), the density satisfies
\[\partial_\tau r_\tau=-\partial_x(br_\tau)+\frac{g^2}{2}\partial_{xx}r_\tau.\]
Substitute \(b=s\) and \(g=\sqrt2\):
\[\partial_\tau r_\tau=-\partial_x(r_\tau s)+\partial_{xx}r_\tau
=-\partial_x J_\tau,\]
where
\[\boxed{J_\tau(x)=\underbrace{r_\tau(x)s(x)}_{\text{drift flux}}
\;\underbrace{-\partial_x r_\tau(x)}_{\text{diffusive flux}}.}\]
The first flux transports particles according to the score vector field. The second describes the net spreading caused by Brownian motion: probability flows down the gradient of the current particle density.
For any fixed interval \([a,b]\), integrate the continuity equation:
\[\frac{d}{d\tau}\Pr(a\leq X_\tau\leq b)
=\int_a^b\partial_\tau r_\tau(x)\,dx
=J_\tau(a)-J_\tau(b).\]
The interval gains probability through its left boundary and loses probability through its right boundary, with signed flux accounting for either direction of movement.


A.3. At the target density, the two fluxes cancel
Set \(r_\tau=p\). By the definition of the score,
\[p(x)s(x)=p(x)\frac{p'(x)}{p(x)}=p'(x).\]
Hence
\[\boxed{J(x)=p(x)s(x)-p'(x)=p'(x)-p'(x)=0.}\]
It follows that
\[\left.\partial_\tau r_\tau(x)\right|_{r_\tau=p}=-\partial_x J(x)=0.\]
Thus, under the stated conditions, \(p\) is an invariant density: if \(X_0\sim p\), then \(X_\tau\sim p\) at every later sampling time. Individual particles continue moving. Their distribution stays unchanged because drift and diffusion balance at every location.
The relative coefficients matter. More generally, \(dX_\tau=c\,s(X_\tau)\,d\tau+\sqrt{2c}\,dW_\tau\), for constant \(c>0\), preserves the same target: both fluxes are multiplied by \(c\). Changing the drift coefficient without the corresponding change in noise generally changes the stationary density.


A.4. Recovering the target from the stationary equation
Conversely, suppose a smooth positive density \(r_*\) is stationary on a connected domain with zero-flux boundary conditions. Then
\[\partial_x J_*=0.\]
The flux is spatially constant, and the boundary condition makes that constant zero. Therefore
\[r_*(x)s(x)-r_*'(x)=0.\]
Divide by \(r_*(x)>0\) and substitute the score:
\[\frac{r_*'(x)}{r_*(x)}=s(x)=\frac{p'(x)}{p(x)},\]
\[\partial_x\log r_*(x)=\partial_x\log p(x).\]
Integrating over the connected domain gives \(r_*(x)=C p(x)\). Since both densities integrate to one, \(C=1\):
\[\boxed{r_*(x)=p(x).}\]
This identifies the stationary density within the stated class. It does not by itself prove convergence from every initial distribution. That requires ergodicity conditions; separated modes can also make convergence very slow.


A.5. Solved example: convergence to a Gaussian
Take \(p=\mathcal N(\mu,1)\). Its score is \(s(x)=-(x-\mu)\), so
\[dX_\tau=-(X_\tau-\mu)\,d\tau+\sqrt2\,dW_\tau.\]
Multiplying the centered process by \(e^\tau\) and integrating gives
\[X_\tau=\mu+e^{-\tau}(X_0-\mu)
+\sqrt2\int_0^\tau e^{-(\tau-u)}\,dW_u.\]
The stochastic integral has mean zero and variance
\[2\int_0^\tau e^{-2(\tau-u)}\,du=1-e^{-2\tau}.\]
Assuming \(X_0\) is independent of the driving Brownian motion, at each fixed time this yields the distributional representation
\[\boxed{X_\tau\overset{d}{=}\mu+e^{-\tau}(X_0-\mu)
+\sqrt{1-e^{-2\tau}}\,Z,\qquad Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1),}\]
where \(Z\) is independent of \(X_0\). As \(\tau\to\infty\), the initial-condition term disappears and \(X_\tau\) converges in distribution to \(\mathcal N(\mu,1)\). If \(X_0\) already has that distribution, the variance at every time is \(e^{-2\tau}+(1-e^{-2\tau})=1\), and the mean remains \(\mu\).
Without Brownian noise, the contraction would collapse all particles toward \(\mu\). With noise, the spreading exactly balances the contraction at unit variance.


A.6. What this guarantees for a numerical sampler
The proof concerns the exact score and the continuous SDE. Euler–Maruyama instead generates
\[x_{k+1}=x_k+\eta s(x_k)+\sqrt{2\eta}\,z_k.\]
For the Gaussian example, the centered update is an autoregression with coefficient \(1-\eta\). At stationarity its variance must satisfy
\[V=(1-\eta)^2V+2\eta
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
V=\frac{1}{1-\eta/2},\qquad 0<\eta<2.\]
Thus even the exact score gives a biased stationary density at a fixed Euler step size. An estimated score introduces another source of error. Small steps and sufficient sampling time are essential qualifications in Song’s discussion of Langevin sampling.
Finally, stationarity describes each sample’s marginal law. Successive observations along one stationary trajectory are generally correlated; they are not independent draws merely because the chain is at equilibrium.
For a different use of a time-dependent score—deterministic transport through a prescribed density path—see the separate Probability-Flow ODE topic.
Continue to Reverse-SDE sampling to follow a changing density path rather than equilibrate at one noise level.

This eleven-part topic develops sampling by transporting a simple distribution into a data distribution. The parts use their own index, 01–11, and can be read in sequence. The notes and worked examples are in development.


For the complete training-and-sampling argument in one place, start with 15 · From Score to Sampling. It develops the algorithmic recipe, a solved scalar example, and the distinction between the reverse-SDE and probability-flow samplers.

Start with particle trajectories and density evolution in one dimension. Then extend the construction to vectors, learn the score from clean/noisy pairs, and implement sampling. title: 01 · Transport in one dimension
text:
Summary: the problem, the sampling procedure, and the main result
The goal is sampling. Given observations from an unknown data density \(p_{\mathrm{data}}\), we want to generate new samples from it. We start from a known prior distribution that is easy to sample, chosen here to be standard normal.
Our sampling procedure is numerical ODE integration. Draw a position at \(t=1\) from the prior, then integrate
\[\frac{dx(t)}{dt}=v(x(t),t)\]
backward to \(t=0\). For a positive step size \(h\), an explicit Euler step is
\[x(t-h)\approx x(t)-h\,v(x(t),t).\]
The initial draw supplies the randomness. Conditional on that draw, the ODE trajectory is deterministic. Given a suitable vector field, we therefore have a numerical procedure for generating samples. Which distribution it produces depends on both the field and the starting law.
The unknown is the vector field. We must construct \(v(x,t)\) so that the population densities induced by its flow satisfy the boundary conditions
\[\boxed{p_0=p_{\mathrm{data}},\qquad
p_1=p_{\mathrm{prior}}=\mathcal N(0,1).}\]
These are conditions on distributions, not prescribed endpoint positions for each particle. If the field defines a well-posed invertible flow with these endpoint laws, drawing from the prior at \(t=1\) and following the flow backward gives a sample from \(p_{\mathrm{data}}\) at \(t=0\).
The central question is how to construct such a vector field. The tutorial develops two constructions. First, in one dimension, we prescribe a density path between the endpoints and recover its velocity using CDFs and conservation of probability. Second, we use forward diffusion to specify a density path, then recover a deterministic field that reproduces it.
The main result for the diffusion construction is
\[\boxed{v(x,t)=-\frac{\beta}{2}\bigl[x+s_t(x)\bigr],
\qquad s_t(x)=\partial_x\log p_t(x).}\]
For training with a time-dependent VP schedule, replace \(\beta\) by \(\beta(t)\) and use \(\alpha_t=\exp[-\frac12\int_0^t\beta(u)du]\) in the forward corruption. These coefficients describe the same process; they cannot be selected independently. Part 3 connects the training examples to this ODE using Song et al. as the primary reference.
Here \(\beta>0\) is the chosen constant rate of the forward diffusion and \(s_t\) is the score of its intermediate density. We will derive this field by expressing the diffusion’s density evolution as a continuity equation. Under suitable regularity assumptions, the resulting probability-flow ODE has the same densities as the stochastic process, although their individual trajectories differ.
This identifies what we need to learn: the intermediate score. Once that function is available, we can evaluate the vector field and use the ODE sampling procedure above. The CDF construction meets the Gaussian endpoint exactly; the finite-rate diffusion construction generally has \(p_1\approx p_{\mathrm{prior}}\). Replacing its actual terminal law by the Gaussian, estimating the score, and numerically integrating the ODE introduce terminal-distribution, estimation, and numerical errors, respectively.
The derivation proceeds in five steps.
The sections below develop these results. Learning the intermediate scores from corrupted data is the subsequent problem.

title: 01 · Transport in one dimension
section: 1. Moving data points: vector fields and trajectories
text:
1. Moving data points: vector fields and trajectories
Represent each data point on the real line as a particle whose position can change with time. If a particle starts at \(x_0\), write \(x(t)\) for its position at time \(t\), so that \(x(0)=x_0\).
We specify a vector field that determines each particle’s velocity as a function of its position and time.

A vector field assigns a local velocity
At each position \(x\) and time \(t\), the vector field specifies a velocity, written as
\[v(x,t).\]
This is a vector field. In one dimension, a vector is simply a signed number:

\(v(x,t)>0\): move to the right.
\(v(x,t)<0\): move to the left.
\(v(x,t)=0\): the velocity is zero at that position and time.

The field describes the rate of positional change, not a displacement by itself. Over a short time interval \(h>0\), the displacement is approximately \(h\,v(x,t)\).
If the vector field does not depend on time, we write \(v(x)\) instead of \(v(x,t)\). This is a time-independent vector field.


Trajectories as solutions of an ODE
The particle’s velocity equals the vector field evaluated at its current position and time:
\[\boxed{\frac{dx(t)}{dt}=v(x(t),t),\qquad x(0)=x_0.}\]
This is an ordinary differential equation (ODE) with an initial condition. The vector field supplies the local rule; solving the ODE gives the trajectory \(t\mapsto x(t)\), the particle’s position over time.
The argument \(x(t)\) on the right is the particle’s current position. Because this position changes, even a time-independent vector field can produce a velocity that varies along the trajectory.
Each starting point supplies a different initial condition. Solving the same ODE for all the data points describes the motion of the entire collection. For the simple fields below, each initial condition has a unique trajectory.


Example 1: a constant vector field
Take
\[v(x)=c,\]
where \(c\) is a constant. The velocity is the same at every position. The ODE and its solution are
\[\frac{dx(t)}{dt}=c,
\qquad\boxed{x(t)=x_0+ct.}\]
For \(c=2\), every particle moves two units to the right per unit time. A particle starting at \(x_0=-1\) is at \(x(0.5)=0\) and \(x(1)=1\). For negative \(c\), the motion is to the left.
Every particle undergoes the same translation, so the distances between particles remain unchanged.



Trajectories for constant velocity \(v(x)=2\). Each curve follows one particle from its marked starting position. The parallel lines show that all particles have the same velocity.


The horizontal axis is time and the vertical axis is position on the line. Each curve is a function \(x(t)\), not a path in two-dimensional space. Its slope at a given time is the particle’s velocity.


Example 2: contraction toward the origin
Now take
\[v(x)=-x.\]
At \(x=2\), the velocity is \(-2\): move left. At \(x=-3\), it is \(+3\): move right. At \(x=0\), it is zero. The velocity is directed toward the origin, with magnitude equal to the distance from it.
The ODE is
\[\frac{dx(t)}{dt}=-x(t),\qquad x(0)=x_0.\]
Its solution is
\[\boxed{x(t)=x_0e^{-t}.}\]
We can check it directly: differentiating gives \(dx(t)/dt=-x_0e^{-t}=-x(t)\), and at \(t=0\) the value is \(x_0\).
A particle starting at \(x_0=2\) has positions \(2\), \(2e^{-1/2}\), and \(2e^{-1}\) at times \(0\), \(0.5\), and \(1\). It moves toward zero and slows down as it gets closer. A particle starting at a negative position approaches zero from the left. A particle starting at zero stays there: zero is an equilibrium.
Unlike constant motion, contraction changes the distances between particles. For two starting points \(x_0\) and \(y_0\),
\[|x(t)-y(t)|=e^{-t}|x_0-y_0|.\]
The collection contracts. Distinct particles approach one another but do not merge at any finite time in this example.



Trajectories for contraction \(v(x)=-x\). Positive and negative starting positions approach zero; the dashed zero trajectory is the equilibrium.


The curves flatten as the particles approach the origin: their speeds decrease. At every finite time the trajectories remain distinct, even when they appear close together in the plot.


Probability induced by transport
So far we have followed individual particles. Now consider the population they form. Suppose their initial positions are sampled from a probability density \(p_0(x)\). The ODE moves every starting position \(x_0\) to a new position \(x(t)\), so it also moves the population into a new density, which we call \(p_t(x)\).
A finite collection of points gives a histogram approximating this density. Strictly, the finite collection itself has point masses; the smooth PDF (probability density function) describes the underlying population. We use this smooth description to study how probability moves.
The motion is deterministic once a starting position is specified. But a random starting position \(X_0\) produces a random position \(X_t\). Its density \(p_t\) is the probability density induced by the transport.
The vector field and the initial density together determine this evolution. The vector field alone does not specify how the particles were initially distributed.

The continuity equation and its interpretation
For particles moving with velocity \(v(x,t)\), conservation of probability gives
\[\boxed{\partial_t p_t(x)=-\partial_x\bigl[p_t(x)v(x,t)\bigr].}\]
This is the continuity equation. Define the probability flux \(J(x,t)=p_t(x)v(x,t)\): the signed rate at which probability crosses position \(x\). Positive flux is rightward; negative flux is leftward. The equation is therefore \(\partial_t p_t=-\partial_xJ\).
At a fixed position, density decreases when more probability leaves a small surrounding interval than enters it. Thus, if flux increases from left to right (\(\partial_xJ>0\)), density decreases (\(\partial_t p_t<0\)). If flux decreases from left to right, density increases. Equal incoming and outgoing flux leaves the interval’s probability unchanged.
For any fixed interval \([x_L,x_R]\), the corresponding balance is
\[\boxed{\frac{d}{dt}\int_{x_L}^{x_R}p_t(x)\,dx
=J(x_L,t)-J(x_R,t).}\]
The partial derivative \(\partial_t\) holds position fixed; \(\partial_x\) holds time fixed. With vanishing flux at infinity, total probability stays one. But preserving total probability alone is not sufficient: the continuity equation also requires the density changes to agree locally with the specified velocity. The word “continuity” here refers to this conservation balance, not merely to continuity of the function \(p_t\).
The conservation argument and derivation are in Appendix A. The simulations in the appendix illustrate the interval balance and its relation to particle motion.


Constant velocity: the density translates
Write \(x_t=x(t)\) for a particle trajectory; \(X_t\) denotes a random particle position. For a smooth flow, conservation in a small moving interval gives
\[p_t(x_t)\frac{\partial x_t}{\partial x_0}=p_0(x_0),\]
as derived in Appendix A.1. This relates local stretching to the transported density in the examples below.
For \(v(x)=c\), the trajectory is \(x_t=x_0+ct\). A small interval keeps its width, because \(\partial x_t/\partial x_0=1\). Conservation therefore gives
\[\boxed{p_t(x)=p_0(x-ct).}\]
The density shifts without changing its shape or height. As a concrete example, start with a standard normal population:
\[p_0(x)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/2}.\]
For \(c=2\),
\[\boxed{p_t(x)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\exp\left[-\frac{(x-2t)^2}{2}\right],\qquad
X_t\sim\mathcal N(2t,1).}\]
The mean moves to the right at speed two; the variance stays one.
Check the continuity equation. Differentiating the translated density,
\[\partial_tp_t=-c\,p_0'(x-ct)
=-\partial_x(cp_t),\]
exactly as required by the velocity field.



Constant motion from a standard normal initial density. Left: PDF snapshots translate to the right with unchanged shape. Right: a time-position map of the same density; color indicates probability density.




Contraction: the density narrows and rises
For \(v(x)=-x\), the trajectory is \(x_t=e^{-t}x_0\). An initial interval shrinks by \(e^{-t}\), so conservation requires the density along it to rise by \(e^t\). Since the starting point that reaches \(x\) is \(x_0=e^tx\),
\[\boxed{p_t(x)=e^t p_0(e^t x).}\]
Starting from the same standard normal density gives
\[\boxed{p_t(x)=\frac{e^t}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\exp\left[-\frac{e^{2t}x^2}{2}\right],\qquad
X_t\sim\mathcal N(0,e^{-2t}).}\]
The mean stays zero. The standard deviation decreases as \(e^{-t}\), while the peak height increases as \(e^t\). The area under the curve stays one. A taller PDF does not mean more total probability: it means the same probability is concentrated into a narrower region.
Check the continuity equation. Differentiating gives
\[\partial_tp_t=p_t+x\partial_xp_t
=\partial_x(xp_t)=-\partial_x((-x)p_t),\]
again matching the particle velocity.



Contraction from a standard normal initial density. Left: the PDF becomes narrower and taller while retaining unit area. Right: the time-position density map concentrates around zero. Each panel uses the same initial density as the constant-motion example.


At every finite time this is still a Gaussian density with positive variance. At the terminal time \(t=1\), its variance is \(e^{-2}>0\); it has not collapsed to a point mass. The narrowing PDF is the population-level description of the converging trajectories plotted above.


A two-component Gaussian population
The transport laws do not require a Gaussian initial density. To see how they move a population with two peaks, take an equal mixture of two Gaussians:
\[p_0(x)=\tfrac12\mathcal N(x;-2,0.5^2)
+\tfrac12\mathcal N(x;2,0.5^2).\]
Here \(\mathcal N(x;\mu,a^2)\) denotes the Gaussian density evaluated at \(x\), with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(a^2\). Half the initial population belongs to each component. The component means are \(-2\) and \(2\), and each component has standard deviation \(0.5\).
Constant motion, \(v(x)=2\). Every particle moves by \(2t\), so both component means shift by \(2t\) while their variances stay fixed:
\[\boxed{p_t(x)=
\tfrac12\mathcal N(x;-2+2t,0.5^2)
+\tfrac12\mathcal N(x;2+2t,0.5^2).}\]
This is again \(p_t(x)=p_0(x-2t)\). The two peaks travel together without changing the overall shape. Their separation stays constant.



Two-component Gaussian mixture under constant motion. PDF snapshots and the time-position density map show both peaks translating to the right with unchanged widths and separation.


Contraction, \(v(x)=-x\). Every position is multiplied by \(e^{-t}\). Both component means and component standard deviations shrink by that factor:
\[\boxed{p_t(x)=
\tfrac12\mathcal N(x;-2e^{-t},0.5^2e^{-2t})
+\tfrac12\mathcal N(x;2e^{-t},0.5^2e^{-2t}).}\]
This is \(p_t(x)=e^tp_0(e^tx)\). Both peaks move toward zero, become narrower, and rise. The weights remain one half, and the total area remains one.



Two-component Gaussian mixture under contraction. Both peaks move inward and become narrower and taller; the density map shows the two concentrating ridges.


The two peaks remain distinct at every finite time: their separation and widths shrink in the same proportion. Thus the ratio of component-mean separation to component standard deviation remains \(4/0.5=8\). At \(t=1\), the mixture still has two distinct peaks and positive component variances.
The continuity equation also holds for this mixture. Each transported component satisfies \(\partial_tp=-\partial_x(pv)\) under the same field \(v\). Adding these equations with weights one half shows that their mixture satisfies it too.



From trajectories to a flow: the transport question
An ODE gives a trajectory for each starting point. Collecting all these trajectories defines a flow map:
\[\boxed{\Psi_{0\to t}(x_0)=x(t).}\]
For a fixed time \(t\), this map tells us where every initial point has moved. As \(t\) varies, we obtain a family of maps. Our two examples give
\[\begin{aligned}
v(x)=2 &: \qquad \Psi_{0\to t}(x_0)=x_0+2t,\\
v(x)=-x &: \qquad \Psi_{0\to t}(x_0)=e^{-t}x_0.
\end{aligned}\]
Now let the starting population be the data distribution:
\[X_0\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\qquad p_0=p_{\mathrm{data}}.\]
Here \(x_0\) is one position; \(X_0\) is a random position with density \(p_{\mathrm{data}}\). Applying the flow to this random starting point gives \(X_t=\Psi_{0\to t}(X_0)\), whose density is \(p_t\).
Previously, we specified a vector field and calculated the resulting density. We now seek a vector field that produces a specified terminal density. On the normalized interval \([0,1]\), our aim is
\[\boxed{p_{\mathrm{data}}\xrightarrow{\Psi_{0\to1}}p_1\approx\mathcal N(0,1).}\]
Can we determine a vector field that transports the data distribution into an approximately standard Gaussian?
This does not happen merely by running any ODE for long enough. Our constant field translates the two-component mixture; our contraction field shrinks it. Neither changes its shape relative to its own scale into that of a single Gaussian. We need a field chosen for the desired transport.
If we can construct such a field, two further questions become natural:

Can we run its flow backward to recover the original distribution?
If we start with a random Gaussian point and follow that backward flow, will the result be a sample from the data distribution?

For exact smooth ODE transport through \(t=0\), assume the data distribution has a smooth positive density. Exact transport, approximate Gaussian endpoints, and the conditions for running backward will need to be distinguished as we answer these questions.


An invertible flow gives a sampling procedure
Suppose we have a vector field whose flow carries the data density into a known terminal density \(p_1\). Assume its trajectories exist uniquely both forward and backward throughout \([0,1]\), so that the flow is invertible. Running backward gives the inverse map:
\[\Psi_{1\to0}=\Psi_{0\to1}^{-1}.\]
To sample from the initial distribution, draw from \(p_1\) and apply the inverse flow:
\[\boxed{X_1\sim p_1,\qquad X_{\mathrm{sample}}=\Psi_{1\to0}(X_1)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad X_{\mathrm{sample}}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}.}\]
The generated sample is random because the terminal position is sampled from \(p_1\). Conditional on that position, the ODE trajectory is deterministic. We do not need to know which original data point produced it: a fresh terminal draw gives a fresh sample from the original distribution. If instead we reverse a particular particle’s forward path, we recover that particle’s particular starting point.

Worked example: standard Gaussian to a shifted, wider Gaussian
Let the data distribution be \(\mathcal N(2,4)\), with mean \(2\) and standard deviation \(2\). Choose the time-independent field
\[v(x)=-(\log 2)(x+2).\]
Here \(\log\) is the natural logarithm. This is contraction toward \(-2\), with rate \(\log 2\). Setting \(y(t)=x(t)+2\) reduces the ODE to \(dy/dt=-(\log 2)y\), so
\[x(t)=-2+(x_0+2)2^{-t}.\]
At time one, the flow is
\[\boxed{\Psi_{0\to1}(x_0)=\frac{x_0-2}{2}.}\]
Thus \(X_0\sim\mathcal N(2,4)\) becomes \(X_1\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) exactly. At intermediate times its mean is \(-2+4\,2^{-t}\) and its standard deviation is \(2\,2^{-t}\): at \(t=1\) these are \(0\) and \(1\).
Reverse this flow starting from a fresh \(X_1\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\):
\[x(t)=-2+(X_1+2)2^{1-t},\qquad t:1\to0.\]
At time zero we obtain
\[\boxed{X_{\mathrm{sample}}=2+2Z\sim\mathcal N(2,4).}\]
The inverse transports the whole Gaussian population to the desired mean and spread. It does not send every particle to the same point.


Simulate sampling with Euler steps backward in time
Usually the inverse flow has no explicit formula. We then approximate backward integration. For a positive step magnitude \(h\), use
\[x(t-h)\approx x(t)-h\,v(x(t),t).\]
In our example this becomes
\[x\leftarrow x+h(\log 2)(x+2),\qquad t\leftarrow t-h.\]
Start at \(t=1\) with independent standard normal draws, and repeat until \(t=0\). The figure uses \(20{,}000\) draws and \(200\) explicit Euler steps backward in time of size \(h=1/200\). The final histogram approximates the target Gaussian; the middle panel follows a small subset of those same simulated particles.



Sampling with an invertible flow. Left: standard normal starting draws at time one. Middle: explicit Euler trajectories in reverse time, with time decreasing from left to right. Right: the generated histogram at time zero, compared with the exact target density.


The explicit inverse gives the exact target law. The simulated histogram has finite-sample fluctuations, and Euler adds numerical error. More generally, starting from standard normal gives exact recovery only if the actual terminal law is standard normal; an approximate terminal match introduces another error.
Given a suitable vector field, we can therefore sample by integrating the ODE backward. We next consider how to construct the vector field.



Designing a vector field through a desired density evolution
We seek a vector field that transports particles drawn from \(p_0=p_{\mathrm{data}}\) so that their final density is approximately standard normal. Reversing that motion would give us a sampling procedure.
The constant and contraction vector fields translate or rescale every particle in the same way. A more general field \(v(x,t)\) can move particles at different speeds in different regions, changing the shape of their density. An ODE can be sufficient for generation, as demonstrated by the Gaussian example above.
For a more complicated data density, one approach is to specify a family of intermediate densities:
