title: 10 · DDPM through the reverse VP SDE
section: 1. DDPM and probability flow share the forward VP SDE
text:
1. DDPM and probability flow share the forward VP SDE
Let \(h_n=t_n-t_{n-1}\) be the length of a forward interval. Subtract the preceding state from the forward DDPM update to obtain
\[X_{t_n}-X_{t_{n-1}}
=(\sqrt{1-b_n}-1)X_{t_{n-1}}+\sqrt{b_n}\,Z_n.\]
To obtain a finite diffusion rate as the grid is refined, the per-step variance must shrink with the interval. For a smooth rate \(\beta\), take \(b_n=\beta(t_n)h_n+O(h_n^2)\). Expanding \(\sqrt{1-b_n}=1-b_n/2+O(b_n^2)\) gives, conditional on \(X_{t_{n-1}}=x\),
\[\mathbb E[X_{t_n}-X_{t_{n-1}}\mid x]
=-\tfrac12\beta(t_n)x h_n+O(h_n^2),\]
\[\operatorname{Var}(X_{t_n}-X_{t_{n-1}}\mid x)
=b_n=\beta(t_n)h_n+O(h_n^2).\]
A Brownian increment over \(h_n\) has variance \(h_n\). These two expressions identify the drift rate and squared diffusion coefficient of the limiting process:
\[\boxed{dX_t=-\frac{\beta(t)}2X_t\,dt+\sqrt{\beta(t)}\,dW_t.}\]
The small-step calculation also has an exact finite-grid counterpart for the forward process. Solving the linear VP SDE over one interval gives contraction \(\exp[-\tfrac12\int_{t_{n-1}}^{t_n}\beta(u)du]\) and conditional noise variance equal to one minus its square. Consequently, one exact grid matching is \(b_n=1-\exp[-\int_{t_{n-1}}^{t_n}\beta(u)\,du]\). The cumulative amplitude then satisfies the same schedule relation as before:
\[\alpha_t=\exp\left[-\frac12\int_0^t\beta(u)\,du\right].\]
The forward chain therefore determines the continuous VP density path as its schedule is refined. The score learned at its noise levels is the score of this path. We can now apply the reverse-time result to that same forward process.
crumbs: 10 · DDPM through the reverse VP SDE

title: 10 · DDPM through the reverse VP SDE
section: 2. Compare ancestral sampling with reverse-SDE Euler–Maruyama
text:
2. Compare ancestral sampling with reverse-SDE Euler–Maruyama

2.1. Reverse the common forward process
For a forward SDE \(dX_t=f(X_t,t)dt+g(t)dW_t\), the reverse-SDE lecture gives, in the increasing generation clock \(\tau=1-t\),
\[dY_\tau=[-f(Y_\tau,t)+g(t)^2s_t(Y_\tau)]d\tau
+g(t)d\overline W_\tau.\]
Here \(s_t=\partial_x\log p_t\) is the true forward marginal score. The minus sign on \(f\) reverses the forward drift, and the score term accounts for the reversal of the probability evolution. Substituting \(f(x,t)=-\beta(t)x/2\) and \(g(t)^2=\beta(t)\) gives
\[\boxed{dY_\tau=\beta(t)\left[\frac12Y_\tau+s_t(Y_\tau)\right]d\tau
+\sqrt{\beta(t)}\,d\overline W_\tau,\qquad t=1-\tau.}\]


2.2. Discretize the reverse SDE
Moving from forward time \(t_n\) to \(t_{n-1}\) advances the reverse clock by the positive amount \(h_n\). Integrate the reverse SDE over this interval and freeze its drift and diffusion coefficients at the current state \(x=x_{t_n}\) and time \(t_n\). The Brownian integral with the frozen coefficient is distributed as \(\sqrt{h_n\beta(t_n)}Z_n\). Replacing the true score by its trained estimate gives the Euler–Maruyama step
\[\boxed{x_{t_{n-1}}=x+h_n\beta(t_n)[x/2+s_\theta(x,t_n)]
+\sqrt{h_n\beta(t_n)}Z_n.}\]
The reversal of forward contraction produces the term \(h_n\beta(t_n)x/2\). The learned score contributes \(h_n\beta(t_n)s_\theta\), and the Brownian increment contributes the Gaussian term. These coefficients are now consequences of the reverse SDE. To interpret DDPM as a solver for this equation, we must check that its ancestral update has the same leading drift and noise variance.


2.3. Expand ancestral sampling and compare the increments
Use the DDPM variance choice \(\nu_n=b_n\), as in Song’s Appendix E comparison. At a positive-time step before final reconstruction,
\[x_{t_{n-1}}^{\mathrm{DDPM}}=
\frac{x+b_ns_\theta(x,t_n)}{\sqrt{1-b_n}}+\sqrt{b_n}Z_n.\]
The Gaussian increment already has variance \(b_n\), which agrees to leading order with \(h_n\beta(t_n)\). The remaining difference lies in the mean. For fixed \(x,t_n\) and bounded score, expand the factor multiplying the state and score:
\[\begin{aligned}
\frac{x+b_ns_\theta}{\sqrt{1-b_n}}
&=(x+b_ns_\theta)\left[1+\frac{b_n}2+O(b_n^2)\right]\\
&=x+b_n[x/2+s_\theta]+O(b_n^2).
\end{aligned}\]
More explicitly, the mean has expansion
\[\frac{x+b_ns_\theta}{\sqrt{1-b_n}}
=x+b_n(x/2+s_\theta)
+b_n^2(3x/8+s_\theta/2)+O(b_n^3).\]
Thus the mean difference from the leading Euler–Maruyama form is \(O(h_n^2)\), and the noise-variance difference is also \(O(h_n^2)\) when \(b_n=\beta(t_n)h_n+O(h_n^2)\). These are statements about the local conditional moments, not a claim that the whole stochastic sample update has a pathwise error of order \(h_n^2\). Define the reverse increment \(\Delta X=x_{t_{n-1}}^{\mathrm{DDPM}}-x\). Dividing its conditional mean and variance by the positive reverse-time increment gives
\[\frac{\mathbb E[\Delta X\mid x]}{h_n}
\longrightarrow\beta(t)[x/2+s_\theta(x,t)],\qquad
\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\Delta X\mid x)}{h_n}
\longrightarrow\beta(t).\]
These limits identify the reverse VP drift and diffusion variance. With the exact score they identify the true reversed process; with an approximate score they identify the corresponding learned reverse SDE. Under the regularity conditions required for numerical convergence, ancestral DDPM is therefore a consistent discretization of those dynamics. It need not equal Euler–Maruyama at a finite grid spacing.
Song’s Appendix E makes the same conclusion by comparing ancestral DDPM with another discretization, called reverse diffusion. Working through that construction makes clear why different finite formulas can belong to the same continuous framework.

title: 10 · DDPM through the reverse VP SDE
section: 3. Match the discrete coefficients in Song’s construction
text:
3. Match the discrete coefficients in Song’s construction

3.1. Insert the DDPM forward displacement and noise coefficient
To express Appendix E in our indexing, write a forward numerical step as
\[x_{t_n}=x_{t_{n-1}}+F_n(x_{t_{n-1}})+G_nZ_n.\]
Here \(F_n\) is the numerical forward displacement and \(G_n^2\) is its noise variance; both already contain the step size. They are not the continuous coefficients \(f\) and \(g\). Song’s construction reverses the numerical displacement at the current state, adds the score correction using that same noise variance, and retains a Gaussian increment:
\[x_{t_{n-1}}=x-F_n(x)+G_n^2s_\theta(x,t_n)+G_nZ_n.\]
For DDPM, \(F_n(x)=(\sqrt{1-b_n}-1)x\) and \(G_n=\sqrt{b_n}\). Substitution gives
\[\boxed{x_{t_{n-1}}^{\mathrm{RD}}
=(2-\sqrt{1-b_n})x+b_ns_\theta(x,t_n)+\sqrt{b_n}Z_n.}\]


3.2. Compare the resulting rule with ancestral DDPM
The substitution has produced Song’s reverse-diffusion update, not Ho’s ancestral update. The coefficient comparison makes the relationship explicit:

DDPM ancestral, \(\nu_n=b_n\)

\(b_n(1-b_n)^{-1/2}\)

Song reverse diffusion
\(2-\sqrt{1-b_n}\)

The table distinguishes the three numerical rules without changing their common limiting target. Expanding each row for a small interval shows that all three have the same leading coefficients as the grid is refined. In particular, \(2-\sqrt{1-b_n}=1+b_n/2+O(b_n^2)\). This is the sense in which Song’s framework includes DDPM as a numerical solver for the reverse VP SDE; it is stronger than merely observing that both methods use a score. Song et al., Section 4.1 and Appendix E
For the two discrete rules using exactly the same \(b_n\), we can make the difference still more explicit. Write \(s=s_\theta(x,t_n)\). Their conditional means expand as
\[\begin{aligned}
\mu_{\mathrm{ancestral}}
&=x+b_n(x/2+s)+b_n^2(3x/8+s/2)+O(b_n^3),\\
\mu_{\mathrm{RD}}
&=x+b_n(x/2+s)+b_n^2x/8+O(b_n^3).
\end{aligned}\]
Consequently,
\[\boxed{\mu_{\mathrm{ancestral}}-\mu_{\mathrm{RD}}
=b_n^2(x/4+s/2)+O(b_n^3).}\]
Their noise variances are both \(b_n\). If the two single-step updates start at the same state and use the same Gaussian draw, only this difference of means remains. This is the direct discrete comparison in the third step: equality of the leading terms, with a generally nonzero finite-step correction.

title: 10 · DDPM through the reverse VP SDE
section: Variance choices and endpoint qualifications
text:
Variance choices and endpoint qualifications
The comparison above uses the variance \(\nu_n=b_n\), matching Song’s Section 2.2 and Appendix E. Ho also considers the forward-posterior variance. For this alternative, \(\nu_n=\widetilde b_n\), at fixed positive time with \(\sigma_{t_n}^2\) bounded away from zero,
\[\widetilde b_n=b_n-
\frac{b_n^2\alpha_{t_{n-1}}^2}{\sigma_{t_n}^2}
=b_n+O(b_n^2).\]
It therefore has the same leading diffusion variance on such intervals. This expansion is not uniform near zero noise. Ho’s final-step convention \(Z_1=0\) is a separate reconstruction operation, not the generic Euler–Maruyama rule.
With the true score and correct terminal initialization, the continuous reverse SDE follows the reversed marginal path. A finite ancestral chain still has kernel and discretization error; a learned score and approximate terminal prior add their own errors. The SDE interpretation explains the sampler without asserting exact finite-step reversal.
The probability-flow route studied earlier is related but uses different dynamics. Written with the same increasing reverse clock, its velocity is
\[\frac{dy}{d\tau}=\frac{\beta(t)}2[y+s_t(y)].\]
Its score coefficient is half the reverse SDE’s, and it contains no Brownian term. With an exact score and matching initialization, the two continuous processes have the same one-time marginals, although their trajectories differ. Simply removing the Gaussian increment from DDPM retains the reverse-SDE drift and does not create this ODE.
We can therefore reuse the learned denoising predictor while changing the numerical sampling problem. This part has shown how Ho’s ancestral rule fits the stochastic problem. The DDIM lecture next derives a particular discretization of the deterministic probability-flow problem.

title: 11 · DDIM and the probability-flow ODE
text:
1. A trained denoising predictor supplies the score
The preceding DDPM reinterpretation takes the reverse-SDE route. This part develops the separate deterministic route.
The probability-flow ODE notes supply the deterministic transport foundation. The separate reverse-SDE note covers stochastic transport. Here we focus on constructing and understanding DDIM.
For the VP schedule used in Part 03,
\[X_t=\alpha_tX_0+\sigma_t\varepsilon,\qquad
\sigma_t=\sqrt{1-\alpha_t^2},\qquad
\alpha_t=\exp\left[-\frac12\int_0^t\beta(u)\,du\right].\]
Here \(\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) is independent of clean data. Squared-error noise regression estimates \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon\mid X_t=x]\), so
\[s_\theta(x,t)=-\frac{\varepsilon_\theta(x,t)}{\sigma_t},
\qquad
D_\theta(x,t)=\frac{x-\sigma_t\varepsilon_\theta(x,t)}{\alpha_t}.\]
These are the same conversions used earlier. A trained noise predictor can therefore supply either a score or a clean-data estimate. The sampling algorithm is an additional choice.
The primary framework is Yang Song et al., Score-Based Generative Modeling through SDEs, especially the reverse SDE, training objective, and probability-flow ODE. Yang Song’s explanatory blog separates the stochastic reverse process from its deterministic counterpart. For the discrete methods, use Ho, Jain, and Abbeel, DDPM and Jiaming Song, Meng, and Ermon, DDIM. Yang Song’s SDE paper and Jiaming Song’s DDIM paper have different first authors.

title: 11 · DDIM and the probability-flow ODE
section: 2. Translate discrete notation before comparing formulas
text:
2. Translate discrete notation before comparing formulas
Let \(0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N=1\). We retain \(\alpha_{t_i}\) for the cumulative signal amplitude. Write the one-step noise variance as \(b_i\) to distinguish it from the continuous rate \(\beta(t)\):
\[b_i=1-\frac{\alpha_{t_i}^2}{\alpha_{t_{i-1}}^2},\qquad
X_{t_i}=\sqrt{1-b_i}\,X_{t_{i-1}}+\sqrt{b_i}\,Z_i.\]
Here the \(Z_i\) are independent standard normals. For a VP SDE sampled exactly on this grid,
\[b_i=1-\exp\left[-\int_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i}\beta(u)\,du\right].\]

The DDIM paper uses its own \(\alpha_i\) for cumulative variance retention. Translate it to our \(\alpha_{t_i}^2\), not our amplitude. This notation difference changes square roots throughout the updates.

2.1. Reuse the trained denoising predictor
The standalone DDPM lecture presents Ho’s Algorithms 1 and 2, their original notation, and the mapping used here. Its training section shows that the simplified noise loss is exactly denoising score matching weighted by the cumulative noise variance. The predictor can therefore supply either stochastic DDPM sampling or deterministic DDIM sampling. Positive time-dependent loss weights preserve the unrestricted population optimum but can change a finite network’s fit.


2.2. The DDIM route from the estimated score





flowchart TD
    A["Trained denoising predictor"] --> B["Estimated marginal score"]
    B --> C["Probability-flow ODE"]
    C --> D["Rescale the state by the signal amplitude"]
    D --> E["Use the noise-to-signal ratio as time"]
    E --> F["Explicit Euler in transformed coordinates"]
    F --> G["Deterministic DDIM update"]






The following sections follow this route. A different choice, direct Euler or Heun in the original coordinates, also discretizes the probability-flow ODE but generally gives different finite updates. DDPM’s stochastic route is developed in its own lecture.

title: 11 · DDIM and the probability-flow ODE
section: 3. The deterministic transport to discretize
text:
3. The deterministic transport to discretize
In increasing generation time \(\tau=1-t\), the VP probability-flow ODE is
\[\frac{dy}{d\tau}=\frac{\beta(t)}2[y+s_t(y)],\qquad t=1-\tau.\]
Its derivation is in the probability-flow ODE lecture. With the exact score, suitable regularity, and matching terminal initialization, this transports the prescribed densities backward to data. The initial sample supplies the randomness; the subsequent trajectory is deterministic.
An Euler step in the original state and time coordinates is
\[x_{t-h}\approx x_t+\frac{h\beta(t)}2[x_t+s_\theta(x_t,t)].\]
DDIM will instead apply Euler after transforming those coordinates. This distinction explains why the finite updates differ while their continuous limit agrees.

title: 11 · DDIM and the probability-flow ODE
section: 4. DDIM: a deterministic update from the same predictor
text:
4. DDIM: a deterministic update from the same predictor
Follow the diagram from the estimated score to the probability-flow ODE and then to Euler in transformed coordinates. DDIM constructs a deterministic coupling; it does not merely iterate the reverse conditional mean. The DDPM lecture explains why that mean-only recursion can collapse variance.
Choose two grid times \(u<t\), possibly skipping intermediate indices. At the current input, compute
\[\widehat x_0=D_\theta(x_t,t)
=\frac{x_t-\sigma_t\varepsilon_\theta(x_t,t)}{\alpha_t}.\]
The deterministic DDIM update is
\[\boxed{x_u=\alpha_u\widehat x_0+\sigma_u\varepsilon_\theta(x_t,t).}\]
Equivalently,
\[x_u=\frac{\alpha_u}{\alpha_t}x_t+
\left(\sigma_u-\frac{\alpha_u}{\alpha_t}\sigma_t\right)
\varepsilon_\theta(x_t,t).\]
The update holds the current predicted clean value and predicted noise fixed over this step, then recombines them at the next noise level. At the next step the predictions are recomputed. It does not recover the particular forward noise realization of an observed image. Randomness comes from the initial terminal sample; no fresh noise is added in this deterministic update.

title: 11 · DDIM and the probability-flow ODE
section: 5. Why deterministic DDIM is an ODE discretization
text:
5. Why deterministic DDIM is an ODE discretization
First, at a fixed positive time away from the zero-noise endpoint, a small-step expansion in ordinary time gives
\[x_{t-h}-x_t
=h\left[-\frac{\alpha_t'}{\alpha_t}x_t+
\left(\frac{\alpha_t'}{\alpha_t}\sigma_t-\sigma_t'\right)
\varepsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\right]+O(h^2).\]
For VP, use \(\alpha_t'/\alpha_t=-\beta(t)/2\) and \(\sigma_t\sigma_t'=\beta(t)\alpha_t^2/2\). The update becomes
\[x_{t-h}-x_t
=\frac{h\beta(t)}2
\left[x_t-\frac{\varepsilon_\theta(x_t,t)}{\sigma_t}\right]+O(h^2)
=\frac{h\beta(t)}2[x_t+s_\theta(x_t,t)]+O(h^2).\]
This is the probability-flow ODE’s backward velocity. There is an even stronger numerical interpretation. Define
\[y_t=\frac{x_t}{\alpha_t},\qquad r_t=\frac{\sigma_t}{\alpha_t}.\]
The transformed corruption is \(y_t=X_0+r_t\varepsilon\). Dividing out signal contraction leaves additive Gaussian noise with standard deviation \(r_t\), which motivates these coordinates. This is a statement about the conditional laws; it does not equate a fixed-noise interpolation with a Brownian trajectory.
For positive noise, \(\alpha_t>0\), and a strictly increasing noise ratio, Appendix A derives
\[\boxed{\frac{dy}{dr}=\varepsilon_\theta(\alpha_t y,t),\qquad t=t(r).}\]
Divide the deterministic DDIM update by \(\alpha_u\):
\[\boxed{y_u=y_t+(r_u-r_t)\varepsilon_\theta(x_t,t).}\]
That is exactly an explicit Euler step for this transformed ODE, with \(r\) decreasing during generation. DDIM is not generally the same finite update as Euler in the original \(x,t\) coordinates. Neither method is generally the exact ODE solution for a finite step. The ODE connection appears in DDIM, Section 4.3.

title: 11 · DDIM and the probability-flow ODE
section: 6. A family connecting deterministic and stochastic updates
text:
6. A family connecting deterministic and stochastic updates
Let \(0\leq\eta\leq1\) and define a step-noise standard deviation
\[\gamma_{t\to u}
=\eta\frac{\sigma_u}{\sigma_t}
\sqrt{1-\frac{\alpha_t^2}{\alpha_u^2}}.\]
The generalized update is
\[x_u=\alpha_u\widehat x_0+
\sqrt{\sigma_u^2-\gamma_{t\to u}^2}\,\varepsilon_\theta(x_t,t)
+\gamma_{t\to u}z.\]

\(\eta=0\) gives deterministic DDIM.
\(\eta=1\) on adjacent grid times gives the DDPM posterior-variance choice \(\nu_i=\widetilde b_i\), with the same noise-prediction mean.
\(\eta=1\) is not the \(\nu_i=b_i\) variance choice at finite steps. For skipped times, it describes a coarsened transition rather than replaying all original adjacent steps.

For any \(\eta>0\) on a step with positive destination noise, it is a stochastic sampler, not a deterministic probability-flow ODE solver. The common conditional corruption marginals allow reuse of the trained predictor; they do not imply that all finite-step generated marginals are exact. This family is developed in DDIM, Eqs. (12) and (16), and Appendix C.1.

title: 11 · DDIM and the probability-flow ODE
section: 7. A Gaussian check that separates exact flows from discretizations
text:
7. A Gaussian check that separates exact flows from discretizations
Take \(p_0=\mathcal N(0,1)\). VP leaves this density unchanged, so
\[s_t(x)=-x,\qquad\varepsilon_*(x,t)=\sigma_t x.\]
The exact probability-flow velocity is zero, hence every ODE particle stays fixed. The reverse SDE is stationary Ornstein–Uhlenbeck dynamics: particles fluctuate but the density remains standard normal.
Deterministic DDIM instead gives the finite step
\[x_u=(\alpha_u\alpha_t+\sigma_u\sigma_t)x_t.\]
The coefficient is the inner product of two unit vectors \((\alpha_u,\sigma_u)\) and \((\alpha_t,\sigma_t)\). It is less than one for distinct noise levels, so this finite step multiplies the variance by \((\alpha_u\alpha_t+\sigma_u\sigma_t)^2\), even with the exact predictor. The contraction can be severe: a single step to \(u=0\) gives \(x_0=\alpha_t x_t\), nearly collapsing the cloud when \(\alpha_t\) is small. Direct Euler in \((x,t)\) is exact for this zero-velocity example. As step sizes shrink, that discretization effect vanishes on regular intervals. This example shows why “same continuous ODE” must not be replaced by “identical finite samples.”
For a complementary case, take clean data to be a fixed point \(c\). Then \(D_*(x,t)=c\) and the exact positive-time ODE paths are \(x_t=\alpha_tc+\sigma_te\) for a fixed Gaussian label \(e\). Deterministic DDIM maps these paths exactly between noise levels, while direct Euler in the original coordinates is generally approximate. The point-mass endpoint is a singular limit, not a regular invertible flow endpoint.
The Gaussian and point-mass checks show that finite-step accuracy depends on both the density and the discretization. DDIM’s deterministic update is neither universally exact nor obtained by suppressing the noise in an ancestral sampler.

title: 11 · DDIM and the probability-flow ODE
section: Appendix A. Deriving the transformed ODE
text:
Appendix A. Deriving the transformed ODE
Write the forward-clock probability-flow ODE using noise prediction:
\[\dot x=-\frac\beta2x+\frac\beta{2\sigma}\varepsilon_\theta(x,t).\]
Since \(\dot\alpha/\alpha=-\beta/2\), differentiation of \(y=x/\alpha\) cancels the linear drift:
\[\dot y=\frac{\dot x}{\alpha}-\frac{x\dot\alpha}{\alpha^2}
=\frac{\beta}{2\alpha\sigma}\varepsilon_\theta(x,t).\]
Also,
\[\begin{aligned}
\dot r&=\frac{\dot\sigma}{\alpha}-\frac{\sigma\dot\alpha}{\alpha^2}\\
&=\frac{\beta\alpha}{2\sigma}+\frac{\beta\sigma}{2\alpha}
=\frac{\beta}{2\alpha\sigma},
\end{aligned}\]
using \(\alpha^2+\sigma^2=1\). Dividing gives \(dy/dr=\varepsilon_\theta(\alpha_t y,t)\). Where \(\beta>0\) the noise ratio is strictly increasing and can parameterize the ODE. For a positive initial rate, \(\dot r\) diverges at zero noise, although the transformed equation need not be singular when its predictor extends regularly to \(r=0\). The derivation at the endpoint requires a limiting interpretation; the finite DDIM formula itself avoids dividing by \(\sigma_u\) at its destination.

title: 11 · DDIM and the probability-flow ODE
section: Appendix B. Checking the stochastic DDIM connection
text:
Appendix B. Checking the stochastic DDIM connection
For adjacent times \(u=t_{i-1}\) and \(t=t_i\), put \(b=b_i=1-\alpha_t^2/\alpha_u^2\). At \(\eta=1\),
\[\gamma^2=b\frac{\sigma_u^2}{\sigma_t^2}=\widetilde b_i.\]
Also \(\sigma_t^2-b=\alpha_t^2\sigma_u^2/\alpha_u^2\), giving
\[\sqrt{\sigma_u^2-\gamma^2}
=\frac{\alpha_t\sigma_u^2}{\alpha_u\sigma_t}.\]
Substitute \(\widehat x_0=(x_t-\sigma_t\varepsilon_\theta)/\alpha_t\) into the generalized mean. The coefficient of \(\varepsilon_\theta\) simplifies to
\[-\frac{\alpha_u\sigma_t}{\alpha_t}
+\frac{\alpha_t\sigma_u^2}{\alpha_u\sigma_t}
=-\frac{\alpha_u}{\alpha_t}\frac b{\sigma_t}.\]
Since \(\alpha_u/\alpha_t=1/\sqrt{1-b}\), the resulting mean and variance are exactly the stated DDPM posterior-variance update. This is a finite-step algebraic identity, unlike the limiting SDE correspondence.

title: 01 · Reverse-SDE sampling
text:
1. From a fixed target to a prescribed density path
Ordinary Langevin dynamics uses the score of one fixed target and attempts to approach its stationary distribution. Reverse diffusion instead follows a time-dependent sequence of target densities, \(p_1,p_{1-h},\ldots,p_0\). It does not wait for equilibrium at each noise level.
Choose a forward process
\[dX_t=f(X_t,t)\,dt+g(t)\,dW_t,\]
and let \(p_t\) be its marginal density. A one-step Euler–Maruyama approximation adds deterministic drift \(h f\) and independent Gaussian noise with standard deviation \(g\sqrt h\). Brownian increments scale with \(\sqrt h\), not \(h\).
Learn \(s_\theta(x,t)\approx\partial_x\log p_t(x)\) using known conditional corruption kernels. The distinction between conditional labels and marginal predictions is the same as in the preceding topic.

title: 01 · Reverse-SDE sampling
section: 2. Reverse the stochastic process
text:
2. Reverse the stochastic process
Write \(Y_\tau=X_{1-\tau}\) for the time-reversed process in law. Under the usual smoothness and time-reversal conditions, and with diffusion coefficient independent of position,
\[\boxed{dY_\tau=
[-f(Y_\tau,t)+g(t)^2s_t(Y_\tau)]\,d\tau
+g(t)\,d\overline W_\tau,\qquad t=1-\tau.}\]
The Brownian motion is defined with respect to the reverse-time information; it is not obtained by simply negating the original Brownian increments. The formula above applies to scalar \(g(t)\); state-dependent diffusion requires additional derivative terms.
In the original decreasing clock, the same reverse dynamics is often written
\[dX_t=[f(X_t,t)-g(t)^2s_t(X_t)]\,dt+g(t)\,d\overline W_t,
\qquad dt<0.\]
Noise increments in this notation have variance proportional to \(|dt|\). We use the increasing reverse clock to avoid negative-variance interpretations. The primary reference is Song et al., Eq. (6); Yang Song’s blog explains the forward and reverse SDEs as separate processes.

title: 01 · Reverse-SDE sampling
section: 3. VP diffusion and an explicit sampler
text:
3. VP diffusion and an explicit sampler
For the VP forward process,
\[f(x,t)=-\tfrac12\beta(t)x,\qquad g(t)=\sqrt{\beta(t)},\]
with the same schedule relation as before:
\[\alpha_t=\exp\left[-\tfrac12\int_0^t\beta(u)\,du\right],
\qquad X_t\mid X_0=x_0\sim\mathcal N(\alpha_tx_0,1-\alpha_t^2).\]
The reverse SDE is
\[dY_\tau=\beta(t)[\tfrac12Y_\tau+s_t(Y_\tau)]\,d\tau
+\sqrt{\beta(t)}\,d\overline W_\tau.\]
For \(h=t_k-t_{k+1}>0\), generate with
\[\boxed{x_{k+1}=x_k+h\beta(t_k)[\tfrac12x_k+s_\theta(x_k,t_k)]
+\sqrt{h\beta(t_k)}\,z_k,\qquad z_k\sim\mathcal N(0,1).}\]
Start from the actual \(p_1\) if available, or a justified approximation such as standard normal after sufficient corruption. Draw fresh independent noise at each step. Stop at a positive cutoff compatible with the trained score if the endpoint is singular. The exact continuous process has the required marginals with the exact score and matched initialization; a learned score, finite steps, and approximate prior introduce errors.

title: 01 · Reverse-SDE sampling
section: 4. Why this is not an ODE with noise simply added
text:
4. Why this is not an ODE with noise simply added
In increasing reverse time, the probability-flow ODE uses
\[b_{\mathrm{ODE}}=-f+\tfrac12g^2s_t,\]
while the reverse SDE uses
\[b_{\mathrm{SDE}}=-f+g^2s_t.\]
Therefore
\[b_{\mathrm{SDE}}=b_{\mathrm{ODE}}+\tfrac12g^2s_t.\]
The extra score drift compensates for the Brownian spreading. Adding \(g\,dW\) to the probability-flow ODE without that drift correction changes the density evolution. Appendix A checks the factors explicitly.

title: 01 · Reverse-SDE sampling
section: 5. A Gaussian example checks the sign and coefficient
text:
5. A Gaussian example checks the sign and coefficient
If the clean law is standard normal, VP preserves it and \(s_t(x)=-x\). The reverse SDE becomes
\[dY_\tau=-\tfrac12\beta(t)Y_\tau\,d\tau
+\sqrt{\beta(t)}\,d\overline W_\tau.\]
At mean zero and variance one, the instantaneous mean and variance derivatives are zero. The density stays standard normal although particles move randomly. The corresponding probability-flow ODE has zero velocity, so its particles remain fixed. The two processes agree on marginals, not trajectories.
For constant \(\beta\) and Euler step \(h\), the stochastic update has stationary variance \(1/(1-h\beta/4)\) when \(0<h\beta<4\). Its deviation from one is a discretization effect, not a failure of the continuous reverse-SDE formula.

title: 01 · Reverse-SDE sampling
section: Appendix A. Check the reversed density evolution
text:
Appendix A. Check the reversed density evolution
The forward Fokker–Planck equation is
\[\partial_tp_t=-\partial_x(fp_t)+\tfrac12g^2\partial_{xx}p_t.\]
Set \(r_\tau=p_{1-\tau}\). Then
\[\partial_\tau r_\tau=\partial_x(fr_\tau)-\tfrac12g^2\partial_{xx}r_\tau,\]
where coefficients and scores are evaluated at \(t=1-\tau\). The proposed reverse SDE gives
\[\begin{aligned}
-\partial_x[(-f+g^2s_t)r_\tau]+\tfrac12g^2\partial_{xx}r_\tau
&=\partial_x(fr_\tau)-g^2\partial_x(r_\tau s_t)
+\tfrac12g^2\partial_{xx}r_\tau\\
&=\partial_x(fr_\tau)-\tfrac12g^2\partial_{xx}r_\tau,
\end{aligned}\]
because \(r_\tau s_t=\partial_xr_\tau\). This verifies the marginal equation. Identifying the full reversed path law requires the time-reversal result cited above; the marginal calculation alone does not establish that joint law.
For comparison, the ODE flux with \(-f+g^2s_t/2\) gives the same marginal equation without a diffusion term. See Probability-Flow ODE, Part 10 for the connection to DDPM and DDIM.

title: Inequalities Worth Knowing
text:
1. Markov: the one everything else comes from
A standalone tutorial, and a short one. Five inequalities that between them justify most of the “and therefore it concentrates” steps in this course. Each is stated, proved in a few lines, and given the job it actually does. The last two sections are the payoff: how a bound that knows only the mean and variance already forces data to cluster, and where that bound is far too pessimistic.
For a non-negative random variable \(X \ge 0\) and any \(a > 0\),
\[
\boxed{\;\mathbb{P}(X \ge a) \;\le\; \frac{\mathbb{E}[X]}{a}.\;}
\]
Proof. Since \(X \ge 0\), we have \(X \ge a\,\mathbf{1}\{X \ge a\}\) pointwise — check the two cases: if \(X \ge a\) the right side is \(a \le X\); otherwise it is \(0 \le X\). Take expectations and use monotonicity: \(\mathbb{E}[X] \ge a\,\mathbb{P}(X \ge a)\). \(\square\)
That is the entire proof, and it is worth noticing how little it uses: only non-negativity and the mean. In exchange, the bound is usually weak. Its value is that it needs almost nothing, and that everything below is a corollary of it applied to a cleverly chosen non-negative quantity.

title: Inequalities Worth Knowing
section: 2. Chebyshev: mean and variance force concentration
text:
2. Chebyshev: mean and variance force concentration
Apply Markov to \((X - \mu)^2\), which is non-negative, with threshold \(k^2\sigma^2\):
\[
\mathbb{P}\big(|X - \mu| \ge k\sigma\big)
= \mathbb{P}\big((X-\mu)^2 \ge k^2\sigma^2\big)
\le \frac{\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2]}{k^2\sigma^2}
= \frac{\sigma^2}{k^2\sigma^2},
\]
so for any random variable with finite variance and any \(k > 0\),
\[
\boxed{\;\mathbb{P}\big(|X - \mu| \ge k\sigma\big) \;\le\; \frac{1}{k^{2}}.\;}
\]
Read what this says. It assumes nothing about the shape of the distribution — not symmetry, not unimodality, not a density. Knowing only the mean and the variance, at most \(1/4\) of the mass can sit two standard deviations or more from the mean, at most \(1/9\) beyond three. Variance is not merely a summary of spread; it is a budget that limits how much mass can be far out.



\(k\)
Chebyshev bound \(1/k^2\)
Actual, if Gaussian

The right column shows how much sharper the Gaussian tail bound is. Chebyshev is tight — there are distributions attaining it — but for the Gaussian it is wildly pessimistic, off by a factor of nearly \(1000\) at \(k=4\). Something much stronger is true for the shapes we actually meet, and asking why leads straight to the normal distribution.

title: Inequalities Worth Knowing
section: 3. Jensen: which way convexity bends an average
text:
3. Jensen: which way convexity bends an average
For a convex \(\varphi\) and integrable \(X\),
\[
\boxed{\;\varphi\big(\mathbb{E}[X]\big) \;\le\; \mathbb{E}\big[\varphi(X)\big].\;}
\]
For concave \(\varphi\) the inequality reverses.
Proof. Convexity means the graph lies above each of its tangent lines. Take the tangent at \(m = \mathbb{E}[X]\): there is a slope \(c\) with \(\varphi(x) \ge \varphi(m) + c(x - m)\) for all \(x\). Take expectations; the linear term has expectation zero. \(\square\)
Three uses you will meet:

\(\mathbb{E}[X^2] \ge (\mathbb{E}X)^2\), i.e. variance is non-negative — Jensen with \(\varphi(x)=x^2\).
\(\log \mathbb{E}[X] \ge \mathbb{E}[\log X]\) — \(\log\) is concave. This single line is what makes the ELBO a lower bound on the log-evidence.
\(\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q) \ge 0\), with equality only when \(p = q\) — Jensen applied to \(-\log\). Every “this divergence is non-negative, so minimising it makes sense” argument is this.

title: Inequalities Worth Knowing
section: 4. Cauchy–Schwarz, and correlation being bounded
text:
4. Cauchy–Schwarz, and correlation being bounded
\[
\boxed{\;\big|\mathbb{E}[XY]\big| \;\le\; \sqrt{\mathbb{E}[X^2]\,\mathbb{E}[Y^2]}.\;}
\]
Proof. For every \(t\), \(0 \le \mathbb{E}[(X - tY)^2] = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - 2t\,\mathbb{E}[XY] + t^2\mathbb{E}[Y^2]\). A quadratic in \(t\) that is never negative has non-positive discriminant: \(4(\mathbb{E}[XY])^2 - 4\mathbb{E}[X^2]\mathbb{E}[Y^2] \le 0\). \(\square\)
Applied to centred variables this says exactly that the correlation coefficient lies in \([-1,1]\), with \(|\rho| = 1\) precisely when \(Y\) is an affine function of \(X\). That is the fact underlying the constraint \(|\rho| < 1\) everywhere in the multivariate Gaussian reference — at \(|\rho| = 1\) the covariance matrix is singular and the ellipse collapses to a line.

title: Inequalities Worth Knowing
section: 5. The union bound
text:
5. The union bound
For any events \(A_1, A_2, \dots\) — no independence required —
\[
\boxed{\;\mathbb{P}\Big(\bigcup_i A_i\Big) \;\le\; \sum_i \mathbb{P}(A_i).\;}
\]
Proof. Countable subadditivity, which follows from countable additivity by disjointifying: replace \(A_i\) by \(A_i \setminus \bigcup_{j<i}A_j\), which is contained in \(A_i\) and hence no more probable. \(\square\)
Crude, and indispensable. It is how you go from “each of \(d\) coordinates is unlikely to be extreme” to “no coordinate is extreme”, at a cost of a factor \(d\). In high dimension that factor is the whole difficulty: with \(d = 784\), an event of probability \(10^{-3}\) per coordinate gives no useful bound at all across coordinates, which is one honest way to see why high-dimensional density estimation is hard.

title: Inequalities Worth Knowing
section: 6. Putting Markov to work: the weak law
text:
6. Putting Markov to work: the weak law
The inequalities are not decoration. Here is a complete theorem in three lines.
Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be i.i.d. with mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2\), and let \(\bar X_n\) be their average. Then \(\mathbb{E}[\bar X_n] = \mu\) and, because variances of independent variables add, \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n) = \sigma^2/n\). Chebyshev gives, for any \(\varepsilon > 0\),
\[
\mathbb{P}\big(|\bar X_n - \mu| \ge \varepsilon\big) \;\le\; \frac{\sigma^2}{n\varepsilon^2}
\;\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\; 0 .
\]
That is the weak law of large numbers, proved entirely from Markov. Note what it does and does not give: it says the average concentrates, but it says nothing about the shape of the fluctuation around \(\mu\). Rescaling by \(\sqrt{n}\) instead of \(n\) and asking what shape survives is the central limit theorem — and the answer being Gaussian, always, is the subject of the next tutorial.






TipKey takeaway



Markov is the whole toolkit: it needs only non-negativity, and Chebyshev, the weak law and most concentration results are Markov applied to a well-chosen non-negative quantity. What you buy with more assumptions is sharpness — Chebyshev’s \(1/k^2\) decay becomes the Gaussian’s \(e^{-k^2/2}\) once you know more than two moments, and closing that gap is exactly the question the Advanced track takes up.

title: Inequalities Worth Knowing
section: Exercises
text:
Exercises

Show Markov is tight: find a non-negative \(X\) and an \(a\) for which \(\mathbb{P}(X \ge a) = \mathbb{E}[X]/a\) exactly. (Two atoms suffice.)
Show Chebyshev is tight at \(k = 2\): construct a distribution with mean \(0\), variance \(1\), and exactly \(1/4\) of its mass at distance \(\ge 2\).
Why does Markov require \(X \ge 0\)? Give a random variable with \(\mathbb{E}[X] = 0\) for which the conclusion fails without it.
Use Jensen to show \(\mathbb{E}[1/X] \ge 1/\mathbb{E}[X]\) for a positive random variable, and give an example where the inequality is strict.
Use Cauchy–Schwarz to prove \(|\rho| \le 1\), and characterise exactly when \(|\rho| = 1\).
A vector has \(d\) coordinates, each of which exceeds \(3\sigma\) with probability at most \(0.0027\). Bound the probability that some coordinate does, for \(d = 10\) and \(d = 784\). At what \(d\) does the union bound stop saying anything?
Compare the Chebyshev bound at \(k=3\) with the true Gaussian tail. By what factor is Chebyshev too pessimistic? Now do the same at \(k=5\) and comment on how the gap grows.

title: The Random Walk: Forward, and Backward
text:
1. The object
A standalone tutorial, and the most economical object in the course. Toss a coin, add \(+1\) for heads and \(-1\) for tails, and keep a running total. That is the forward process of a diffusion model with the noise made as simple as noise can possibly be — and because it is that simple, every single thing we will later have to learn or approximate can here be done exactly, by counting.
The companion sheet Practice 1 built the machinery. This one spends it. The full derivations, with the small cases written out and the induction in full, are in Practice 2; the Walk Lab below is the same object to play with.
Let \(X_1, X_2, \dots\) be independent with \(\mathbb{P}(X_i = +1) = \mathbb{P}(X_i = -1) = \tfrac12\), and set
\[S_n = \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i .\]
This is the simple symmetric random walk. Put its update rule beside the one from note 01 and the resemblance is the entire point:
\[\underbrace{S_n = S_{n-1} + X_n}_{\text{here}}
\qquad\qquad
\underbrace{x_t = \sqrt{\alpha_t}\,x_{t-1} + \sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\,\varepsilon_t}_{\text{a diffusion model}}\]
Both are discrete-time Markov chains in which noise accumulates and nothing removes it; both run forward with no training required; and both end somewhere structureless. The difference is one multiplicative factor. The walk has no shrinkage, so its variance grows without bound — variance exploding; the DDPM update shrinks the old state just enough to hold the total variance at 1 — variance preserving. Both are used in practice, and the choice is a design decision rather than a mathematical necessity.
crumbs: The Random Walk: Forward, and Backward

title: The Random Walk: Forward, and Backward
section: 2. Variances add, so the walk spreads like \(\sqrt{n}\)
text:
2. Variances add, so the walk spreads like \(\sqrt{n}\)
Each increment has mean \(0\), and since \(X_i^2 = 1\) always, variance \(1\). The increments are independent, so variances add:
\[\mathbb{E}[S_n] = 0, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(S_n) = n, \qquad \operatorname{sd}(S_n) = \sqrt{n}.\]






NoteThis is the \(\sqrt{t}\) envelope



The W01 demo Progressively Adding Noise draws a cloud of walkers spreading with a \(\sqrt{t}\) curve over it. That curve is the line above. A walk does not travel a distance proportional to the number of steps — it travels proportional to the square root of it, because the steps cancel in a way that lets variances rather than distances accumulate.
Everything in this course that spreads like \(\sqrt{t}\) spreads for this reason.
crumbs: The Random Walk: Forward, and Backward

title: The Random Walk: Forward, and Backward
section: 3. The exact law, and where the binomial comes from
text:
3. The exact law, and where the binomial comes from
Here it matters what the underlying sample space actually is, because the answer is a counting argument and counting needs something to count.
An outcome is a whole path, not a position:
\[\Omega_n = \{-1,+1\}^n, \qquad \omega = (\omega_1,\dots,\omega_n), \qquad |\Omega_n| = 2^n,\]
with every path equally likely, \(\mathbb{P}(\{\omega\}) = 2^{-n}\). On this space \(S_n(\omega) = \sum_i \omega_i\) is a random variable in the sense of note 02 — an honest function — and the interesting thing about it is that it is massively many-to-one: it crushes \(2^n\) paths onto at most \(n+1\) positions.
The event \(\{S_n = k\}\) is therefore a set of paths, the preimage \(S_n^{-1}(\{k\})\), and because the measure is uniform,
\[\mathbb{P}(S_n = k) \;=\; \frac{\big|S_n^{-1}(\{k\})\big|}{2^n}
\;=\; \frac{\text{paths ending at } k}{\text{all paths}} .\]
Probability has become combinatorics, not by choice but because the coin is fair.
Now count. A path with \(j\) up-steps and \(n-j\) down-steps ends at \(j - (n-j) = 2j-n\), so ending at \(k\) is the same condition as having exactly \(j = (n+k)/2\) up-steps. The paths ending at \(k\) are in bijection with the ways of choosing which \(j\) of the \(n\) steps went up, and there are \(\binom{n}{j}\) of those:
\[\boxed{\;\mathbb{P}(S_n = k) = \binom{n}{\tfrac{n+k}{2}}\,2^{-n},
\qquad k \in \{-n, -n+2, \dots, n-2, n\}.\;}\]
Note the parity constraint: each step changes \(S\) by an odd amount, so after \(n\) steps only positions of the same parity as \(n\) are reachable. \(\mathbb{P}(S_4 = 1)\) is not small — it is exactly zero.






TipThis is the discrete \(q(x_t \mid x_0)\)



Note 05’s closed-form marginal is what lets a diffusion model jump to any noise level in one step rather than simulating the chain. The boxed formula is that same property, with a binomial coefficient where the Gaussian would be. Without it, sampling \(S_{1000}\) would mean tossing a thousand coins.


Interactive — The Walk Lab runs all of this. Act I stacks the counts up column by column and draws the distribution on the same \(k\) axis, so it reads as the column of counts turned on its side. Act II is §7 below — observe an endpoint and watch path space collapse. Act III is §6, the reverse step.
crumbs: The Random Walk: Forward, and Backward

title: The Random Walk: Forward, and Backward
section: 4. The equation the density obeys
text:
4. The equation the density obeys
Stop watching the walker and watch the distribution. Write \(p_n(k) = \mathbb{P}(S_n = k)\). There are exactly two ways to be at \(k\) at time \(n+1\), so
\[p_{n+1}(k) = \tfrac12\,p_n(k-1) + \tfrac12\,p_n(k+1).\]
Subtract \(p_n(k)\) from both sides and regroup:
\[\underbrace{p_{n+1}(k) - p_n(k)}_{\text{difference in time}}
\;=\; \tfrac12 \underbrace{\big[\,p_n(k+1) - 2p_n(k) + p_n(k-1)\,\big]}_{\text{second difference in space}}\]
The left side is a discrete time derivative; the right is the three-point second difference, the discrete \(\partial_x^2\). In the continuum,
\[\boxed{\;\frac{\partial p}{\partial t} = \frac12\,\frac{\partial^2 p}{\partial x^2}\;}\]






ImportantThat is the heat equation



It is the Fokker–Planck equation for Brownian motion — Module 5’s centrepiece — derived from a coin toss with nothing but addition and subtraction.
Read it rather than merely verifying it: where \(p\) is concave (a peak) the second difference is negative and the density falls; where it is convex (a trough) it rises. Peaks flatten, troughs fill, the whole thing spreads. That is what “adding noise” does to a distribution, as opposed to what it does to a sample.


Where \(\sqrt{\Delta t}\) comes from. Take lattice spacing \(h\) and time step \(\Delta t\), so after time \(t\) the walker has taken \(n = t/\Delta t\) steps and, by §2, has variance \(n h^2 = t h^2/\Delta t\). Only one choice of \(h\) survives the limit:








choice
variance at time \(t\)
limit




\(h = \Delta t\)
\(t\,\Delta t \to 0\)
the walk dies


\(h = \sqrt{\Delta t}\)
\(t\)
Brownian motion


\(h = (\Delta t)^{1/4}\)
\(t/\sqrt{\Delta t} \to \infty\)
the walk explodes



This is why an SDE is written \(dX = b\,dt + \sigma\,dW\) with \(dW\) of size \(\sqrt{dt}\) and not \(dt\) — and it is the same fact that puts a square root on the noise coefficient \(\sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\), since that coefficient multiplies the variable while variances scale by its square.
crumbs: The Random Walk: Forward, and Backward

title: The Random Walk: Forward, and Backward
section: 5. The Gaussian is a limit, not an assumption
text:
5. The Gaussian is a limit, not an assumption
\(S_n\) is a sum of \(n\) i.i.d. terms with mean \(0\) and variance \(1\), so \(S_n/\sqrt{n} \Rightarrow \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) — equivalently, the binomial of §3, once centred and scaled, approaches a Gaussian density.
The increments here are as un-Gaussian as a random variable can be: two atoms, no density at all. After enough steps the marginal is Gaussian anyway. So the Gaussian noise in a diffusion model is not a modelling restriction being smuggled in — after many small steps you would arrive at a Gaussian whatever the increments looked like. Choosing Gaussians only buys closed forms at every \(t\) rather than asymptotically.
Run \(d\) independent walks and a second fact appears: \(\mathbb{E}\lVert S_n\rVert^2 = nd\), and the relative spread of \(\lVert S_n \rVert\) shrinks like \(1/\sqrt{2d}\). In high dimension essentially every sample sits in a thin shell at radius \(\sqrt{nd}\), even though the origin is the single most likely point. That is the Gaussian annulus of note 06, and it is why \(x_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I_d)\) is a sphere rather than a blob — the reverse process starts on a shell.
crumbs: The Random Walk: Forward, and Backward

title: The Random Walk: Forward, and Backward
section: 6. Backward: the reverse step is exactly solvable
text:
6. Backward: the reverse step is exactly solvable
Now the diffusion question, asked of a coin: you are told where the walk ended; what was the last step?
By Bayes. To have \(S_n = k\) with \(X_n = +1\) the walk must have been at \(k-1\) after \(n-1\) steps. With \(j = (n+k)/2\),
\[\mathbb{P}(X_n = +1 \mid S_n = k)
= \frac{\mathbb{P}(S_{n-1}=k-1)\cdot\tfrac12}{\mathbb{P}(S_n = k)}
= \frac{\binom{n-1}{j-1}}{\binom{n}{j}} = \frac{j}{n} = \frac{n+k}{2n},\]
the powers of two cancelling and the last step being \(\binom{n}{j} = \tfrac{n}{j}\binom{n-1}{j-1}\).
By symmetry, in one line. Given \(S_n = k\), every path with \(j\) up-steps has the same probability — a path’s probability depends on how many up-steps it has, not where they fall. So the increments are conditionally exchangeable, \(\mathbb{E}[X_i \mid S_n = k]\) is the same number \(c\) for every \(i\), and they must sum to \(k\). Hence \(nc = k\) and
\[\boxed{\;\mathbb{E}\big[X_i \mid S_n = k\big] = \frac{k}{n} \quad\text{for every } i.\;}\]
The expected step is the average step. Same theorem; one derivation takes a blackboard and the other takes a sentence.






NoteThis is a denoiser



A hidden quantity, a noisy observation, a posterior, and its mean — and note 07’s best-predictor theorem says the conditional mean is exactly what squared-error training converges to. So \(k/n\) is what a network trained to predict the increment from the endpoint would learn. Here we have it in closed form, so we can check the answer a network would otherwise have to discover.
A question worth sitting with: does the answer change if the coin is biased? It does not. Conditioning on the endpoint fixes the number of up-steps, all arrangements stay equally likely whatever \(p\) is, and exchangeability is untouched. The forward process depends on the bias; the reverse step given the endpoint does not.


Reverse sampling. The reverse step is all you need to run the process backwards. From \(S_n = k\): set \(j = (n+k)/2\), declare the last step \(+1\) with probability \(j/n\) (else \(-1\)), update \(k\) and \(n\), repeat. This produces a trajectory distributed exactly as a forward walk conditioned to end at \(k\) — a complete diffusion model, in nine lines of code, with nothing trained. Act III of the lab runs it.
crumbs: The Random Walk: Forward, and Backward

title: The Random Walk: Forward, and Backward
section: 7. What the observation actually did
text:
7. What the observation actually did
This is the part the lab is built to make visible, and it is worth stating carefully because it is the idea the whole course rests on.
Before you observe anything, all \(2^n\) paths are equally likely. Ranking paths by probability gives one enormous tie. The distribution of \(S_n\) is peaked in the middle not because those paths are likelier, but because more paths land there.
Observing \(S_n = k\) then reweights nothing. It rules paths out. The \(\binom{n}{j}\) survivors remain exactly as likely as one another — a perfect tie, just a smaller one. And the size of what survives measures how much you learned:

The extreme case is the clearest. \(S_n = n\) can be reached by exactly one path, all \(+1\)s, so the observation determines the entire history and the reverse process is deterministic. At the other end, the most likely endpoint is also the least informative: more paths survive there than anywhere else.

title: The Random Walk: Forward, and Backward
section: 8. Where learning has to enter
text:
8. Where learning has to enter
Everything above was exact. It is worth being precise about which step stops being exact when the data stops being a coin, because that step is the rest of the course.
The reverse process needs \(\mathbb{P}(x_0 \mid x_t)\). Here we could write it down because the possibilities could be enumerated. Replace the coin with images and three things break at once: there is no formula for \(p(x_0)\) — note 06 is a catalogue of failed attempts to get one; the sum over possible \(x_0\) becomes an intractable integral over \(\mathbb{R}^d\); and by §5 the relevant region is a thin shell in a huge space, so no amount of sampling covers it.
So the posterior mean is not computable. But note 07 §1 says it is exactly what squared-error regression converges to — and a regression target is available, because the forward process is known and we can noise a real image ourselves.






TipThe whole idea, assembled



A forward process that is free to run and has a closed-form marginal (§3); a reverse process that is a posterior over what was added (§6); and a training objective that reaches that posterior without ever writing it down (note 07).
Modules 3 to 6 replace the coin with a Gaussian and the enumeration with a network. Nothing else changes.

title: The Random Walk: Forward, and Backward
section: Exercises
text:
Exercises
The full set, with the small cases enumerated and the induction written out, is in Practice 2. A representative few:

Compute \(\mathbb{P}(S_6 = k)\) for every \(k\) and check the values sum to 1. Which \(k\) are unreachable, and why?
Prove the recursion \(N_{n+1}(k) = N_n(k-1) + N_n(k+1)\) by deleting the last step, and show it is Pascal’s rule in disguise.
A walker starts at 0. Estimate how many steps until it is typically 100 away, then 1000 away, and comment on the ratio.
Show \(\mathbb{E}[X_i \mid S_n = k] = k/n\) for every \(i\), not just \(i = n\). Why does this not contradict the increments being unconditionally independent?
Let \(\mathbb{P}(X_i = +1) = p\). Show \(\mathbb{E}[S_n] = n(2p-1)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(S_n) = 4np(1-p)\), and then that \(\mathbb{P}(X_n = +1 \mid S_n = k)\) is still \((n+k)/2n\), independent of \(p\).
Which choice of \(\alpha_t\) turns the DDPM update of §1 into this walk? What does that say about variance-preserving versus variance-exploding processes?
